docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
PostgreSQL is the most advanced open-source relational database available. In this module, you'll learn how to design and work with PostgreSQL for production backend systems.

What you'll master: - PostgreSQL architecture and how it guarantees data reliability - Creating robust schema with proper types, constraints, and relationships - Designing efficient indexes for query performance - Writing production-ready SQL queries with proper error handling - Understanding transaction semantics and isolation levels - Best practices for backend data models

By the end of this module, you'll be able to design complete production database schemas and understand why each decision matters for reliability and performance.

docs.title: What PostgreSQL Actually Does
docs.text:
PostgreSQL is a process-based relational database that:

  1. Manages concurrent connections via separate processes - Each client connection gets its own backend process. This provides true isolation but uses more memory than threaded approaches.

  2. Uses WAL (Write-Ahead Logging) for crash recovery - Before any data is modified on disk, the change is written to a log. If the server crashes, it replays this log to recover. This is why your data survives crashes.

  3. Implements MVCC (Multi-Version Concurrency Control) for transactions - Multiple transactions see different versions of the same data simultaneously. Readers never block writers, and writers don't block readers. This is why concurrent access is fast.

  4. Stores data in 8KB pages on disk - Data is organized in fixed-size pages. This affects how indexes work and query planning.

What matters for your application: - PostgreSQL handles concurrency extremely well (thousands of simultaneous users) - It's fully ACID-compliant (your data is safe) - It scales vertically (better hardware = better performance) - It's not designed for massive horizontal scaling (but works fine for most applications)

docs.title: Installation (Linux)
docs.text:
The installation process varies slightly by distribution. Here's the most common approach:

# Ubuntu/Debian/Linux Mint
sudo apt update
sudo apt install -y postgresql postgresql-contrib postgresql-client

# Verify installation
sudo -u postgres psql --version

# Start PostgreSQL service
sudo systemctl start postgresql

# Enable auto-start on boot
sudo systemctl enable postgresql

# Verify it's running
sudo systemctl status postgresql

On a development machine, PostgreSQL starts automatically after installation.

On a server, you might need to configure: 

# Allow remote connections (CAUTION: requires authentication)
sudo nano /etc/postgresql/15/main/postgresql.conf
# Find and change: listen_addresses = 'localhost' to listen_addresses = '*'

# Allow remote authentication
sudo nano /etc/postgresql/15/main/pg_hba.conf
# Add: host    all             all             0.0.0.0/0            md5

docs.title: Creating a Database
docs.text:
The postgres user is the superuser created during installation. You'll use it to create your application user and database.

-- Connect as superuser
sudo -u postgres psql

-- Create database for application
CREATE DATABASE backend_db ENCODING 'UTF8';

-- Create user with password (for application to use)
CREATE USER backend_user WITH PASSWORD 'strong_password_here';

-- Grant privileges on database
GRANT CONNECT ON DATABASE backend_db TO backend_user;
GRANT USAGE ON SCHEMA public TO backend_user;
GRANT CREATE ON SCHEMA public TO backend_user;

-- Grant all privileges on all tables (current and future)
ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES IN SCHEMA public GRANT ALL ON TABLES TO backend_user;

-- If you created tables as postgres, transfer ownership
-- ALTER TABLE table_name OWNER TO backend_user;

-- Verify user was created
\du

-- Connect to new database as new user
\c backend_db backend_user

-- Exit
\q

Connection string for application: 

# Flask/SQLAlchemy
DATABASE_URL = "postgresql://backend_user:password@localhost/backend_db"

# Or with environment variable (recommended)
import os
DATABASE_URL = os.getenv('DATABASE_URL', 'postgresql://backend_user:password@localhost/backend_db')

docs.title: Creating Tables
docs.text:
A table is the fundamental structure in PostgreSQL. Each table represents an entity (users, posts, orders), and each row is an instance of that entity.

-- Users table - core entity
CREATE TABLE users (
id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,                              -- Auto-incrementing ID
email VARCHAR(255) UNIQUE NOT NULL,                 -- Email must be unique
password_hash VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL,                -- Password hash (never store plaintext)
full_name VARCHAR(255),                             -- Optional full name
is_active BOOLEAN DEFAULT TRUE,                     -- Active status, defaults to TRUE
created_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT NOW(),                 -- Timestamp when created
updated_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT NOW(),                 -- Timestamp of last update

-- Optional: explicitly name primary key
-- CONSTRAINT pk_users PRIMARY KEY (id)
);

-- Posts table - depends on users
CREATE TABLE posts (
id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
user_id INTEGER NOT NULL,                           -- Foreign key to users
title VARCHAR(500) NOT NULL,
content TEXT,                                       -- Unlimited length
published BOOLEAN DEFAULT FALSE,
view_count INTEGER DEFAULT 0,
created_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT NOW(),

-- Relationship: each post belongs to one user
CONSTRAINT fk_posts_user_id FOREIGN KEY (user_id)
REFERENCES users(id) ON DELETE CASCADE
-- ON DELETE CASCADE: Delete posts when user is deleted
);

-- Comments table - multiple relationships
CREATE TABLE comments (
id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
post_id INTEGER NOT NULL,
user_id INTEGER NOT NULL,
content TEXT NOT NULL,
created_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT NOW(),

-- Relationships
CONSTRAINT fk_comments_post_id FOREIGN KEY (post_id)
REFERENCES posts(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,

CONSTRAINT fk_comments_user_id FOREIGN KEY (user_id)
REFERENCES users(id) ON DELETE SET NULL
-- ON DELETE SET NULL: Keep comment but remove user reference
);

Common table creation mistakes to avoid:

-- BAD: Missing NOT NULL constraints
CREATE TABLE users (
email VARCHAR(255),  -- Can be NULL (useless)
password_hash VARCHAR(255)  -- Can be NULL (security issue!)
);

-- GOOD: Enforce required fields
CREATE TABLE users (
email VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL,  -- Must be provided
password_hash VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL
);

-- BAD: No defaults for timestamps
CREATE TABLE posts (
created_at TIMESTAMP,  -- Have to set manually (error-prone)
);

-- GOOD: Automatic timestamps
CREATE TABLE posts (
created_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT NOW(),  -- Automatically set
updated_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT NOW()
);

-- BAD: VARCHAR with no size limit
CREATE TABLE users (
name VARCHAR  -- PostgreSQL allows unlimited, but wasteful
);

-- GOOD: Reasonable limit
CREATE TABLE users (
name VARCHAR(255)  -- Enough for real names
);

docs.title: Data Types (What Actually Matters)
docs.text: PostgreSQL has many data types. Focus on these 10 that cover 95% of real applications:

docs.title: Data Types (What Actually Matters)
docs.text:
PostgreSQL has many data types. Focus on these 10 that cover 95% of real applications:

Text Types: - VARCHAR(n) - Variable length string, max n characters - Use for: emails, usernames, names, phone numbers, URLs - Example: VARCHAR(255) for email (RFC 5321 limit is 254) - Don't use: VARCHAR without size (allows unlimited, causes bloat)

CREATE TABLE users (
email VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL,  -- Good: reasonable limit
username VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL  -- Good: short usernames
);
  • TEXT - Unlimited length string
  • Use for: descriptions, content, bio, comments
  • Example: Blog post content, user bio, product description
  • Benefits: No need to guess max length
  • Costs: Slightly slower than VARCHAR for very short strings (usually negligible)
CREATE TABLE posts (
title VARCHAR(500) NOT NULL,  -- Short, bounded
content TEXT NOT NULL          -- Long, unbounded
);

Numeric Types: - INTEGER - 32-bit signed integer: -2,147,483,648 to 2,147,483,647 - Use for: counts, ages, quantities, status codes - Sufficient for: Most applications (2B users? probably don't need it yet) - Size: 4 bytes

CREATE TABLE products (
stock INTEGER DEFAULT 0,       -- Number in stock
reorder_point INTEGER,          -- Reorder threshold
views INTEGER DEFAULT 0
);
  • BIGINT - 64-bit signed integer: -9.2 quintillion to 9.2 quintillion
  • Use for: When you'll definitely exceed 2B values
  • Example: Total hits counter for viral sites, high-frequency trading
  • Size: 8 bytes (twice as much disk/memory)
  • When to use: 1M+ events per day × 10 years = probably need BIGINT
CREATE TABLE events (
id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,      -- Use BIGSERIAL for auto-increment
event_count BIGINT DEFAULT 0
);
  • SERIAL / BIGSERIAL - Auto-incrementing integer (use for primary keys)
  • Use for: Primary key IDs
  • SERIAL: Starts at 1, increments by 1, max 2B values
  • BIGSERIAL: Same but up to 9.2 quintillion
  • Creates a sequence automatically (don't worry about details)
CREATE TABLE users (
id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,          -- Auto-increment from 1
email VARCHAR(255) UNIQUE
);

-- Or explicit with BIGSERIAL
CREATE TABLE events (
id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY        -- For very high volume
);
  • DECIMAL(p, s) - Exact decimal number
  • Use for: Money, prices, precise calculations
  • NEVER use FLOAT for money (rounding errors!)
  • p = total digits, s = digits after decimal
  • Size: Depends on precision (up to 38 digits)
CREATE TABLE orders (
total DECIMAL(10, 2) NOT NULL,     -- Max 10 digits: $99,999,999.99
tax DECIMAL(10, 2),                -- Always 2 decimals for cents
discount_percent DECIMAL(5, 2)    -- Up to 999.99%
);

-- BAD: Don't use float for money!
price FLOAT  -- Results in 19.99 becoming 19.989999... or 20.000001...

-- GOOD: Always DECIMAL
price DECIMAL(10, 2)  -- Exactly 19.99

Boolean Type: - BOOLEAN - TRUE or FALSE (not NULL-safe) - Use for: Flags, boolean states, yes/no values - In SQL: TRUE, FALSE, 't', 'f', 1, 0 - In Python: True, False, None - Size: 1 byte

CREATE TABLE users (
is_active BOOLEAN DEFAULT TRUE,      -- Active by default
is_verified BOOLEAN DEFAULT FALSE,   -- Not verified by default
is_admin BOOLEAN NOT NULL            -- Required field
);

-- Usage
UPDATE users SET is_active = FALSE WHERE id = 123;
SELECT * FROM users WHERE is_verified = TRUE;

Date/Time Types: - TIMESTAMP - Date and time with timezone awareness - Use for: Timestamps when things happened (created_at, updated_at, logged_in_at) - Includes: Year, month, day, hour, minute, second, millisecond - Size: 8 bytes - Best practice: Always use DEFAULT NOW() to auto-set

CREATE TABLE users (
created_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT NOW(),           -- When record created
updated_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT NOW(),           -- When last updated
last_login TIMESTAMP                          -- Can be NULL (never logged in)
);

-- Query time ranges
SELECT * FROM users WHERE created_at > NOW() - INTERVAL '30 days';
SELECT * FROM users WHERE last_login < NOW() - INTERVAL '6 months';
  • DATE - Date only, no time component
  • Use for: Birthdays, deadlines, dates when time doesn't matter
  • Example: User birthdate (9:45am birthday is same as 11:20pm)
  • Size: 4 bytes (saves space if time not needed)
CREATE TABLE users (
birthdate DATE,                 -- Just the date
account_expiry_date DATE
);

JSON Type: - JSONB - Binary JSON (optimized for queries) - Use for: Flexible data, metadata, nested structures - Better than TEXT JSON (JSONB is indexed and queryable) - Supports: Objects, arrays, primitives

CREATE TABLE users (
metadata JSONB DEFAULT '{}'::jsonb    -- Flexible schema
);

-- Insert
INSERT INTO users (email, metadata) VALUES (
'user@example.com',
'{"preferences": {"theme": "dark", "language": "en"}, "tags": ["vip", "beta"]}'::jsonb
);

-- Query JSONB
SELECT * FROM users WHERE metadata -> 'preferences' ->> 'theme' = 'dark';
SELECT * FROM users WHERE metadata @> '{"tags": ["vip"]}'::jsonb;

Type Selection Summary:

Need Type Example Small integer INTEGER age, stock count Huge count BIGINT total events, impressions Auto ID SERIAL/BIGSERIAL Primary key Money DECIMAL(10,2) Price, salary Flag/Status BOOLEAN is_active, published Timestamp TIMESTAMP created_at, updated_at Date only DATE birthdate, deadline Short text VARCHAR(n) email, name, username Long text TEXT description, content, bio Flexible JSONB metadata, preferences
  • DATE - Date only (use for birthdays, deadlines)

JSON: - JSONB - Binary JSON (use for flexible data, metadata)

docs.title: Backend Example: User Model
docs.text:
CREATE TABLE users (
id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
email VARCHAR(255) UNIQUE NOT NULL,
password_hash VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL,
full_name VARCHAR(255),
is_active BOOLEAN DEFAULT TRUE,
is_verified BOOLEAN DEFAULT FALSE,
metadata JSONB,  -- Flexible data
created_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT NOW(),
updated_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT NOW()
);

-- Insert user
INSERT INTO users (email, password_hash, full_name, metadata)
VALUES (
'user@example.com',
'$2b$12$...',  -- bcrypt hash
'John Doe',
'{"preferences": {"theme": "dark"}}'::jsonb
);

-- Query user
SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = 'user@example.com';

docs.title: Primary Keys
docs.text:
Purpose: Uniquely identify each row

-- Auto-incrementing ID (most common)
CREATE TABLE products (
id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
name VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL
);

-- UUID (for distributed systems)
CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS "uuid-ossp";

CREATE TABLE sessions (
id UUID PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT uuid_generate_v4(),
user_id INTEGER NOT NULL,
token VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL,
expires_at TIMESTAMP NOT NULL
);

-- Composite primary key (rare)
CREATE TABLE user_roles (
user_id INTEGER,
role_id INTEGER,
PRIMARY KEY (user_id, role_id)
);

When to use UUID vs SERIAL: - SERIAL: Single database, simpler, faster - UUID: Distributed systems, merge databases, public-facing IDs

docs.title: Foreign Keys
docs.text:
Purpose: Enforce relationships between tables

CREATE TABLE orders (
id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
user_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES users(id),
total DECIMAL(10, 2) NOT NULL,
created_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT NOW()
);

-- What this does:
-- 1. Prevents inserting order with non-existent user_id
-- 2. Prevents deleting user who has orders (by default)

docs.title: Foreign Key Actions
docs.text:
CREATE TABLE comments (
id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
post_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES posts(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
user_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES users(id) ON DELETE SET NULL,
content TEXT NOT NULL
);

-- ON DELETE CASCADE: Delete comments when post is deleted
-- ON DELETE SET NULL: Set user_id to NULL when user is deleted
-- ON DELETE RESTRICT: Prevent deletion if comments exist (default)

Production pattern: 

-- Good: Explicit foreign key with name
ALTER TABLE orders
ADD CONSTRAINT fk_orders_user
FOREIGN KEY (user_id) REFERENCES users(id) ON DELETE RESTRICT;

-- Bad: No foreign key (data integrity issues)
CREATE TABLE orders (
user_id INTEGER  -- Nothing prevents invalid user_id
);

docs.title: Why Indexes Exist
docs.text:
Without index: 

SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = 'user@example.com';
-- Scans ALL rows (slow for large tables)

With index: 

CREATE INDEX idx_users_email ON users(email);
SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = 'user@example.com';
-- Uses B-tree index (fast, O(log n))

docs.title: When to Create Indexes
docs.text:
Always index: - Primary keys (automatic) - Foreign keys - Columns in WHERE clauses - Columns in JOIN conditions - Columns in ORDER BY

Example: 

-- Users table
CREATE INDEX idx_users_email ON users(email);  -- WHERE email = ?
CREATE INDEX idx_users_created_at ON users(created_at);  -- ORDER BY created_at

-- Orders table
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_user_id ON orders(user_id);  -- Foreign key
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_created_at ON orders(created_at);  -- Date range queries

docs.title: Index Types
docs.text:
B-tree (default): Use for most cases 

CREATE INDEX idx_users_email ON users(email);

Unique index: Enforce uniqueness 

CREATE UNIQUE INDEX idx_users_email_unique ON users(email);
-- Same as: ALTER TABLE users ADD CONSTRAINT users_email_unique UNIQUE (email);

Partial index: Index subset of rows 

-- Only index active users
CREATE INDEX idx_active_users_email ON users(email) WHERE is_active = TRUE;

Composite index: Multiple columns 

-- For queries like: WHERE user_id = ? AND created_at > ?
CREATE INDEX idx_posts_user_created ON posts(user_id, created_at);

GIN index: For JSONB and arrays 

CREATE INDEX idx_users_metadata ON users USING GIN (metadata);

-- Query JSONB
SELECT * FROM users WHERE metadata @> '{"preferences": {"theme": "dark"}}';

docs.title: Index Gotchas
docs.text:
Problem 1: Too many indexes slow down writes 

-- Bad: Index everything
CREATE INDEX idx1 ON users(email);
CREATE INDEX idx2 ON users(full_name);
CREATE INDEX idx3 ON users(created_at);
CREATE INDEX idx4 ON users(updated_at);
CREATE INDEX idx5 ON users(is_active);
-- Every INSERT/UPDATE must update 5 indexes

Problem 2: Wrong column order in composite index 

-- Bad: created_at first
CREATE INDEX idx_posts_created_user ON posts(created_at, user_id);
-- Doesn't help: WHERE user_id = ?

-- Good: user_id first
CREATE INDEX idx_posts_user_created ON posts(user_id, created_at);
-- Helps both: WHERE user_id = ? AND WHERE user_id = ? AND created_at > ?

Rule: Most selective column first (column that narrows down results most)

docs.title: NOT NULL
docs.text:
CREATE TABLE products (
id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
name VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL,  -- Must have a name
description TEXT  -- Optional
);

-- Prevents:
INSERT INTO products (description) VALUES ('...');  -- Error: name is NULL

docs.title: UNIQUE
docs.text:
CREATE TABLE users (
id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
email VARCHAR(255) UNIQUE NOT NULL,  -- No duplicate emails
username VARCHAR(50) UNIQUE NOT NULL  -- No duplicate usernames
);

-- Prevents:
INSERT INTO users (email, username) VALUES ('user@example.com', 'john');
INSERT INTO users (email, username) VALUES ('user@example.com', 'jane');  -- Error

docs.title: CHECK
docs.text:
CREATE TABLE products (
id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
name VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL,
price DECIMAL(10, 2) CHECK (price >= 0),  -- Price can't be negative
stock INTEGER CHECK (stock >= 0)
);

-- Prevents:
INSERT INTO products (name, price, stock) VALUES ('Widget', -10.00, 5);  -- Error

docs.title: DEFAULT
docs.text:
CREATE TABLE orders (
id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
status VARCHAR(50) DEFAULT 'pending',  -- Default status
created_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT NOW()  -- Auto-set timestamp
);

-- No need to specify status or created_at
INSERT INTO orders DEFAULT VALUES;

docs.text:
CREATE TABLE users (
id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
email VARCHAR(255) UNIQUE NOT NULL,
password_hash VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL,
full_name VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL,

);

id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
user_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES users(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
title VARCHAR(500) NOT NULL,

published BOOLEAN DEFAULT FALSE,

);

docs.text:
-- CREATE
INSERT INTO users (email, password_hash, full_name)
VALUES ('user@example.com', '$2b$12$...', 'John Doe')
RETURNING id, email, created_at;  -- Return inserted data

-- READ
SELECT id, email, full_name, created_at
FROM users
WHERE email = 'user@example.com';

SET full_name = 'Jane Doe', updated_at = NOW()
WHERE id = 1
RETURNING *;

docs.title: Joins
docs.text:
-- Get user with their posts
SELECT u.email, p.title, p.created_at
FROM users u
INNER JOIN posts p ON u.id = p.user_id
WHERE u.id = 1
ORDER BY p.created_at DESC;

-- Get users who have never posted
SELECT u.id, u.email
FROM users u
LEFT JOIN posts p ON u.id = p.user_id
WHERE p.id IS NULL;

docs.title: Aggregations
docs.text:
-- Count posts per user
SELECT u.email, COUNT(p.id) as post_count
FROM users u
LEFT JOIN posts p ON u.id = p.user_id
GROUP BY u.id, u.email
HAVING COUNT(p.id) > 5
ORDER BY post_count DESC;

-- Total revenue per day
SELECT DATE(created_at) as date, SUM(total) as revenue
FROM orders
WHERE created_at >= NOW() - INTERVAL '30 days'
GROUP BY DATE(created_at)
ORDER BY date;

docs.text:
1. What is the purpose of a foreign key constraint? a) To make queries faster b) To enforce referential integrity between tables c) To create indexes automatically d) To prevent NULL values

  2. Which index type should you use for JSONB columns? a) B-tree b) Hash c) GIN d) GIST

  3. What does ON DELETE CASCADE do? a) Deletes all rows in the table b) Prevents deletion of referenced rows c) Automatically deletes dependent rows d) Creates a backup before deletion

  4. When should you use SERIAL vs UUID for primary keys? a) Always use UUID for better performance b) Use SERIAL for single database, UUID for distributed systems c) Use UUID for better security d) They are interchangeable

docs.title: Incident Scenario
docs.text:
Scenario: Your Flask API is timing out on a query that fetches user orders:

@app.route('/users/<int:user_id>/orders')
def get_user_orders(user_id):
    orders = db.session.query(Order).filter_by(user_id=user_id).all()
    return jsonify([o.to_dict() for o in orders])

The orders table has 10 million rows. The query takes 30 seconds.

Questions: 1. What is the likely cause? 2. How would you diagnose it using PostgreSQL tools? 3. What is the fix? 4. How would you prevent this in the future?

docs.title: The NoSQL Philosophy
docs.text:
NoSQL databases solve different problems than relational databases:

Aspect SQL (PostgreSQL) NoSQL (MongoDB, Redis) Schema Fixed, enforced Flexible, dynamic Consistency ACID transactions Eventually consistent (usually) Scaling Vertical (bigger server) Horizontal (more servers) Joins Built-in, powerful No joins (data embedding/duplication) Data Model Tables & rows Documents, key-value, graphs Query Language SQL Database-specific (MongoDB: aggregation) Best For Transactional data, complex relationships High-volume writes, flexible schemas, caching

docs.title: Key Principle
docs.text:
Don't replace PostgreSQL with NoSQL. Complement it.

A robust production system uses PostgreSQL for core transactional data and NoSQL for specific problems it solves better.

docs.title: What You'll Learn
docs.text:
• MongoDB: Document storage for flexible schemas, logging, catalogs
  • Redis: In-memory caching, sessions, real-time data
  • Architecture patterns: Combining SQL + NoSQL effectively
  • Production-ready code: Monitoring, error handling, scaling
  • Common mistakes: Anti-patterns to avoid

docs.title: What is MongoDB?
docs.text: MongoDB stores data as JSON-like documents (BSON internally) rather than tables and rows. Each document can have a different structure, making it ideal for evolving schemas.

docs.title: Visual Comparison: SQL vs Document Model
docs.text:
PostgreSQL (Structured):
┌─ users table ───────────────────────┐
│ id │ email              │ age │ name  │
├────┼────────────────────┼─────┼───────┤
│ 1  │ john@example.com   │ 30  │ John  │
│ 2  │ jane@example.com   │ 28  │ Jane  │
└─────────────────────────────────────┘

MongoDB (Flexible):
{
  "_id": ObjectId("..."),
  "email": "john@example.com",
  "age": 30,
  "name": "John",
  "skills": ["Python", "Kubernetes"],    ← Different structure
  "verified": true
}

{
  "_id": ObjectId("..."),
  "email": "jane@example.com",
  "age": 28,
  "name": "Jane",
  "certifications": [{name: "CKA", year: 2023}],  ← Can differ
  "verified": false,
  "phone": "+1234567890"  ← Additional field, not in other docs
}

docs.title: Core Characteristics
docs.text: Feature Advantage Trade-off Flexible Schema Add fields without migration Risk of inconsistent data Nested Documents No joins needed, single query Data duplication, update complexity Horizontal Scaling Handle massive data volumes Sharding complexity Eventually Consistent Faster writes by default Stale reads possible Rich Documents Store arrays, objects, dates Larger documents = more memory

docs.title: Basic Example
docs.text:
{
"_id": ObjectId("507f1f77bcf86cd799439011"),  // Auto-generated ID
"email": "user@example.com",

// Nested object (can be queried)
"profile": {
"firstName": "John",
"lastName": "Doe",
"age": 30,
"location": "New York"
},

// Array of values
"skills": ["Python", "Kubernetes", "DevOps"],

// Array of objects
"experience": [
{
"company": "TechCorp",
"role": "DevOps Engineer",
"years": 5
},
{
"company": "CloudInc",
"role": "SRE",
"years": 2
}
],

// Standard types
"isActive": true,
"joinedAt": ISODate("2023-01-15T10:30:00Z"),
"salary": 120000
}

docs.title: Design Guidelines
docs.text: Document Size: MongoDB has a 16MB limit per document Nesting: Usually 2-3 levels deep maximum Arrays: Unbounded arrays should reference instead (see patterns below)

wget -qO - https://www.mongodb.org/static/pgp/server-7.0.asc | sudo apt-key add -

# 2. Add MongoDB repository
echo "deb [ arch=amd64,arm64 ] https://repo.mongodb.org/apt/ubuntu focal/mongodb-org/7.0 multiverse" | \

docs.title: Python Setup
docs.text:
# backend/app/db/mongo.py
from pymongo import MongoClient
from pymongo.errors import DuplicateKeyError, ConnectionFailure
import os

class MongoDatabase:
    def __init__(self):
"""Initialize MongoDB connection."""
        uri = os.getenv('MONGO_URI', 'mongodb://localhost:27017/')
        try:
            self.client = MongoClient(uri, serverSelectionTimeoutMS=5000)
            # Verify connection
            self.client.admin.command('ping')
            self.db = self.client[os.getenv('MONGO_DB', 'devops_db')]
        except ConnectionFailure as e:
            raise RuntimeError(f"Failed to connect to MongoDB: {e}")

    def get_collection(self, collection_name):
"""Get a collection object."""
        return self.db[collection_name]

    def close(self):
"""Close the connection."""
        self.client.close()

# Singleton instance
mongo_db = MongoDatabase()

docs.title: Create (Insert)
docs.text:
from app.db.mongo import mongo_db
from datetime import datetime

collection = mongo_db.get_collection('users')

# Insert single document
user_doc = {
    "email": "john@example.com",
    "name": "John Doe",
    "role": "engineer",
    "created_at": datetime.utcnow()
}
result = collection.insert_one(user_doc)
print(f"Inserted ID: {result.inserted_id}")

# Insert multiple documents
users = [
    {"email": "jane@example.com", "name": "Jane Doe"},
    {"email": "bob@example.com", "name": "Bob Smith"}
]
result = collection.insert_many(users)
print(f"Inserted {len(result.inserted_ids)} documents")

docs.title: Read (Query)
docs.text:
# Find single document
user = collection.find_one({"email": "john@example.com"})

# Find by ID
from bson import ObjectId
user = collection.find_one({"_id": ObjectId("507f1f77bcf86cd799439011")})

# Find multiple documents
all_users = collection.find()
for user in all_users:
    print(user['email'])

# Query with filters
engineers = collection.find({"role": "engineer"})
active_users = collection.find({"isActive": True})

# Query nested fields
users_in_nyc = collection.find({"profile.location": "New York"})

# Query arrays
python_devs = collection.find({"skills": "Python"})

docs.title: Update
docs.text:
# Update single document
collection.update_one(
    {"email": "john@example.com"},
    {"$set": {"role": "senior engineer", "updated_at": datetime.utcnow()}}
)

# Update multiple documents
result = collection.update_many(
    {"role": "engineer"},
    {"$set": {"department": "Platform"}}
)
print(f"Modified {result.modified_count} documents")

# Array operations
collection.update_one(
    {"email": "john@example.com"},
    {"$push": {"skills": "Docker"}}  # Add to array
)

collection.update_one(
    {"email": "john@example.com"},
    {"$pull": {"skills": "Python"}}  # Remove from array
)

docs.title: Delete
docs.text:
# Delete single document
result = collection.delete_one({"email": "john@example.com"})

# Delete multiple documents
result = collection.delete_many({"role": "intern"})
print(f"Deleted {result.deleted_count} documents")

# Delete all documents (use carefully!)
collection.delete_many({})

docs.title: Indexing for Performance
docs.text:
Indexes are crucial for MongoDB query performance:

collection = mongo_db.get_collection('users')

# Single field index
collection.create_index("email", unique=True)
collection.create_index("created_at")

# Compound index (multiple fields)
collection.create_index([("role", 1), ("created_at", -1)])
# 1 = ascending, -1 = descending

# Text search index (full-text search)
collection.create_index([("bio", "text"), ("skills", "text")])

# TTL index (auto-delete documents after time)
collection.create_index("created_at", expireAfterSeconds=2592000)  # 30 days

# List all indexes
collection.list_indexes()

# Drop an index
collection.drop_index("email_1")

docs.title: Pattern 1: Embedding (Denormalization)
docs.text:
Use when related data is always accessed together:

# Good: Address embedded in User
user = {
    "_id": ObjectId("..."),
    "email": "user@example.com",
    "addresses": [
        {
            "type": "shipping",
            "street": "123 Main St",
            "city": "NYC",
            "zip": "10001"
        },
        {
            "type": "billing",
            "street": "456 Secondary Ave",
            "city": "LA",
            "zip": "90001"
        }
    ]
}

# Query embedded field
users_in_nyc = collection.find({"addresses.city": "NYC"})

When to use embedding: - Data accessed together - 1-to-few relationships - Limited array size - Data doesn't change frequency

docs.title: Pattern 2: Referencing (Normalization)
docs.text:
Use when data is accessed independently:

# User document
{
    "_id": ObjectId("user123"),
    "email": "user@example.com",
    "name": "John Doe"
}

# Order document (references user)
{
    "_id": ObjectId("order456"),
    "user_id": ObjectId("user123"),  # Reference, not embedding
    "total": 99.99,
    "items": [
        {"product_id": "prod1", "quantity": 2}
    ]
}

# Query: Find user's orders
orders = orders_collection.find({"user_id": ObjectId("user123")})

# Note: MongoDB doesn't do automatic joins, you must manually fetch
user = users_collection.find_one({"_id": ObjectId("user123")})
orders = orders_collection.find({"user_id": user['_id']})

When to use referencing: - Large or unbounded arrays - Data accessed separately - Many-to-many relationships - Frequent updates

docs.title: Example 1: Application Logging
docs.text:
# backend/app/repositories/log_repository.py
from app.db.mongo import mongo_db
from datetime import datetime, timedelta
from enum import Enum

class LogLevel(Enum):
    INFO = "INFO"
    WARNING = "WARNING"
    ERROR = "ERROR"
    DEBUG = "DEBUG"

class LogRepository:
    def __init__(self):
        self.collection = mongo_db.get_collection('logs')
        # Create indexes for common queries
        self.collection.create_index('timestamp')
        self.collection.create_index('level')
        self.collection.create_index('service')
        # Auto-delete logs after 30 days
        self.collection.create_index('timestamp', expireAfterSeconds=2592000)

    def insert_log(self, level: LogLevel, message: str, service: str, 
                   metadata: dict = None):
"""Insert a log entry."""
        doc = {
            'level': level.value,
            'message': message,
            'service': service,
            'metadata': metadata or {},
            'timestamp': datetime.utcnow()
        }
        result = self.collection.insert_one(doc)
        return str(result.inserted_id)

    def get_logs(self, level: LogLevel = None, service: str = None, 
                 hours: int = 24, limit: int = 100):
"""Retrieve logs with optional filtering."""
        query = {}

        if level:
            query['level'] = level.value
        if service:
            query['service'] = service

        # Filter by time range
        cutoff = datetime.utcnow() - timedelta(hours=hours)
        query['timestamp'] = {'$gte': cutoff}

        return list(self.collection\
            .find(query)\
            .sort('timestamp', -1)\
            .limit(limit))

    def get_error_summary(self, hours: int = 24):
"""Get count of errors by service."""
        cutoff = datetime.utcnow() - timedelta(hours=hours)

        # Aggregation pipeline
        pipeline = [
            {
                '$match': {
                    'level': 'ERROR',
                    'timestamp': {'$gte': cutoff}
                }
            },
            {
                '$group': {
                    '_id': '$service',
                    'count': {'$sum': 1}
                }
            },
            {
                '$sort': {'count': -1}
            }
        ]

        return list(self.collection.aggregate(pipeline))

docs.title: Example 2: Product Catalog
docs.text:
# backend/app/repositories/product_repository.py
from app.db.mongo import mongo_db
from datetime import datetime

class ProductRepository:
    def __init__(self):
        self.collection = mongo_db.get_collection('products')
        # Create indexes
        self.collection.create_index('sku', unique=True)
        self.collection.create_index('category')
        self.collection.create_index([('name', 'text'), ('description', 'text')])

    def create_product(self, sku: str, name: str, price: float, 
                      category: str, attributes: dict = None):
"""Create a new product."""
        doc = {
            'sku': sku,
            'name': name,
            'price': price,
            'category': category,
            'attributes': attributes or {},
            'inventory': 0,
            'created_at': datetime.utcnow(),
            'updated_at': datetime.utcnow()
        }
        result = self.collection.insert_one(doc)
        return str(result.inserted_id)

    def get_product_by_sku(self, sku: str):
"""Get product by SKU."""
        return self.collection.find_one({'sku': sku})

    def search_products(self, query: str, category: str = None, limit: int = 20):
"""Full-text search products."""
        search_filter = {'$text': {'$search': query}}

        if category:
            search_filter['category'] = category

        return list(self.collection\
            .find(search_filter)\
            .limit(limit))

    def get_by_category(self, category: str):
"""Get all products in a category."""
        return list(self.collection.find({'category': category}))

    def update_price(self, sku: str, new_price: float):
"""Update product price."""
        self.collection.update_one(
            {'sku': sku},
            {'$set': {'price': new_price, 'updated_at': datetime.utcnow()}}
        )

    def update_inventory(self, sku: str, quantity_change: int):
"""Increment or decrement inventory."""
        self.collection.update_one(
            {'sku': sku},
            {'$inc': {'inventory': quantity_change}}
        )

docs.text:
# WRONG: User authentication in MongoDB
def register_user(email: str, password: str):
    users = mongo_db.get_collection('users')

    # Problems:
    # - No transaction guarantees
    # - No foreign key constraints
    # - Race conditions possible
    # - Cannot rollback on error

    users.insert_one({
        'email': email,
        'password_hash': hash_password(password)
    })

Solution: Use PostgreSQL for user authentication

docs.title: ❌ Anti-Pattern 2: Unbounded Array Growth
docs.text:
# WRONG: Embedding all orders in user document
{
    "_id": ObjectId("user123"),
    "email": "user@example.com",
    "orders": [
        {order1},
        {order2},
        ...
        {order1000000}  # Document grows forever!
    ]
}

# Problems:
# - Violates 16MB document limit
# - Entire document loaded into memory
# - Slow queries

Solution: Reference instead of embedding

# RIGHT: Reference orders separately
# users collection
{
    "_id": ObjectId("user123"),
    "email": "user@example.com"
}

# orders collection
{
    "_id": ObjectId("order1"),
    "user_id": ObjectId("user123"),
    "total": 99.99
}

# Solution: Create indexes

docs.title: What is Redis?
docs.text: Redis is an in-memory key-value store that's extremely fast, built for caching, sessions, and real-time data. It's not a database replacement—it's a complement to your primary database.

docs.title: Redis vs Databases
docs.text: Aspect Redis PostgreSQL Storage RAM (all data) Disk + memory Speed ~0.1ms ~1-5ms Data Types Strings, Lists, Sets, Sorted Sets, Hashes Tables, Complex types Persistence Optional (RDB/AOF) Default Transactions Single-threaded atomicity Full ACID Use Case Caching, sessions, real-time Persistent storage

docs.title: Performance Comparison
docs.text:
Operation         | PostgreSQL | Redis
──────────────────────────────────────────
Simple read       | 1-5ms      | 0.05-0.1ms (10-100x faster)
Sequential reads  | 1-5ms each | 0.05-0.1ms each
Complex query     | 10-100ms   | N/A (no SQL)
Memory usage/GB   | Scalable   | All in RAM (expensive)
Data size         | TB+ easy   | Limited by RAM

docs.title: Data Structures
docs.text: Redis offers more than key-value pairs:

docs.title: 1. Strings (Simple Values)
docs.text:
import redis

r = redis.Redis(host='localhost', port=6379, decode_responses=True)

# Set and get
r.set('user:1:name', 'John')
name = r.get('user:1:name')  # → 'John'

# Increment counter
r.incr('page:views')  # → 1
r.incrby('page:views', 5)  # → 6

# Append to string
r.append('message', ' world')

# With expiration (auto-delete)
r.setex('session:abc123', 3600, 'session_data')  # Expires in 1 hour
r.expire('cache:key', 300)  # Set expiration

# Delete
r.delete('user:1:name')

docs.title: 2. Lists (Ordered Collections)
docs.text:
# LIFO queue (like stack)
r.lpush('stack:tasks', 'task1', 'task2', 'task3')  # Add to left
task = r.lpop('stack:tasks')  # Remove from left → 'task3'

# FIFO queue
r.rpush('queue:emails', 'email1', 'email2')  # Add to right
email = r.lpop('queue:emails')  # Remove from left → 'email1'

# Get range
r.lrange('queue:emails', 0, -1)  # All items
r.llen('queue:emails')  # Length

docs.title: 3. Sets (Unordered Unique Members)
docs.text:
# Add members
r.sadd('tags:python', 'user1', 'user2', 'user3')

# Check membership
r.sismember('tags:python', 'user1')  # → True
r.scard('tags:python')  # Count → 3

# Get all members
r.smembers('tags:python')  # → {'user1', 'user2', 'user3'}

# Set operations
r.sinter('tags:python', 'tags:devops')  # Intersection
r.sunion('tags:python', 'tags:devops')  # Union
r.sdiff('tags:python', 'tags:devops')  # Difference

docs.title: 4. Sorted Sets (Ordered by Score)
docs.text:
# Add members with scores
r.zadd('leaderboard', {
    'user1': 100,
    'user2': 95,
    'user3': 90
})

# Get top N (highest to lowest)
r.zrange('leaderboard', 0, 2, withscores=True, desc=True)
# → [('user1', 100.0), ('user2', 95.0), ('user3', 90.0)]

# Get user's rank
rank = r.zrevrank('leaderboard', 'user1')  # → 0 (first place)

# Get members in score range
r.zrangebyscore('leaderboard', 90, 100)

docs.text:
# Set multiple fields
r.hset('user:1', mapping={
    'email': 'john@example.com',
    'name': 'John Doe',
    'age': '30'
})

# Get single field
r.hget('user:1', 'email')  # → 'john@example.com'

# Get all fields
r.hgetall('user:1')  # → {'email': '...', 'name': '...', 'age': '30'}

# Check if field exists
r.hexists('user:1', 'email')  # → True

# Delete field

# Increment field value

# backend/app/db/redis.py
import redis
from typing import Any, Optional
import os
import json

class RedisClient:
    def __init__(self):
"""Initialize Redis connection."""
        self.client = redis.Redis(
            host=os.getenv('REDIS_HOST', 'localhost'),
            port=int(os.getenv('REDIS_PORT', 6379)),
            db=int(os.getenv('REDIS_DB', 0)),
            password=os.getenv('REDIS_PASSWORD'),
            decode_responses=True,  # Return strings, not bytes
            socket_connect_timeout=5,
            socket_keepalive=True
        )

        # Test connection
        try:
            self.client.ping()
        except redis.ConnectionError as e:
            raise RuntimeError(f"Failed to connect to Redis: {e}")

    def get(self, key: str) -> Optional[str]:
"""Get value by key."""
        return self.client.get(key)

    def set(self, key: str, value: str, ex: int = None) -> bool:
"""Set key-value with optional expiration (seconds)."""
        return self.client.set(key, value, ex=ex)

    def delete(self, *keys: str) -> int:
"""Delete one or more keys."""
        return self.client.delete(*keys)

    def exists(self, key: str) -> bool:
"""Check if key exists."""
        return self.client.exists(key) > 0

    def incr(self, key: str) -> int:
"""Increment counter."""
        return self.client.incr(key)

    def expire(self, key: str, seconds: int) -> bool:
"""Set expiration on existing key."""
        return self.client.expire(key, seconds)

    def ttl(self, key: str) -> int:
"""Get TTL in seconds (-1 if no expiration, -2 if not exists)."""
        return self.client.ttl(key)

# Singleton
redis_client = RedisClient()

# backend/app/services/user_service.py
from app.db.redis import redis_client
from app.models import User
import json

class UserService:
    CACHE_TTL = 300  # 5 minutes

    def get_user(self, user_id: int):
"""Get user with Redis caching."""
        cache_key = f'user:{user_id}'

        # Try cache first
        cached = redis_client.get(cache_key)
        if cached:
            return json.loads(cached)

        # Cache miss: query database
        user = User.query.get(user_id)
        if not user:
            return None

        user_dict = {
            'id': user.id,
            'email': user.email,
            'name': user.name,
            'role': user.role
        }

        # Store in cache
        redis_client.set(
            cache_key,
            json.dumps(user_dict),
            ex=self.CACHE_TTL
        )

        return user_dict

    def update_user(self, user_id: int,  **kwargs):
"""Update user and invalidate cache."""
        user = User.query.get(user_id)

        for key, value in kwargs.items():
            if hasattr(user, key):
                setattr(user, key, value)

        db.session.commit()

        # Invalidate cache
        redis_client.delete(f'user:{user_id}')

        return user.to_dict()

# backend/app/services/session_service.py
from app.db.redis import redis_client
import secrets
import json
from datetime import datetime

class SessionService:
    SESSION_TTL = 86400  # 24 hours

    def create_session(self, user_id: int, ip_address: str = None):
"""Create a new session."""
        session_id = secrets.token_urlsafe(32)
        session_data = {
            'user_id': user_id,
            'created_at': datetime.utcnow().isoformat(),
            'ip_address': ip_address
        }

        redis_client.set(
            f'session:{session_id}',
            json.dumps(session_data),
            ex=self.SESSION_TTL
        )

        return session_id

    def get_session(self, session_id: str):
"""Retrieve session data."""
        data = redis_client.get(f'session:{session_id}')
        return json.loads(data) if data else None

    def delete_session(self, session_id: str):
"""Logout: delete session."""
        redis_client.delete(f'session:{session_id}')

    def extend_session(self, session_id: str):
"""Extend session TTL (on activity)."""
        key = f'session:{session_id}'
        if redis_client.exists(key):
            redis_client.expire(key, self.SESSION_TTL)
            return True
        return False

# backend/app/middleware/rate_limit.py
from app.db.redis import redis_client
from flask import request, jsonify
from functools import wraps

def rate_limit(max_requests: int = 100, window_seconds: int = 60):
"""Rate limit decorator by IP address."""
    def decorator(f):
        @wraps(f)
        def wrapped(*args, **kwargs):
            # Use IP as key
            ip = request.remote_addr
            key = f'rate:{ip}:{f.__name__}'

            # Increment request counter
            current = redis_client.incr(key)

            # Set expiration on first request
            if current == 1:
                redis_client.expire(key, window_seconds)

            # Check if exceeded limit
            if current > max_requests:
                retry_after = redis_client.ttl(key)
                return jsonify({
                    'error': 'Rate limit exceeded',
                    'retry_after_seconds': retry_after
                }), 429

            return f(*args, **kwargs)
        return wrapped
    return decorator

# Usage in Flask app
@app.route('/api/expensive-operation')
@rate_limit(max_requests=10, window_seconds=60)
def expensive_operation():
    return jsonify({'result': 'success'})

docs.text:
# backend/app/services/email_queue.py
from app.db.redis import redis_client
import json
from datetime import datetime

class EmailQueue:
    QUEUE_KEY = 'queue:emails'

    def enqueue(self, to: str, subject: str, body: str,  priority: int = 1):
"""Add email to queue."""
        email_data = {
            'to': to,
            'subject': subject,
            'body': body,
            'priority': priority,
            'queued_at': datetime.utcnow().isoformat()
        }

        # Use sorted set for priority
        score = -priority  # Negative so lower numbers = higher priority
        redis_client.client.zadd(
            self.QUEUE_KEY,
            {json.dumps(email_data): score}
        )

    def dequeue(self):
"""Get next email from queue."""
        # Get highest priority (lowest score)
        data = redis_client.client.zrange(self.QUEUE_KEY, 0, 0)
        if data:
            email = json.loads(data[0])
            redis_client.client.zrem(self.QUEUE_KEY, data[0])
            return email
        return None

    def queue_size(self):
"""Get pending email count."""
        return redis_client.client.zcard(self.QUEUE_KEY)

# Worker process
import time

def email_worker():
"""Background worker that processes emails."""
    queue = EmailQueue()
    while True:
        email = queue.dequeue()
        if email:
            try:
                send_email(email['to'], email['subject'], email['body'])
            except Exception as e:
                # Log error and requeue
                queue.enqueue(email['to'], email['subject'], email['body'])
        else:
            time.sleep(1)  # Wait before checking again

docs.title: Redis Persistence Options
docs.text:
Redis can optionally save to disk so data survives restarts:

# Edit /etc/redis/redis.conf

# Option 1: RDB (Snapshot-based)
# Pros: Compact, fast recovery
# Cons: Loss of data between snapshots
save 900 1      # Save if 1 key changed in 900 seconds
save 300 10     # Save if 10 keys changed in 300 seconds
save 60 10000   # Save if 10000 keys changed in 60 seconds

# Option 2: AOF (Append-Only File)
# Pros: Detailed history, safer
# Cons: Larger files, slower writes
appendonly yes
appendfsync everysec  # Sync to disk every second

# Option 3: No persistence (fastest)
# (Don't set any save directives)

docs.text: Use Case Persistence TTL Session storage Yes (AOF) 24 hours Rate limits No Auto-expire Caching No Auto-expire Leaderboards Yes (RDB) No Task queue Yes (AOF) No

docs.title: Pattern 1: Read-Through Cache
docs.text:
# backend/app/patterns/read_through_cache.py
from app.db.postgres import db
from app.db.redis import redis_client
import json

class ReadThroughCache:
"""
    Cache layer between app and database.
    App always reads from cache.
    Cache handles database interaction.
    """

    def __init__(self, namespace: str, ttl: int = 300):
        self.namespace = namespace
        self.ttl = ttl

    def get(self, key: str, loader_func):
"""
        Get from cache or load from database.

        Args:
            key: Cache key
            loader_func: Function to call if cache miss

        Returns:
            Cached or loaded data
        """
        cache_key = f'{self.namespace}:{key}'

        # Try cache
        cached = redis_client.get(cache_key)
        if cached:
            return json.loads(cached)

        # Cache miss: load from database
        data = loader_func()

        # Store result
        if data:
            redis_client.set(
                cache_key,
                json.dumps(data),
                ex=self.ttl
            )

        return data

    def invalidate(self, key: str):
"""Remove from cache."""
        redis_client.delete(f'{self.namespace}:{key}')

# Usage
user_cache = ReadThroughCache('user', ttl=300)

def get_user(user_id):
    return user_cache.get(
        f'id:{user_id}',
        loader_func=lambda: User.query.get(user_id).to_dict()
    )

def update_user(user_id, **kwargs):
    user = User.query.get(user_id)
    for k, v in kwargs.items():
        setattr(user, k, v)
    db.session.commit()

    user_cache.invalidate(f'id:{user_id}')  # Invalidate cache
    return user.to_dict()

docs.title: Pattern 2: Write-Behind Cache
docs.text:
# ADVANCED: Cache writes and batch updates to database
# Use for high-write scenarios (analytics, metrics)

class WriteBehindCache:
"""
    Write to cache immediately, flush to DB periodically.
    Fast writes, eventual consistency.
    """

    def __init__(self, namespace: str, flush_interval: int = 60):
        self.namespace = namespace
        self.flush_interval = flush_interval

    def write(self, key: str, data: dict):
"""Write to cache only."""
        cache_key = f'{self.namespace}:{key}'
        redis_client.set(cache_key, json.dumps(data))

    def flush_to_db(self):
"""
        Periodically write cache to database.
        Run as background task.
        """
        keys = redis_client.client.keys(f'{self.namespace}:*')
        for key in keys:
            data = json.loads(redis_client.get(key))
            # Write to database
            # Clear from cache after flush
            redis_client.delete(key)

# backend/app/patterns/hybrid_database.py

class HybridStorage:
"""
    Use SQL for transactional data, MongoDB for supplementary data.
    """

    class UserProfile:
"""
        SQL Table: users (id, email, password_hash, created_at)
        MongoDB: user_profiles (user_id, bio, skills, certifications)
        """

        @staticmethod
        def get_full_profile(user_id: int):
"""Get SQL + MongoDB data together."""
            # SQL query
            user = User.query.get(user_id)
            if not user:
                return None

            # MongoDB query
            profiles = mongo_db.get_collection('user_profiles')
            profile = profiles.find_one({'user_id': user_id})

            # Combine
            return {
                'user_id': user.id,
                'email': user.email,
                'bio': profile.get('bio') if profile else None,
                'skills': profile.get('skills') if profile else [],
                'certifications': profile.get('certifications') if profile else []
            }

        @staticmethod
        def update_profile(user_id: int, bio: str = None,  skills: list = None):
"""MongoDB: Update profile data."""
            profiles = mongo_db.get_collection('user_profiles')

            update_doc = {}
            if bio:
                update_doc['bio'] = bio
            if skills:
                update_doc['skills'] = skills

            profiles.update_one(
                {'user_id': user_id},
                {'$set': update_doc},
                upsert=True
            )

class MongodbMonitor:

# backend/app/db/error_handlers.py
from pymongo import errors as mongo_errors
from pymongo import RetryWriteFailed
import redis

def handle_mongo_error(func):
"""Decorator for MongoDB error handling."""
    def wrapper(*args, **kwargs):
        try:
            return func(*args, **kwargs)
        except mongo_errors.DuplicateKeyError:
            raise ValueError("Document with this value already exists")
        except mongo_errors.OperationFailure as e:
            raise RuntimeError(f"MongoDB operation failed: {e}")
        except mongo_errors.ConnectionFailure:
            raise RuntimeError("MongoDB connection lost")
    return wrapper

def handle_redis_error(func):
"""Decorator for Redis error handling."""
    def wrapper(*args, **kwargs):
        try:
            return func(*args, **kwargs)
        except redis.ConnectionError:
            # Fall back to database query
            return None
        except redis.TimeoutError:
            # Timeout on Redis, don't crash
            return None
    return wrapper

docs.title: Decision Tree
docs.text:
Do you need flexible schema?
├─ YES: Document data with arrays/objects?
│   ├─ YES: Use MongoDB
│   └─ NO: Use PostgreSQL (JSONB)
└─ NO: Use PostgreSQL

Need microsecond latency caching?
├─ YES: Use Redis
└─ NO: Use database

Need to store sessions/temporary data?
├─ YES: Use Redis
└─ NO: Use database

Need full-text search?
├─ YES: MongoDB (moderate scale) or Elasticsearch (large scale)
└─ NO: Use PostgreSQL (text search)

Need real-time leaderboard/ranking?
├─ YES: Use Redis (sorted sets)
└─ NO: Use database with indexes

docs.title: Use MongoDB For:
docs.text:
• ✅ Logging - Flexible schema, high write volume, time-windowed queries
  • ✅ Product catalogs - Varying attributes per product
  • ✅ Content management - Articles with different structures
  • ✅ Analytics events - High-volume, flexible structure
  • ✅ Cache of API responses - Fast read, can be recreated

docs.title: DO NOT Use MongoDB For:
docs.text:
• ❌ User authentication - Needs ACID guarantees
  • ❌ Financial transactions - Needs constraints and rollback
  • ❌ Data with complex relationships - Avoid denormalization
  • ❌ Data requiring joins - SQL is simpler
  • ❌ Anything with integrity constraints - PostgreSQL enforces at database level

docs.title: Use Redis For:
docs.text:
• ✅ Caching - Reduce database load
  • ✅ Sessions - Fast reads, auto-expiration
  • ✅ Rate limiting - Atomic counters
  • ✅ Leaderboards - Sorted sets, fast ranking
  • ✅ Real-time counters - Page views, metrics
  • ✅ Task queues - Inter-process communication
  • ✅ Pub/Sub messaging - Real-time notifications

docs.title: DO NOT Use Redis For:
docs.text:
• ❌ Persistent storage - Data lost on restart
  • ❌ Large datasets - Limited by RAM
  • ❌ Complex queries - No SQL
  • ❌ Unstructured data - No schema validation

    "level": "ERROR",
    "service": "api",
    "message": "...",
    "timestamp": "...",
    "expires": 30 days

Question 1: When should you use MongoDB over PostgreSQL? - a) Always - it's faster - b) When you need flexible schema and don't need ACID transactions - c) For user authentication - d) For financial data

Correct: b

docs.title: When MongoDB is a BAD Idea
docs.text:
Don't use MongoDB for:

  1. Transactional data 

    # BAD: User registration in MongoDB
def register_user(email, password):
    users = mongo.get_collection('users')
    # No transaction guarantees
    # No foreign key constraints
    # Race conditions possible
    users.insert_one({
        'email': email,
        'password_hash': hash_password(password)
    })

  2. Complex relationships 

    # BAD: E-commerce orders in MongoDB
{
  "order_id": 1,
  "user": {  # Duplicated user data
    "email": "user@example.com",
    "name": "John"
  },
  "items": [
    {
      "product": {  # Duplicated product data
        "name": "Widget",
        "price": 10.00
      }
    }
  ]
}
# Problem: Update user email → must update ALL orders

  3. Financial data 

    # BAD: Payment processing in MongoDB
# No ACID guarantees across documents
# Risk of data inconsistency

Use PostgreSQL instead for these cases.

docs.text:
Pattern 1: Embedding (denormalization) 

# User with embedded addresses
{
  "_id": ObjectId("..."),
  "email": "user@example.com",
  "addresses": [  # Embedded
    {
      "type": "shipping",
      "street": "123 Main St",
      "city": "NYC"
    },
    {
      "type": "billing",
      "street": "456 Oak Ave",
      "city": "LA"
    }
  ]
}

# Good when:
# - Addresses are always accessed with user
# - Limited number of addresses per user
# - Addresses rarely change

Pattern 2: Referencing (normalization) 

# User document
{
  "_id": ObjectId("507f1f77bcf86cd799439011"),
  "email": "user@example.com"
}

# Order documents (reference user)
{
  "_id": ObjectId("..."),
  "user_id": ObjectId("507f1f77bcf86cd799439011"),
  "total": 100.00,
  "items": [...]
}

# Good when:
# - Data is accessed independently
# - Large or unbounded arrays
# - Data changes frequently

# backend/app/repositories/product_repository.py
from app.db.mongo import mongo
from bson import ObjectId

class ProductRepository:
    def __init__(self):
        self.collection = mongo.get_collection('products')
        # Indexes
        self.collection.create_index('sku', unique=True)
        self.collection.create_index('category')
        self.collection.create_index([('name', 'text')])  # Text search

    def create_product(self, sku, name, price, category, attributes=None):
        doc = {
            'sku': sku,
            'name': name,
            'price': price,
            'category': category,
            'attributes': attributes or {},
            'created_at': datetime.utcnow()
        }
        result = self.collection.insert_one(doc)
        return str(result.inserted_id)

    def get_product(self, sku):
        return self.collection.find_one({'sku': sku})

    def search_products(self, query, category=None):
        filter_doc = {'$text': {'$search': query}}

            filter_doc['category'] = category

    def update_price(self, sku, new_price):

            {'sku': sku},
            {'$set': {'price': new_price, 'updated_at': datetime.utcnow()}}

docs.title: What Redis Actually Is
docs.text:
Redis is an in-memory key-value store that's extremely fast. It's not a replacement for databases—it's a complement. Think of it as a turbocharger for your application.

How it works: - Data stored in RAM (memory) - 100-1000x faster than disk databases - Single-threaded - No race conditions, atomic operations - Optional persistence - Can save to disk, or lose on restart - Data structures - Not just strings, but lists, sets, sorted sets, hashes

Performance comparison: 

Operation         | PostgreSQL | Redis
─────────────────────────────────────────
Simple read       | 1-5ms      | 0.01-0.1ms (100-500x faster)
Write             | 1-5ms      | 0.01-0.1ms
Complex query     | 10-100ms   | N/A (no SQL)
Memory usage      | On disk    | All in RAM (expensive)

Data structures (why Redis is powerful):

import redis

r = redis.Redis(host='localhost', port=6379)

# 1. String - Simple value
r.set('user:1:name', 'John')              # SET
r.get('user:1:name')                      # GET → 'John'

# 2. List - Ordered collection (like array)
r.lpush('queue:jobs', job1, job2, job3)  # Add to left (push)
r.rpop('queue:jobs')                      # Remove from right (pop)

# 3. Set - Unordered unique collection
r.sadd('tags:python', 'user1', 'user2')  # Add tag
r.smembers('tags:python')                 # Get all users with tag
r.sismember('tags:python', 'user1')       # Check membership

# 4. Sorted Set - Ordered by score
r.zadd('leaderboard', {'user1': 100, 'user2': 95})  # Score is ranking
r.zrange('leaderboard', 0, -1, withscores=True)     # Top to bottom

# 5. Hash - Dictionary/object
r.hset('user:1', mapping={                # SET multiple fields
    'name': 'John',
    'email': 'john@example.com',
    'age': 30
})
r.hget('user:1', 'name')                  # GET single field → 'John'
r.hgetall('user:1')                       # GET all fields

docs.title: Real-World Redis Patterns
docs.text:
Pattern 1: Caching 

def get_user(user_id):
    # Try Redis first (fast)
    cached = redis.get(f'user:{user_id}')
    if cached:
        return json.loads(cached)

    # Cache miss: load from PostgreSQL
    user = User.query.get(user_id)
    if user:
        # Cache for 5 minutes
        redis.setex(
            f'user:{user_id}',
            300,
            json.dumps(user.to_dict())
        )

    return user.to_dict() if user else None

Pattern 2: Rate Limiting 

def check_rate_limit(user_id, limit=100, window=60):
"""Allow 100 requests per 60 seconds"""
    key = f'rate:{user_id}'

    # Increment counter
    current = redis.incr(key)

    # Set expiration on first request
    if current == 1:
        redis.expire(key, window)

    # Check if exceeded
    return current <= limit

Pattern 3: Session Storage 

def create_session(user_id):
    session_id = secrets.token_urlsafe(32)
    session_data = {
        'user_id': user_id,
        'created_at': datetime.utcnow().isoformat(),
        'ip': request.remote_addr
    }

    # Store in Redis with 24-hour expiration
    redis.hset(
        f'session:{session_id}',
        mapping=session_data
    )
    redis.expire(f'session:{session_id}', 86400)  # 24 hours

    return session_id

def get_session(session_id):
    return redis.hgetall(f'session:{session_id}')  # Returns dict

Pattern 4: Leaderboard 

def update_score(user_id, score):
    # Sorted set: user → score
    redis.zadd('leaderboard', {f'user:{user_id}': score})

def get_leaderboard(limit=10):
    # Get top 10 (highest scores first)
    return redis.zrange(
        'leaderboard',
        0, limit-1,
        withscores=True,
        desc=True  # Reverse order
    )

def get_user_rank(user_id):
    # Returns rank (0 = top)
    return redis.zrevrank('leaderboard', f'user:{user_id}')

docs.title: Redis Persistence Options
docs.text:
Redis can optionally save to disk so data survives restarts:

# In Redis configuration file (/etc/redis/redis.conf):

# Option 1: RDB (Snapshot)
# Saves entire dataset to disk periodically
save 900 1      # Save if 1 key changed in 900 seconds
save 300 10     # Save if 10 keys changed in 300 seconds
save 60 10000   # Save if 10000 keys changed in 60 seconds

# Option 2: AOF (Append-Only File)
# Logs every write operation
appendonly yes
appendfsync everysec  # Sync to disk every second

# Option 3: No persistence (fastest, loses data on restart)
# Don't set any save directives

When to enable persistence: - Yes: Session data, important cache data - No: Throwaway cache, rate limit counters, ephemeral data

redis.lpush('queue:emails', 'email1') # List redis.sadd('tags:python', 'user1', 'user2') # Set redis.hset('user:1', 'name', 'John', 'email', 'john@example.com') # Hash 

**Key characteristics**:
- In-memory (very fast, but expensive)
- Data structures (lists, sets, hashes, sorted sets)
- Persistence optional (RDB snapshots, AOF logs)
- Single-threaded (no race conditions)

docs.title: Caching Pattern
docs.text:
# backend/app/services/user_service.py
from app.db.postgres import db
from app.db.redis import redis_client
from app.models import User
import json

class UserService:
    CACHE_TTL = 300  # 5 minutes

    def get_user(self, user_id):
        # Try cache first
        cache_key = f'user:{user_id}'
        cached = redis_client.get(cache_key)

        if cached:
            return json.loads(cached)

        # Cache miss - query database
        user = User.query.get(user_id)
        if not user:
            return None

        user_data = user.to_dict()

        # Store in cache
        redis_client.set(
            cache_key,
            json.dumps(user_data),
            ex=self.CACHE_TTL
        )

        return user_data

    def update_user(self, user_id, **kwargs):
        user = User.query.get(user_id)
        for key, value in kwargs.items():
            setattr(user, key, value)
        db.session.commit()

        # Invalidate cache
        redis_client.delete(f'user:{user_id}')

        return user.to_dict()

# backend/app/services/session_service.py
from app.db.redis import redis_client
import secrets
import json

class SessionService:
    SESSION_TTL = 86400  # 24 hours

    def create_session(self, user_id):
        session_id = secrets.token_urlsafe(32)
        session_data = {
            'user_id': user_id,
            'created_at': datetime.utcnow().isoformat()
        }

        redis_client.set(
            f'session:{session_id}',
            json.dumps(session_data),
            ex=self.SESSION_TTL
        )

        return session_id

    def get_session(self, session_id):
        data = redis_client.get(f'session:{session_id}')
        return json.loads(data) if data else None

    def delete_session(self, session_id):
        redis_client.delete(f'session:{session_id}')

    def extend_session(self, session_id):
        key = f'session:{session_id}'
        if redis_client.exists(key):
            redis_client.expire(key, self.SESSION_TTL)

docs.title: Rate Limiting
docs.text:
# backend/app/middleware/rate_limit.py
from app.db.redis import redis_client
from flask import request, jsonify
from functools import wraps

def rate_limit(max_requests=100, window=60):
"""
    Rate limit decorator
    max_requests: Maximum requests allowed
    window: Time window in seconds
    """
    def decorator(f):
        @wraps(f)
        def wrapped(*args, **kwargs):
            # Use IP address as key
            ip = request.remote_addr
            key = f'rate_limit:{ip}:{f.__name__}'

            # Increment counter
            current = redis_client.client.incr(key)

            # Set expiration on first request
            if current == 1:
                redis_client.client.expire(key, window)

            # Check limit
            if current > max_requests:
                return jsonify({
                    'error': 'Rate limit exceeded',
                    'retry_after': redis_client.client.ttl(key)
                }), 429

            return f(*args, **kwargs)
        return wrapped
    return decorator

# Usage
@app.route('/api/expensive-operation')
@rate_limit(max_requests=10, window=60)
def expensive_operation():
    return jsonify({'result': 'success'})

docs.title: Queue Pattern (Simple)
docs.text:
# backend/app/services/email_queue.py
from app.db.redis import redis_client
import json

class EmailQueue:
    QUEUE_KEY = 'queue:emails'

    def enqueue(self, to, subject, body):
        email_data = {
            'to': to,
            'subject': subject,
            'body': body,
            'queued_at': datetime.utcnow().isoformat()
        }
        redis_client.client.lpush(self.QUEUE_KEY, json.dumps(email_data))

    def dequeue(self):
        data = redis_client.client.rpop(self.QUEUE_KEY)
        return json.loads(data) if data else None

    def queue_size(self):
        return redis_client.client.llen(self.QUEUE_KEY)

# Worker process
def email_worker():
    queue = EmailQueue()
    while True:
        email = queue.dequeue()
        if email:
            send_email(email['to'], email['subject'], email['body'])
        else:
            time.sleep(1)
