docs.title: Module 0: Linux Networking Essentials for Backend Engineers
docs.text:
Duration: 2–3 hours | Level: Beginner→Intermediate | Prerequisites: Basic command-line comfort, ability to SSH into a Linux box

What This Module Is: An exhaustive, hands-on guide to the Linux networking tools and concepts that every backend and DevOps engineer must know. You will learn how to inspect, troubleshoot, configure, and optimize network behavior on any Linux system.

docs.title: Why You Need This
docs.text:
Linux powers approximately 96% of the cloud infrastructure on the planet. When your Flask API mysteriously drops connections, when a Kubernetes pod can't reach the database, or when a load balancer returns 502 errors — the problem is almost always solved by understanding and inspecting the Linux networking layer.

Most networking tutorials focus on protocols (TCP/IP theory), cloud services (AWS VPCs), or web frameworks. But they skip the actual tools you will use at 3 AM to debug production. This module fills that gap.

docs.title: The Reality of Production Debugging
docs.text:
You will encounter these scenarios:

  1. "The database connection timed out" — You SSH into the application host and discover port 5432 is not being routed correctly.
  2. "WebSocket connections drop every 5 minutes" — You use tcpdump to find that a firewall rule is silently killing idle connections.
  3. "Kubernetes DNS works from one pod but not another" — You hop into the pod's network namespace and inspect interface configuration.
  4. "The API is slow but CPU and memory look fine" — You check ethtool statistics and discover the network card is dropping packets due to buffer overflow.

In all these cases, the Linux tools in this module are your only path to truth.

docs.title: Historical Evolution of Linux Networking Tools
docs.text:
Linux has had several generations of networking tools:

Era Tools Limitation Current Status 1990s–2000s ifconfig, route, netstat, arp Slow (parses /proc), poor IPv6 support Deprecated 2000s–2010s iproute2 suite (ip, ss) Fast, complete, but steeper learning curve Current standard 2010s–Present ip, ss, nftables, bpf tools Modern, scriptable, kernel-aware Actively maintained

You will see the old tools in legacy documentation and older systems, but know ip and ss first.

docs.title: Mental Model for This Module
docs.text:
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  Application (Flask, Node.js, Go)                    │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  System Call Layer (bind, listen, connect, send)     │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  Linux Kernel Networking Stack                       │
│  ├─ Socket management                                │
│  ├─ Protocol handlers (TCP, UDP, ICMP)               │
│  ├─ Routing decisions                                │
│  ├─ Firewall rules (iptables/nftables)               │
│  └─ Interface drivers                                │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  Network Hardware (NIC driver, physical interface)    │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  Physical Network (switches, routers, cables)         │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Throughout this module, we inspect each layer. Most problems live in the kernel and hardware layers, not in your application code.

docs.title: What Is a Network Interface?
docs.text:
A network interface is an abstraction representing how your host connects to a network. It may be:

  • Physical – a real ethernet port (eth0), wifi card (wlan0)
  • Virtual – created by software for containers (veth123...), tunnels (tun0), or bridges (br0)
  • Loopback – only for localhost traffic (lo)

Each interface has: - A name (eth0, docker0, wlan0) - MAC address (hardware layer, 00:11:22:33:44:55) - IPv4 address(es) (192.168.1.100/24) - IPv6 address(es) (fe80::1/64) - State (UP, DOWN) - MTU (maximum transmission unit, usually 1500 bytes)

docs.title: Inspecting Interfaces: The ip Command
docs.text: The ip suite of tools is the modern standard. Think of it as a single powerful binary with subcommands.

docs.title: Basic Inspection
docs.text:
# Show all interfaces with addresses
ip addr show

# output:
# 1: lo: <LOOPBACK,UP,LOWER_UP> mtu 65536 qdisc noqueue state UNKNOWN group default qlen 1000
#     inet 127.0.0.1/8 scope host lo
#     inet6 ::1/128 scope host
#
# 2: eth0: <BROADCAST,MULTICAST,UP,LOWER_UP> mtu 1500 qdisc fq_codel state UP group default qlen 1000
#     link/ether a2:34:56:78:90:ab brd ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff
#     inet 192.168.1.100/24 brd 192.168.1.255 scope global dynamic eth0
#     inet6 fe80::a034:56ff:fe78:90ab/64 scope link

Breaking down the output:

  • <LOOPBACK,UP,LOWER_UP> = flags indicating state
  • UP = interface is administrative up (layer 3)
  • LOWER_UP = physical/driver layer is operational (layer 1)
  • LOOPBACK = reserved for localhost
  • BROADCAST = can send broadcast frames

  • MULTICAST = can send multicast frames

  • mtu 1500 = maximum frame size before fragmentation (1500 is standard Ethernet)

  • inet 192.168.1.100/24 = IPv4 address with CIDR, brd is broadcast address

  • inet6 fe80::1/64 = IPv6 address (link-local by default on Ethernet)

  • scope values:

  • global = routable on external networks
  • link = only on local segment
  • host = localhost only

docs.title: Show a Specific Interface
docs.text:
# Show only eth0
ip addr show eth0

# Show only IPv4
ip -4 addr show

# Show only IPv6
ip -6 addr show

docs.title: Add an Address (Temporarily)
docs.text:
# Add a second IP to eth0
sudo ip addr add 192.168.1.50/24 dev eth0

# Verify
ip addr show eth0 | grep "inet 192.168.1.50"

# Remove it
sudo ip addr del 192.168.1.50/24 dev eth0

docs.title: Check Interface Statistics
docs.text:
# Show RX/TX statistics
ip -s link show eth0

# output:
# 2: eth0: <BROADCAST,MULTICAST,UP,LOWER_UP> mtu 1500 qdisc fq_codel state UP mode DEFAULT group default qlen 1000
#     link/ether a2:34:56:78:90:ab brd ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff
#     RX: bytes  packets  errors  dropped overrun mcast
#     268402    1843     0       12      0       0
#     TX: bytes  packets  errors  dropped carrier collsns
#     198761    1204     0       0       0       0

What the metrics mean:

  • RX bytes/packets = total data received / number of frames received
  • errors = corrupted frames (usually hardware issues)
  • dropped = frames discarded by kernel (usually insufficient buffer or firewall DROP rule)
  • overrun = interface couldn't keep up with incoming traffic (ring buffer too small)

docs.title: Understanding the Routing Table
docs.text: The routing table is a list of rules: "To reach network X, send packets through gateway G via interface I".

docs.title: Inspecting Routes: The ip route Command
docs.text:
# Show entire routing table
ip route show

# output:
# default via 192.168.1.1 dev eth0 proto dhcp metric 100
# 192.168.1.0/24 dev eth0 proto kernel scope link src 192.168.1.100
# 10.0.0.0/8 via 192.168.1.254 dev eth0 metric 200

Breaking it down:

  • default via 192.168.1.1 dev eth0 = "For any address not listed below, send to 192.168.1.1 via eth0"
  • proto dhcp/kernel/static = how the route was added (DHCP server, kernel auto-detect, manual)
  • metric 100 = cost (lower = preferred). When multiple routes match, lowest metric wins
  • 192.168.1.0/24 dev eth0 scope link = directly connected subnet (no gateway needed)

docs.title: How Routing Works: A Walkthrough
docs.text:
When your application sends a packet to 8.8.8.8:

  1. Kernel checks routing table for longest matching prefix
  2. 8.8.8.8 doesn't match 192.168.1.0/24 or 10.0.0.0/8
  3. Falls back to default via 192.168.1.1
  4. Sends packet to 192.168.1.1 (your gateway/router) via eth0
  5. Router decides where to forward it next

Key insight: Routing is prefix matching, not exact matching. The most specific (longest prefix) match wins.

docs.title: Adding and Deleting Routes
docs.text:
# Add a route to a specific network via a gateway
sudo ip route add 192.168.50.0/24 via 192.168.1.254 dev eth0

# Verify
ip route show

# Delete the route
sudo ip route del 192.168.50.0/24

# Add a default route (if none exists)
sudo ip route add default via 192.168.1.1

docs.title: Temporary vs Persistent Routes
docs.text:
The routes you add with ip route are temporary — they vanish when you reboot.

For persistence, edit /etc/network/interfaces (Debian/Ubuntu) or /etc/sysconfig/network-scripts/ifcfg-eth0 (RHEL/CentOS), or use netplan on modern systems.

docs.title: Routing Table Pitfalls
docs.text:
Critical: You Can Lock Yourself Out

If you're SSH'd into a remote server and you delete the default route, you lose connectivity immediately. Always test local systems first.

# DANGEROUS on remote system!
sudo ip route del default
# ... now you can't connect to the server anymore!

docs.title: What Is a Socket?
docs.text:
A socket is an endpoint for network communication — the kernel's representation of a connection or listener.

Think of it like a mailbox: - Server socket (LISTEN) = a mailbox accepting incoming letters - Established socket (ESTABLISHED) = an open letter being exchanged - Connecting socket (SYN_SENT) = you're writing a letter, waiting for reply

docs.title: Inspecting Sockets: The ss Command
docs.text: The ss (socket statistics) command supersedes the old netstat. It's faster and more powerful.

docs.title: Show All Listeners
docs.text:
# Show all listening sockets (TCP and UDP)
ss -tuln

# output:
# Netid  State      Recv-Q Send-Q  Local Address:Port       Peer Address:Port Process
# tcp    LISTEN     0      128     0.0.0.0:22              0.0.0.0:*            users:(("sshd",pid=456))
# tcp    LISTEN     0      50      127.0.0.1:5432          0.0.0.0:*            users:(("postgres",pid=789))
# tcp    LISTEN     0      511     0.0.0.0:80              0.0.0.0:*            users:(("nginx",pid=1234))
# udp    UNCONN     0      0       0.0.0.0:53              0.0.0.0:*            users:(("systemd-resolve",pid=567))

Flag explanations:

  • -t = TCP sockets
  • -u = UDP sockets
  • -l = listening sockets only
  • -n = numeric addresses (don't resolve names to avoid DNS lookups)

Columns:

  • Recv-Q = bytes queued for the application to read (should be small)
  • Send-Q = bytes queued in the TCP send buffer (normal varies)
  • Local Address:Port = which interface and port this is bound to
  • Peer Address:Port = remote address (0.0.0.0 means listening to all)

docs.title: Show Established Connections
docs.text:
# All established sockets
ss -tn state established

# output:
# Netid  State      Recv-Q Send-Q  Local Address:Port       Peer Address:Port
# tcp    ESTAB      0      0       192.168.1.100:443       203.0.113.50:52344
# tcp    ESTAB      0      0       192.168.1.100:5432      10.0.0.50:42891

docs.title: Count Connections by State
docs.text:
# How many connections in each state?
ss -tn | awk '{print $2}' | sort | uniq -c

# output:
#      1 State
#     42 ESTAB
#     12 TIME_WAIT
#      3 LISTEN
#      1 SYN_RECV

This shows you have 42 active connections, 12 that are closing (TIME_WAIT), 3 listeners, etc.

docs.title: Understanding Socket States
docs.text:
State Meaning Normal Duration If Stuck = Problem LISTEN Waiting for connections Until service stops Service not running SYN_SENT Initiating connection < 1 second Remote not responding SYN_RECV Received SYN, not yet accepted < 1 second Application not accepting ESTAB Connection active Minutes to hours Data flowing FIN_WAIT_1 We sent FIN, waiting for ack < 1 second Remote not closing FIN_WAIT_2 We acked their FIN, waiting < 1 second Remote not responding TIME_WAIT Waiting before cleanup Default 60 seconds Normal, but if thousands stuck = problem CLOSE_WAIT Remote closed, we haven't < 1 second Application leak (not closing sockets)

Critical fact: If you see thousands of CLOSE_WAIT sockets, your application is leaking connections — it's not properly closing them.

docs.title: Finding Which Process Owns a Socket
docs.text:
# Show process names for each socket
ss -tulnp | grep 5432

# output:
# tcp  LISTEN  0  50  127.0.0.1:5432  0.0.0.0:*  users:(("postgres",pid=789,fd=5))

Or if you know the port:

# Which process is listening on port 8080?
lsof -i :8080

# output:
# COMMAND  PID  USER  FD  TYPE DEVICE          SIZE/OFF NODE NAME
# python  1234  app   3u  IPv4 0x12345678          0t0  TCP localhost:8080 (LISTEN)

docs.title: What Is a Firewall Rule?
docs.text:
A firewall rule is a kernel-level filter: "For packets matching X properties, perform Y action (ACCEPT, DROP, REJECT, etc.)".

Linux has two firewall subsystems:

  1. iptables – older, still widely used
  2. nftables – modern replacement, but iptables still dominates

docs.title: List All Rules
docs.text:
# Show all rules in human-readable form
sudo iptables -L

# or more verbose
sudo iptables -L -v

# Show raw format (useful for scripts)
sudo iptables -S

docs.title: Basic Rule Structure
docs.text:
# Default policy: if no rule matches, DROP incoming packets
sudo iptables -P INPUT DROP

# Allow established connections
sudo iptables -A INPUT -m state --state ESTABLISHED,RELATED -j ACCEPT

# Allow SSH (port 22)
sudo iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 22 -j ACCEPT

# Allow HTTP/HTTPS (ports 80, 443)
sudo iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 80 -j ACCEPT
sudo iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 443 -j ACCEPT

# Allow ICMP (ping)
sudo iptables -A INPUT -p icmp -j ACCEPT

# Allow localhost
sudo iptables -A INPUT -i lo -j ACCEPT

# Log dropped packets (for debugging)
sudo iptables -A INPUT -j LOG --log-prefix "Dropped: " --log-level 7

# Default policy: drop anything not explicitly allowed
sudo iptables -P INPUT DROP

docs.title: Flags Explained
docs.text:
• -A = append rule to chain
  • -I = insert at beginning
  • -D = delete rule
  • -P = set default policy
  • -p = protocol (tcp, udp, icmp)
  • --dport = destination port
  • -i = incoming interface
  • -j = target/action (ACCEPT, DROP, REJECT, LOG)
  • -m state = match connection state

docs.title: Practical Example: Secure Web Server
docs.text:
# Flush existing rules (start clean)
sudo iptables -F
sudo iptables -X  # delete custom chains

# Default: deny all incoming
sudo iptables -P INPUT DROP
sudo iptables -P FORWARD DROP
sudo iptables -P OUTPUT ACCEPT

# Allow loopback (needed for localhost services)
sudo iptables -A INPUT -i lo -j ACCEPT

# Allow established connections
sudo iptables -A INPUT -m state --state ESTABLISHED,RELATED -j ACCEPT

# Allow SSH (from anywhere — change to restrict)
sudo iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 22 -j ACCEPT

# Allow HTTP
sudo iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 80 -j ACCEPT

# Allow HTTPS
sudo iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 443 -j ACCEPT

# Verify
sudo iptables -L -v

docs.title: Making iptables Persistent
docs.text:
Rules are temporary (lost on reboot). To persist:

On Ubuntu/Debian: 

sudo apt-get install iptables-persistent
sudo iptables-save | sudo tee /etc/iptables/rules.v4

On RHEL/CentOS: 

sudo systemctl enable iptables
sudo systemctl restart iptables

docs.title: nftables: The Modern Alternative
docs.text:
nftables is the successor, with simpler syntax:

# List rules
sudo nft list ruleset

# Add a simple rule
sudo nft add rule inet filter input tcp dport 22 accept

However, iptables is still ubiquitous. Learn both, but prioritize iptables for production systems.

docs.title: Why Capture Packets?
docs.text:
When a connection mysteriously fails, the only ground truth is what packets actually crossed the network. Logs can lie, but packets don't.

Use packet capture to: - Verify that traffic reaches the host (or diagnose why it doesn't) - Inspect protocol negotiation (TLS handshake, HTTP headers) - Identify duplicate packets or out-of-order delivery - Find where connections are being reset

docs.title: tcpdump Basics
docs.text:
# Capture packets on eth0 and print to screen
sudo tcpdump -i eth0

# Capture only HTTP traffic (port 80)
sudo tcpdump -i eth0 port 80

# Capture only HTTPS (port 443)
sudo tcpdump -i eth0 port 443

# Capture traffic to/from a specific host
sudo tcpdump -i eth0 host 192.168.1.100

# Capture only outgoing traffic (-i eth0 src 192.168.1.100)
sudo tcpdump -i eth0 src 192.168.1.100

# Capture in binary format (for Wireshark)
sudo tcpdump -i eth0 -w /tmp/capture.pcap port 443

# Limit to first 100 packets
sudo tcpdump -i eth0 -c 100

# Show packet contents (be careful, will show passwords!)
sudo tcpdump -i eth0 -A port 80

docs.title: Real-World Debugging Scenario
docs.text:
Problem: "Client can't reach our API on port 8080"

# Step 1: Capture traffic
sudo tcpdump -i eth0 -w /tmp/api.pcap port 8080

# Step 2: Have client attempt connection
# (in another terminal: curl http://192.168.1.100:8080/api)

# Step 3: Stop capture (Ctrl-C) and analyze
sudo tcpdump -r /tmp/api.pcap -nn

# output might show:
# 192.168.1.50.52344 > 192.168.1.100.8080: Flags [S], seq 0
# (SYN sent but no reply)
# Conclusion: Server on port 8080 not responding at all

docs.title: Wireshark for Deep Analysis
docs.text:
For complex issues, use Wireshark (GUI):

# Capture to file for later analysis
sudo tcpdump -i eth0 -w /tmp/full_capture.pcap

# Open on your local machine
# Download the file, open in Wireshark, analyze graphically

Wireshark shows:

  • TCP handshake and connection states
  • Complete DNS queries/responses
  • HTTP request/response headers and bodies
  • TLS certificate negotiation
  • Retransmissions and packet loss

docs.title: Bandwidth and Throughput: iftop and nethogs
docs.text:
# Show real-time bandwidth by connection
sudo iftop -i eth0

# Show bandwidth by process
sudo nethogs -i eth0

docs.title: Network Namespace Inspection
docs.text:
Containers and Kubernetes pods use network namespaces for isolation:

# List namespaces
ip netns list

# Run command in namespace
sudo ip netns exec backend ss -tulnp

# Enter namespace shell
sudo nsenter --net=/var/run/netns/backend /bin/bash
# Now all commands run inside that namespace

docs.title: Ethtool: Hardware-Level Diagnostics
docs.text:
# Show interface speed/duplex
sudo ethtool eth0

# Check for packet drops
sudo ethtool -S eth0 | grep -i drop

# Optimize ring buffer to prevent drops
sudo ethtool -G eth0 rx 4096 tx 4096

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
Best Practices: Linux Networking

  1. Use ip and ss, not ifconfig or netstat – They are faster and more complete.
  2. Capture packets on the server side – Client captures often miss the problem.
  3. Comment iptables rules – Future you (and your team) will thank you.
  4. Test routes locally before enabling – Use a test network interface.
  5. Use network namespaces for testing – Avoid breaking production.
  6. Automate with Ansible/Terraform – Manual ip commands are error-prone.
  7. Monitor packet drops – A silent ring-buffer overflow can tank performance.

docs.title: Scenario 1: Application Can't Reach Database
docs.text:
# 1. Check if database service is listening
ss -tulnp | grep 5432

# 2. If yes, check if route exists
ip route show | grep database_subnet

# 3. If yes, check firewall
sudo iptables -L | grep 5432

# 4. If still blocked, capture packets
sudo tcpdump -i eth0 host database_ip -w /tmp/db.pcap

docs.title: Scenario 2: Port Is Listening but Connections Fail
docs.text:
# Check socket state
ss -tnp | grep :8080

# Check how many connections are in CLOSE_WAIT (application leak?)
ss -tn | grep CLOSE_WAIT | wc -l

# Check if application is accepting
lsof -i :8080

# Monitor connections in real-time
watch -n 1 'ss -tn state established | wc -l'

docs.title: Scenario 3: Random Connection Drops
docs.text:
# Check for packet loss on the wire
sudo tcpdump -i eth0 -c 1000 > /tmp/packets.txt
# Count retransmissions
grep "retransmit" /tmp/packets.txt

# Check ring buffer overflow
sudo ethtool -S eth0 | grep -i "rx.*error\|drop"

# If overflowing, increase buffer
sudo ethtool -G eth0 rx 4096

docs.title: Tools Quick Reference
docs.text: Problem Command Output Which ports are listening? ss -tulnp List of sockets in LISTEN state How many active connections? ss -tn \| grep ESTAB \| wc -l Count Is a host reachable? ping -c 4 host ICMP response (or timeout) What traffic crosses the wire? sudo tcpdump -i eth0 -c 20 Raw packets Which process owns port 8080? lsof -i :8080 Process name/PID Is DNS working? dig example.com IP address (or NXDOMAIN) Can I reach database? telnet db.example.com 5432 Connection success or refused What's the routing path? traceroute 8.8.8.8 Hops to destination

docs.title: Legacy Tools vs Modern Tools
docs.text: Task Legacy Tool Modern Tool Which to Use Show interfaces ifconfig ip addr show ip (faster) Show routes route ip route show ip (more control) Show sockets netstat ss ss (much faster) Firewall rules iptables (only) iptables or nftables iptables (more standard) Packets tcpdump tcpdump Same (still best)

docs.title: 0.10 Summary & Connection to Next Module
docs.text:
You now understand the fundamental tools and concepts for Linux networking:

  • Network interfaces – where packets enter/leave
  • Routing – how packets find their way
  • Sockets – where applications bind and listen
  • Firewalls – how to filter traffic
  • Packet capture – how to see what's actually happening

These tools are used in every subsequent module of this tutorial. When we cover HTTP, REST APIs, load balancing, and TLS, we will use tcpdump, ss, and ip to understand and debug at the Linux level.

In Module 1: Networking Fundamentals, you will learn the protocol layer (TCP/IP, ports, sockets from an application perspective). You'll apply the Linux tools from this module to verify protocol behavior.

docs.title: 📚 Lecture Notes — Module 0: Linux Networking Essentials
🎯 Learning Objectives
docs.text: By the end of this module, you should be able to: - [ ] Use ip addr, ip route, and ss to inspect the complete network configuration of a Linux host - [ ] Diagnose connectivity failures by checking interfaces, routes, firewall rules, and capturing packets - [ ] Configure temporary network interfaces, addresses, and routes for testing - [ ] Write and troubleshoot basic iptables firewall rules - [ ] Use tcpdump to capture and analyze network traffic at the packet level - [ ] Map socket states to connection lifecycle and identify application connection leaks - [ ] Apply these tools to debug real production networking problems

docs.title: 🧠 Key Concepts Summary
docs.text: Concept One-Line Definition Importance Module Coverage Network Interface System abstraction for NIC or virtual network device Without it, no addressing or packet flow 0.2 Routing Kernel decision tree for determining where packets go Critical for cross-network communication 0.3 Socket Kernel endpoint for network communication Foundation of all network applications 0.4 Socket States Stages of connection lifecycle (LISTEN, SYN_SENT, ESTAB, etc.) Reveals what's happening in connections 0.4 Firewall Rules Kernel-level packet filtering with policies Controls who can reach your services 0.5 Packet Capture Recording raw network traffic for analysis Holy grail for debugging network issues 0.6 Namespace Isolated network stack (used by containers) Essential for understanding Kubernetes 0.7 Ring Buffer Hardware queue for incoming packets Often causes silent packet loss 0.7

docs.title: 💡 Core Takeaways
docs.text:
✅ Remember this: Most network problems are solved not by reading code, but by inspecting what the kernel and hardware are actually doing using ip, ss, and tcpdump.

  • Know your tools cold. Muscle memory matters at 3 AM when the API is down.
  • Interfaces and routes are foundational. If traffic doesn't reach the host or doesn't leave it, the app is blameless.
  • Socket states tell the full story. CLOSE_WAIT means applications leak; TIME_WAIT is normal.
  • Packet capture is the ultimate truth. When everything else is unclear, tcpdump never lies.
  • Firewall rules are evaluated in order. A single DROP rule before ACCEPT rules silently blocks traffic.
  • Persistent configuration matters. Manual ip commands vanish on reboot; automate with Ansible/Terraform.

docs.title: 🧪 Hands-On Exercise
docs.text:
Task: Diagnose why a local Flask API cannot be reached from a remote client.

Scenario: You have a Flask app running on 127.0.0.1:5000 on a Linux server. A remote client at 192.168.1.50 attempts to connect to 192.168.1.100:5000 but gets "Connection refused".

Step-by-step instructions:

  1. Check if Flask is actually listening: 

    ss -tulnp | grep 5000
    Result: You notice Flask is bound to 127.0.0.1:5000, not 0.0.0.0:5000. Issue found: It's only listening on localhost.

  2. Verify the application configuration (code change needed, not network): 

    # Wrong:
app.run(host='127.0.0.1', port=5000)

# Correct:
app.run(host='0.0.0.0', port=5000)

  3. Restart Flask and verify: 

    ss -tulnp | grep 5000
# Now shows: 0.0.0.0:5000

  4. From the remote client, test: 

    curl http://192.168.1.100:5000/
# Success!

  5. Capture and observe the traffic: 

    # On server:
sudo tcpdump -i eth0 port 5000 -c 10

# On client (in another terminal):
curl http://192.168.1.100:5000/

# Observe SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK in the capture

Expected Output (before fix): 

Client → Server: SYN (trying to connect)
Server: No response (port 5000 not listening on 0.0.0.0, only on 127.0.0.1)
Client: Retries, then timeout

Expected Output (after fix): 

Client → Server: SYN
Server → Client: SYN-ACK
Client → Server: ACK (connection established)
HTTP GET request from client
HTTP 200 response from Flask

Reflection Question: If the Flask app was bound to 0.0.0.0:5000 but still didn't respond, what would be your next debugging step? (Answer: Check firewall rules with sudo iptables -L to see if port 5000 is blocked.)

docs.title: ❓ Review Questions
docs.text:
1. What command shows all listening sockets with process names?
  2. How do you add a second IP address to interface eth0 temporarily?
  3. If ss -tn shows thousands of CLOSE_WAIT sockets, what is the likely problem?
  4. What does the routing table do, and how is it used when sending a packet to 8.8.8.8?
  5. Why is tcpdump on the server more useful than tcpdump on the client?
  6. What's the difference between iptables -A and iptables -I?
  7. If a rule like iptables -A INPUT -j DROP is placed before an ACCEPT rule, what happens?

Answers:

Click to reveal answers

  1. ss -tulnp or ss -tulnp | grep LISTEN

  2. sudo ip addr add 192.168.1.50/24 dev eth0 (or other CIDR). Remove with sudo ip addr del ...

  3. The application is not properly closing sockets — it's a connection leak. The application may have a bug or resource exhaustion.

  4. The routing table is a list of rules: "To reach network A, use gateway G via interface I". When sending to 8.8.8.8, the kernel searches for matching rules (longest prefix wins) and forwards packets accordingly. If no specific rule matches, the default gateway is used.

  5. The server capture shows both directions of traffic (arriving and leaving), whereas the client only sees its own traffic. Server-side captures reveal whether the server received the packet or a firewall dropped it.

  6. -A appends the rule to the end of the chain; -I inserts it at the beginning. Rule order matters because evaluation stops at the first match.

  7. The DROP rule will match everything, and the chain stops there. The later ACCEPT rule is unreachable. Always put more-specific rules before more-general ones.

docs.title: ⚠️ Common Exam / Interview Questions
docs.text:
• "Which command would you use to find which process is listening on port 3000?" Answer: ss -tulnp | grep 3000 or lsof -i :3000

  • "Your API server is running on 0.0.0.0:8080 but clients can't reach it. How do you debug?" Answer: Check routes (ip route show), firewall (sudo iptables -L), and packet capture (sudo tcpdump -i eth0 port 8080).

  • "Explain the difference between ESTABLISHED and CLOSE_WAIT socket states." Answer: ESTABLISHED = connection active and healthy. CLOSE_WAIT = remote side closed, but application hasn't closed yet. Many CLOSE_WAIT = app bug.

  • "You accidentally deleted the default route on a remote server. How do recovery without physical access?" Answer: You can't (that's why you should always test locally first). Prevention: use configuration management to define routes persistently.

  • "Why should you prefer ip and ss over ifconfig and netstat?" Answer: ip/ss are faster (don't parse /proc), support full IPv6, handle virtual interfaces better, and have consistent syntax.

docs.title: 🔗 What Comes Next
docs.text:
After mastering this section, proceed to: Module 1: Networking Fundamentals

You now understand how to inspect the Linux networking layer. In Module 1, you will learn what the protocols are (TCP, UDP, ports, IP addressing) and apply these Linux tools to verify that protocols work as expected.

The connection: Module 0 teaches visibility (tools), Module 1 teaches understanding (protocols). Together, they form the foundation for every subsequent module.

# list all interfaces with their addresses
ip addr show

# output snippet:
# 2: eth0: <BROADCAST,MULTICAST,UP,LOWER_UP> mtu 1500
#     inet 192.168.1.100/24 brd 192.168.1.255 scope global eth0
#     inet6 fe80::1/64 scope link

An interface can have multiple addresses (IPv4/IPv6) and multiple states (UP, DOWN). Understanding interfaces is the first step in troubleshooting connectivity.

docs.title: Routing Table
docs.text:
Linux maintains a routing table that decides where packets go.

$ ip route show

default via 192.168.1.1 dev eth0 proto dhcp metric 100
192.168.1.0/24 dev eth0 proto kernel scope link src 192.168.1.100

The default route handles traffic to any address not covered by a more specific route. You can add, modify or delete routes with ip route add/del.

docs.title: Socket States & Connections
docs.text:
The ss command displays socket information much faster than the legacy netstat. It shows TCP/UDP listeners, established connections, and statistics.

$ ss -tuln
Netid  State      Recv-Q Send-Q Local Address:Port               Peer Address:Port
tcp    LISTEN     0      128      0.0.0.0:22                        0.0.0.0:*
tcp    ESTAB      0      0        192.168.1.100:443                203.0.113.5:52344

Filter by state: ss -tn state established shows only active TCP connections.

docs.title: Namespaces and Virtual Devices
docs.text: Containers and network virtualization use namespaces to provide isolated network stacks. The ip netns command lets you inspect and run commands inside a namespace.

docs.title: Firewalls (iptables/nftables)
docs.text: Linux uses iptables or nftables to filter packets. A basic rule set can block, allow or log traffic. We will cover the most common patterns below.

docs.title: Packet Capture
docs.text: tcpdump and wireshark let you capture and inspect raw packets on an interface. This is the go‑to tool when connections mysteriously fail.

docs.title: Tools Summary
docs.text: Tool Purpose Common Flags When to Use ip configure interfaces, addresses, routes, rules addr, route, link, rule any interface or routing change ss socket statistics -tuln, state established examine open ports/connections netstat legacy; same as ss — troubleshooting older scripts ifconfig legacy interface tool — when working on very old systems iptables/nft firewall/packet filtering -L, -A, -F firewall policy management tcpdump capture packets -i, -w, port deep packet analysis ping/traceroute connectivity & path -c, -I test reachability dig/host DNS lookup +short debug DNS issues

docs.title: Comparison Table: iproute2 vs Legacy Tools
docs.text: Feature iproute2 (ip, ss) Legacy (ifconfig, route, netstat) Performance Fast, built-in kernel queries Slow (parses /proc files) IPv6 support First-class Limited Scripting Single binary, subcommands Multiple binaries, inconsistent syntax Maintenance Actively maintained Deprecated in many distros

docs.title: Beginner Example – Check Your IP and Connectivity
docs.text:
# Show addresses
ip addr show eth0

# Ping your gateway
ping -c 4 192.168.1.1

# Check DNS resolution
dig +short example.com

docs.title: Intermediate Example – Diagnose a Dropped Connection
docs.text:
# Start a packet capture on port 80
sudo tcpdump -i eth0 port 80 -w /tmp/http.pcap

# In another shell, attempt curl
curl http://192.168.1.200/

# Stop tcpdump (Ctrl-C) then open file in wireshark or analyze with:
sudo tcpdump -r /tmp/http.pcap -nn

docs.title: Advanced/Real-World Example – Track a 502 Error Through Namespaces
docs.text:
# List namespaces
ip netns list

# Enter backend namespace
sudo ip netns exec backend ss -tuln

# Capture traffic inside namespace
sudo ip netns exec backend tcpdump -i eth0 host 10.0.0.5

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
Best Practices: Linux Networking

  • Always use ip and ss on modern systems; only fall back to old tools when you have no choice.
  • Keep firewall rules as simple, ordered lists; comment each rule.
  • Use network namespaces or nsenter to isolate testing environments.
  • Capture packets on the server side when debugging production issues; client captures are less useful.
  • Script ip commands for reproducibility and include them in configuration management (Ansible, Terraform).

docs.title: Common Mistakes & Pitfalls
docs.text:
Mistake: Forgetting to bring interface UP

A new interface created with ip link add ... will be DOWN by default. You must ip link set dev eth1 up or you will see no traffic.

Pitfall: Overwriting iptables chains

Running iptables -F without understanding the default policy can lock you out of a remote host. Always check iptables -L first.

Misreading CIDR notation

192.168.1.0/24 includes addresses .0–.255 — the .0 network address and .255 broadcast. Don’t assign them to hosts.

docs.title: Real-World Use Cases
docs.text:
1. Post-deployment connectivity check: After deploying a new service, SSH into the host, run ss -tan | grep LISTEN, and verify the port is bound.
  2. Firewall troubleshooting: A web app suddenly returns 403. Use sudo tcpdump -ni eth0 port 443 to see if packets arrive; then inspect iptables -L for unwanted drop rules.
  3. Performance optimization: High packet drop on 10GbE interface? ethtool -S eth0 shows ring buffer overflow counters; increase rx/tx buffer sizes with ethtool -G.
  4. Container networking: Diagnose Kubernetes pod network by entering the pod’s network namespace and running ip a / ss.

docs.title: Networking Basics: A-to-Z Premodule
docs.text:
Duration: 2-3 hours | Level: Beginner | Prerequisites: None

What This Module Is: A complete A-to-Z introduction to networking concepts for backend engineers. If you're completely new to networking or need a refresher, start here before Module 1.

docs.title: Table of Contents (A-Z)
docs.text:
• A: Addressing & IP
  • B: Bandwidth & Bytes
  • C: Clients & Connections
  • D: Datagrams & DNS
  • E: Ethernet & Encapsulation
  • F: Firewalls & Flow
  • G: Gateways & Routing
  • H: Headers & Hops
  • I: Internet & Interfaces
  • J: Jumbo Frames (Jumbograms)
  • K: Keyed Sockets (Keying)
  • L: Latency & Layers
  • M: MAC & Multiplexing

docs.title: IPv4 Addresses
docs.text:
An IPv4 address is a 32-bit number written as 4 decimal numbers (0-255) separated by dots.

192.168.1.1
  ↑   ↑  ↑  ↑
  |   |  |  └── Host (0-255)
  |   |  └───── Subnet (0-255)
  |   └──────── Network (0-255)
  └──────────── Class (0-255)

Public vs Private: - Public IPs: Routable on the internet (e.g., 8.8.8.8) - Private IPs: Not routable (only within local networks) - 10.0.0.0 - 10.255.255.255 - 172.16.0.0 - 172.31.255.255 - 192.168.0.0 - 192.168.255.255

docs.title: IPv6 Addresses
docs.text:
Modern replacement for IPv4. 128-bit address written in hexadecimal.

2001:0db8:85a3:0000:0000:8a2e:0370:7334

Why it matters for backends: Your server likely has both IPv4 and IPv6. Most apps still use IPv4.

# See your machine's addresses
ip addr show

# Output:
# 2: eth0: ...
#     inet 192.168.1.100/24 scope global
#     inet6 fe80::1/64 scope link

docs.title: CIDR Notation
docs.text:
Shorthand for IP ranges. /24 means "first 24 bits are the network, last 8 bits are hosts."

192.168.1.0/24 = all IPs from 192.168.1.0 to 192.168.1.255
10.0.0.0/8 = all IPs from 10.0.0.0 to 10.255.255.255
172.16.0.0/12 = all IPs from 172.16.0.0 to 172.31.255.255

Why this matters: VPCs, subnets, and firewall rules use CIDR notation.

docs.title: Bandwidth
docs.text:
The maximum data rate a connection can handle.

1 Mbps (megabit/second) = 1,000,000 bits/second = 125 KB/second
1 Gbps = 1,000 Mbps = 125 MB/second

docs.title: Throughput
docs.text: Actual data transferred (always less than bandwidth due to overhead).

docs.title: Latency
docs.text:
Time for data to travel from A to B (measured in milliseconds or microseconds).

Localhost: < 1 ms
Same data center: 1-5 ms
Same region (AWS): 5-50 ms
Across continents: 100-300 ms

docs.title: Practical Example for Backend
docs.text:
If you call an API across the world:
- Latency adds 150 ms (one-way)
- 300 KB response / 50 Mbps bandwidth = 48 ms transfer
- Total: ~150 + 48 = 200+ ms before your backend gets the response

docs.title: Clients
docs.text:
Any device initiating a network request (your web browser, mobile app, or another backend service).

Your Flask Server Perspective:
- A client connects to your server
- Sends: GET /api/users HTTP/1.1
- Receives: 200 OK with JSON
- Connection closes (or stays open for HTTP/1.1 keep-alive)

docs.title: Connection States
docs.text:
CLOSED → SYN_SENT (client sends) → SYN_RECEIVED (server receives)
→ ESTABLISHED (both sides ready) → FIN_WAIT/CLOSE_WAIT (closing)
→ CLOSED

docs.title: Connection Limits
docs.text:
Every server has limits:

# Check max open files (connections)
ulimit -n
# Output: 1024 (on many Linux systems)

# See current connections
netstat -an | grep ESTABLISHED | wc -l

Why this matters: If you have 10,000 users, you need more than 1024 file descriptors.

docs.title: Datagrams
docs.text:
Individual packets of data (used by UDP). Unlike TCP, they're sent independently and may arrive out of order or not at all.

UDP Datagram = Header (8 bytes) + Payload (up to 65,527 bytes)

docs.title: DNS (Domain Name System)
docs.text:
Translates human-readable names to IP addresses.

www.example.com → 93.184.216.34

DNS Query Process: 

1. Browser: "What IP is example.com?"
2. Resolver (ISP): "Let me ask root nameserver"
3. Root: "Ask TLD server for .com"
4. TLD: "Ask authoritative nameserver for example.com"
5. Authoritative: "93.184.216.34"
6. Browser gets IP and connects

Common DNS Records:

Type Purpose Example A IPv4 address example.com → 93.184.216.34 AAAA IPv6 address example.com → 2001:db8::1 CNAME Alias www.example.com → example.com MX Mail server Mail goes to mail.example.com NS Nameserver Points to authoritative nameserver TXT Text record For SPF, DKIM, verification 
# Check DNS records
nslookup example.com
dig example.com
dig example.com A      # IPv4
dig example.com AAAA   # IPv6
dig example.com MX     # Mail servers

docs.title: Ethernet
docs.text:
The physical/link layer protocol for LANs (local area networks).

Your server talks to other servers on the same network via Ethernet.

docs.title: Encapsulation (Layering)
docs.text:
Data wraps through layers, each adding headers:

Application Layer (HTTP)
    ↓ (Add HTTP headers)
Transport Layer (TCP)
    ↓ (Add TCP headers: source/dest port, sequence numbers)
Network Layer (IP)
    ↓ (Add IP headers: source/dest IP address)
Link Layer (Ethernet)
    ↓ (Add MAC headers: source/dest MAC address)
Physical (Copper cable, fiber)

When you send HTTP request: 

[HTTP headers][HTTP body]
    ↓ TCP wraps it
[TCP header][HTTP headers][HTTP body]
    ↓ IP wraps it
[IP header][TCP header][HTTP headers][HTTP body]
    ↓ Ethernet wraps it
[Ethernet][IP header][TCP header][HTTP headers][HTTP body][Checksum]
    ↓ Sent on wire

Unwrapping on receive: 

Receiver removes Ethernet → IP → TCP → gets HTTP message

docs.title: Firewalls
docs.text:
Software or hardware that controls traffic based on rules.

Inbound Rules: What traffic is allowed INTO your server
Outbound Rules: What traffic is allowed OUT of your server

Example: 

Allow port 80 (HTTP) from anywhere
Allow port 443 (HTTPS) from anywhere
Allow port 3306 (MySQL) only from 10.0.0.0/8
Block everything else

docs.title: Firewall Tools on Linux
docs.text:
# Check firewall status
sudo ufw status    # On Ubuntu/Debian
sudo firewall-cmd --list-all  # On RHEL/CentOS

# Open a port
sudo ufw allow 80/tcp
sudo ufw allow 443/tcp

# Close a port
sudo ufw deny 3306/tcp

# See active connections
netstat -an
ss -an              # Modern replacement for netstat

docs.title: Connection Tracking
docs.text:
Stateful firewalls remember connections:

Outbound traffic:
Your server → External API (port 443)
    ↓
Firewall remembers this connection
    ↓
Return traffic from API → Your server is ALLOWED
(Without this, you couldn't receive responses!)

docs.title: Gateways
docs.text:
Entry/exit points for networks.

Your home network gateway = your WiFi router
In AWS, NAT Gateway = how private subnet servers reach internet

docs.title: Routing
docs.text:
How packets find their way from source to destination.

Step 1: Check routing table
        "Is destination on my local network? YES → send directly via Ethernet"
        "Is destination NOT local? NO → send to gateway/router"

Step 2: Router checks its routing table
        "I know how to reach that destination → forward"

Step 3: Repeat until destination reached

Check your routing table:

route -n     # Simple view
ip route     # Modern view

# Output example:
# default via 192.168.1.1 dev eth0     (default gateway)
# 192.168.1.0/24 dev eth0              (local network)
# 172.17.0.0/16 dev docker0            (Docker bridge)

Interpretation: 

"If destination is 192.168.1.x → use eth0 directly (local)"
"Otherwise → send to 192.168.1.1 (my router)"

docs.title: Headers
docs.text:
Metadata added by each layer.

HTTP Header example:
GET /api/users HTTP/1.1
Host: example.com
Content-Length: 42
Authorization: Bearer token123

TCP Header contains:
- Source port: 54321
- Destination port: 443
- Sequence number: 1000
- Acknowledgment number: 2000
- Flags: SYN, ACK, FIN, etc.

IP Header contains:
- Source IP: 192.168.1.100
- Destination IP: 8.8.8.8
- TTL (Time To Live): 64

docs.title: Hops
docs.text:
Each router the packet passes through = 1 hop.

# See the path from your machine to google.com
traceroute google.com

# Output:
#  1  router.home (192.168.1.1) 1ms
#  2  isp-gateway (203.0.113.1) 15ms
#  3  backbone1 (198.51.100.1) 20ms
#  4  google-router (172.217.0.1) 25ms
#  5  google.com (142.251.41.14) 25ms

Default hop limit (TTL): 64 on Linux, 128 on Windows. Each hop decrements by 1. When TTL reaches 0, packet is discarded (prevents infinite loops).

docs.title: Internet
docs.text:
Global system of interconnected networks. The "network of networks."

Your server is connected to the internet through:
ISP → Backbone → Regional routes → Local networks → Your server

docs.title: Network Interfaces
docs.text:
Virtual or physical connections to networks.

# See all interfaces
ip link show
ifconfig

# Output:
# lo: loopback (127.0.0.1)        [purely local, not on internet]
# eth0: ethernet (192.168.1.100)   [actual network connection]
# docker0: bridge (172.17.0.1)     [Docker's virtual network]
# veth1234: virtual eth            [Docker container interface]

Important: A server can have multiple interfaces, each with its own IP.

# Server with multiple IPs
ip addr show eth0

# Output:
# inet 192.168.1.100/24           (primary)
# inet 192.168.1.101/24           (secondary)
# inet 10.0.0.50/24               (on different network)

docs.title: Standard Frame Size
docs.text: Normal Ethernet frame: 1,500 bytes (MTU = Maximum Transmission Unit)

docs.title: Jumbo Frames
docs.text:
Larger frames: 9,000+ bytes for high-performance networks (data centers).

Why it matters: 

With 1,500 byte frames:
  100 MB file = 66,667 packets

With 9,000 byte frames:
  100 MB file = 11,112 packets

Fewer packets = less overhead, faster transfer
But: Requires all equipment to support jumbo frames

Check your MTU:

ip link show eth0
# Output: ... mtu 1500 ...

# Change MTU (for high-speed local networks)
sudo ip link set dev eth0 mtu 9000

When you need this: Data warehouse transfers, HPC (high-performance computing), not for typical web backends.

docs.title: Socket Pairs
docs.text:
A connection is uniquely identified by a 4-tuple (5-tuple including protocol):

(Source IP, Source Port, Destination IP, Destination Port)

Example:
(192.168.1.100, 54321, 93.184.216.34, 443)

This identifies ONE conversation between client and server

docs.title: Why This Matters
docs.text:
# Multiple connections to same server are tracked separately
netstat -an | grep :443
# Shows all connections to port 443
# Each has different source port (54321, 54322, 54323, ...)

docs.title: Maximum Connections
docs.text:
Per source IP to destination IP:port combo: 65,535 ports available
(Ports 0-65535, but 1-1023 are reserved)

So: One client IP can have ~64,000 simultaneous connections to one server port

If you have 1,000 clients: 1,000 × 64,000 = 64 million possible connections
(But servers rarely need more than 100,000 connections)

docs.title: Latency
docs.text:
Time for data to travel from A to B (or round trip RTT = round trip time).

Local network: 1 ms
Same AWS region: 1-10 ms
Different AWS region: 50-150 ms
Intercontinental: 150-300 ms

docs.title: Layers (OSI Model)
docs.text:
7 layers of networking:

Layer 7: Application (HTTP, DNS, SMTP)
Layer 6: Presentation (Encryption, compression)
Layer 5: Session (Establishing/maintaining connection)
Layer 4: Transport (TCP, UDP)
Layer 3: Network (IP routing)
Layer 2: Link/Data (Ethernet, MAC addresses)
Layer 1: Physical (Cables, signals)

Backend engineers usually care about: - Layer 4 (TCP/UDP): Connection type - Layer 3 (IP): Routing, network configuration - Layer 7 (HTTP/HTTPS): APIs, protocols

docs.title: MAC Addresses
docs.text:
Media Access Control: physical hardware address (48-bit).

Format: 00:1a:2b:3c:4d:5e
        ↑  ↑  ↑  ↑  ↑  ↑
        Vendor Unique per device

Use: Identifying devices on the same local network.

# See your MAC address
ip link show
# OR
ifconfig

# See other devices' MAC addresses
arp -a  # ARP table (IP ↔ MAC mapping)

# Output example:
# 192.168.1.1 at 00:11:22:33:44:55 [ether]

Difference from IP: 

IP address: "Where to send it" (global, routable)
MAC address: "Who to send to directly" (local, physical)

Analogy:
IP = mailing address (route through postal system)
MAC = person's name (when you're talking face-to-face)

docs.title: Multiplexing
docs.text:
Multiple conversations sharing one connection.

HTTP/1.1 Keep-Alive:
Request 1: GET /api/users
Response 1: [JSON]
Request 2: GET /api/posts
Response 2: [JSON]
[All over same TCP connection]

HTTP/2:
Multiple requests/responses simultaneously on same connection

docs.title: Networks
docs.text:
Logically grouped computers connected together.

Your home WiFi network: 192.168.1.0/24
Your office network: 10.0.0.0/8
AWS VPC: 172.31.0.0/16

docs.title: Namespaces (Linux)
docs.text:
Isolation mechanism so containers/processes have their own: - Network interfaces - IP addresses - Routing tables - Firewall rules

# See namespaces
ip netns list

# Execute command in namespace
sudo ip netns exec <namespace> ip addr show

# Docker containers use namespaces for isolation
docker inspect <container> | grep -i namespace

Why it matters: Docker containers use network namespaces so each can have its own IP address and network configuration.

docs.title: Open Systems
docs.text:
Systems that follow published standards (interoperable).

OSI model = Open Systems Interconnection

A standard model for how networking should work, enabling different vendors' equipment to talk to each other.

docs.title: OSI Recap
docs.text: Layer Name Protocol Examples What Backend Engineers Use 7 Application HTTP, HTTPS, DNS, SSH, SMTP APIs, protocols 6 Presentation TLS/SSL, JPEG, MP4 Encryption 5 Session HTTP/HTTPS sessions Connection state 4 Transport TCP, UDP Sockets, connection type 3 Network IP, ICMP, routing Addresses, routing 2 Link Ethernet, ARP, MAC Physical network, switching 1 Physical Fiber, copper, WiFi Hardware

docs.title: Ports
docs.text:
Virtual "endpoints" on a server (0-65535).

Port 0-1023: Well-known (reserved for system processes)
  - Port 80: HTTP
  - Port 443: HTTPS
  - Port 22: SSH
  - Port 3306: MySQL
  - Port 5432: PostgreSQL

Port 1024-49151: Registered (less reserved)
  - Port 3000: Node.js dev server
  - Port 5000: Flask dev server
  - Port 8000: Django dev server

Port 49152-65535: Dynamic (temporary, used by clients)

Why both source and destination ports matter:

Client connects to Server:
Client: 192.168.1.100:54321 → Server: 93.184.216.34:443
                    ↑
            Dynamic source port (assigned automatically)

Server knows to send response back to:
93.184.216.34:443 → 192.168.1.100:54321

docs.title: Protocols
docs.text:
Rules for communication.

HTTP:  Request-response, stateless, text-based
HTTPS: HTTP + encryption (TLS/SSL)
TCP:   Reliable, ordered delivery (most common)
UDP:   Fast, unreliable (video streaming, online games)
ICMP:  Diagnostic (ping, traceroute)

docs.title: QoS (Quality of Service)
docs.text:
Prioritizing certain traffic over others.

Example:
Video streaming: LOW priority (can be buffered)
VOIP/Calls: HIGH priority (must be real-time)
Database queries: MEDIUM priority

docs.title: Queues
docs.text:
Packets waiting to be sent/received.

# See queue depth
netstat -s | grep "segments retransmitted"

# If high retransmissions = network congestion

Backpressure:

When queue fills up:
1. New packets are dropped
2. Sender doesn't get acknowledgment
3. Sender retransmits
4. Network is congested
5. Latency increases

docs.title: Routing
docs.text:
How packets find their way.

# Linux routing table
route -n
ip route show

# Find path to destination
traceroute 8.8.8.8

docs.title: Routing Types
docs.text:
Direct routing: Destination is on my local network → send directly
Indirect routing: Destination is NOT local → send to gateway
Default route: "If you don't know, send to this gateway"
Static routing: Administrator sets routes manually
Dynamic routing: Routers learn routes from each other (OSPF, BGP)

docs.title: Requests (HTTP)
docs.text:
Request = Client asking server for something

HTTP Methods:
GET:    Retrieve data
POST:   Create new resource
PUT:    Update existing resource
PATCH:  Partial update
DELETE: Remove resource
HEAD:   Same as GET but no response body

docs.title: Sockets
docs.text:
Endpoint for network communication (file descriptor).

"A socket is like a telephone jack - the interface to the network"

Types: 

SOCK_STREAM:   TCP (reliable, ordered)
SOCK_DGRAM:    UDP (unreliable, fast)

Socket states: 

LISTEN:        Waiting for connections (server)
ESTABLISHED:   Connected and communicating
CLOSE_WAIT:    Waiting to close (after remote closed)
TIME_WAIT:     Waiting before fully closing (2MSL timeout)


# See all sockets
netstat -an
ss -an          # Modern alternative

# Filter to specific port
netstat -an | grep :3000

# Count connections
netstat -an | grep ESTABLISHED | wc -l

docs.title: Servers
docs.text:
Programs listening for incoming connections on a socket.

Flask/Django:
1. Bind to IP:Port (0.0.0.0:5000)
2. Listen for connections
3. Accept client connections
4. Process request
5. Send response
6. Close connection (or keep alive)

docs.title: TCP (Transmission Control Protocol)
docs.text:
Reliable, ordered delivery. Guarantees: 

- All data arrives
- In correct order
- No duplicates

TCP Connection: 

3-Way Handshake (SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK)
Client: SYN (synchronize, seq=1000)
Server: SYN-ACK (acknowledge, seq=2000, ack=1001)
Client: ACK (acknowledge, seq=1001, ack=2001)
[Connection established]

Closing: 

FIN → Acknowledge → FIN → Acknowledge
[Connection closed]

docs.title: TCP Window (Flow Control)
docs.text:
Sender says: "I can send up to 65,536 bytes before you must acknowledge"
This prevents overwhelming the receiver

docs.title: IP (Internet Protocol)
docs.text:
Addressing and routing.

IPv4: 32-bit addresses (4 billion possible)
IPv6: 128-bit addresses (340 undecillion possible)

docs.title: UDP (User Datagram Protocol)
docs.text:
Fast, unreliable delivery. No guarantees.

UDP Characteristics:
- Connectionless (no handshake)
- No flow control
- No ordering guarantee
- Lower overhead
- Suitable for real-time: video, audio, gaming

UDP Packet: 

[UDP Header: 8 bytes]
[Data: up to 65,527 bytes]

docs.title: When to Use
docs.text:
TCP: Email, file transfer, web pages (HTTPS)
     Correctness more important than speed

UDP: Video streaming, online games, VoIP
     Speed more important than perfection
     Missing 1 frame = no big deal

docs.title: Virtual Networks
docs.text:
Networks that exist in software, not physical hardware.

Docker bridge network (docker0):
- Virtual network interface
- Virtual switching
- All containers on same "network" can talk directly

docs.title: VLANs (Virtual LANs)
docs.text:
Logical grouping of devices on physical network.

Physical: One Ethernet switch
Virtual: Multiple logical networks on that switch

VLAN 100: Finance (IP range 10.1.x.x)
VLAN 200: Engineering (IP range 10.2.x.x)
VLAN 300: HR (IP range 10.3.x.x)

Even on same switch, VLANs can't talk without a router

Not typically needed for web backends, but good to know.

docs.title: Wireshark
docs.text:
Network packet analyzer/sniffer. Captures and displays packets.

# Capture on eth0 interface
sudo wireshark -i eth0 &

# Or command-line (tcpdump):
sudo tcpdump -i eth0 -w capture.pcap

# Filter for HTTP
sudo tcpdump -i eth0 'port 80'

# Filter for HTTPS
sudo tcpdump -i eth0 'port 443'

# Filter for specific IP
sudo tcpdump -i eth0 'host 192.168.1.100'

Uses: 

- Debugging network issues
- Learning how protocols work
- Troubleshooting slow connections
- Security analysis

docs.title: Web (HTTP/HTTPS)
docs.text:
The primary protocol for backend engineers.

HTTP: Plain text (insecure)
HTTPS: HTTP + TLS encryption (secure)

HTTP/1.0: One request per connection
HTTP/1.1: Keep-alive, pipelining
HTTP/2: Multiplexing, compression, push
HTTP/3: Based on UDP instead of TCP

docs.title: X.509
docs.text:
Standard format for public key certificates (encryption/identity).

Certificate contains: 

- Public key
- Subject (who owns this cert)
- Issuer (who signed it)
- Validity dates
- Digital signature

How HTTPS works: 

1. Client connects to server (port 443)
2. Server sends X.509 certificate
3. Client verifies certificate is trusted and valid
4. Client and server establish encrypted connection (TLS)
5. Data is encrypted: only client and server can read


# View certificate details
openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -showcerts

# Check certificate expiration
openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 | \
openssl x509 -noout -dates

docs.title: Protocol Standards
docs.text:
The internet is built on open standards and RFCs (Requests for Comments).

TCP/IP: RFC 793 (TCP), RFC 791 (IP)
HTTP/1.1: RFC 7230-7237
HTTPS/TLS: RFC 5246 (TLS 1.2), RFC 8446 (TLS 1.3)
DNS: RFC 1035

Why it matters: 

Different vendors' equipment can interoperate because they follow same standards
You can predict how networks behave because behavior is standardized

docs.title: REST (Representational State Transfer)
docs.text:
Standard way to design web APIs.

Resource = "thing" (users, posts, comments)
Representation = "how it looks" (JSON, XML)
State Transfer = "changing the thing"

GET /users → List all users
POST /users → Create new user
GET /users/123 → Get user 123
PUT /users/123 → Update user 123
DELETE /users/123 → Delete user 123

docs.title: Zero-Knowledge
docs.text:
Security concept: Prove something without revealing the information.

Blockchain example:
- Prove you own Bitcoin without revealing your private key
- Prove you're over 18 without revealing your exact age

docs.title: Basic Security Concepts
docs.text:
Authentication: "Who are you?" 

Username/password
Certificate
Token (JWT)
OAuth

Authorization: "What are you allowed to do?" 

User can only access their own data
Admin can access everything
Guest can only view public data

Encryption: "Keep secrets secret" 

TLS/SSL: Encrypts data in transit
Password hashing: Doesn't store plaintext passwords

Examples for backends:

# Authentication: verify user
user = authenticate_user(username, password)

# Authorization: check permissions
if not user.can_delete_other_users():
    return 403 Forbidden

# Delete user
delete_user(target_user_id)

docs.title: Scenario: A User Loads a Website
docs.text:
User types: https://example.com/products

1. DNS (D): Browser resolves example.com → 93.184.216.34
2. IP/Routing (A, G, R): Browser finds route to 93.184.216.34
3. Interfaces (I): Uses eth0 to connect
4. TCP (T): Establishes TCP connection (3-way handshake)
5. TLS/X.509 (X): Verifies server certificate
6. Ports (P): Connects to port 443 (HTTPS)
7. HTTP Request (W): Sends GET request
8. Headers (H): Headers wrapped by each layer
9. Hops (H): Request travels through routers
10. Latency (L): Depending on distance
11. Sockets (S): Server's socket receives data
12. Server Processing: Generates response
13. Response: Travels back through layers 9-1
14. Browser displays: HTML, CSS, JS loads
15. Browser makes more requests: CSS, JavaScript, images
16. Multiplexing (M): HTTP/2 sends all simultaneously
17. Connection closes: TCP teardown (FIN, ACK)

docs.title: Lab: Check Your Network
docs.text:
# 1. See your IP
ip addr show

# 2. See your gateway
route -n

# 3. Test connectivity
ping 8.8.8.8

# 4. See what's listening
netstat -an | grep LISTEN

# 5. See active connections
netstat -an | grep ESTABLISHED

# 6. Resolve DNS
nslookup example.com

# 7. Trace route to destination
traceroute google.com

# 8. Check certificate
openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -showcerts

# 9. Capture packets
sudo tcpdump -i eth0 -n 'port 80'

# 10. List interfaces
ip link show

docs.title: Can You Explain?
docs.text:
• What's an IP address and why we have both IPv4 and IPv6
  • Difference between TCP and UDP
  • How DNS works (all 5 steps)
  • What a port is and why we need them
  • How a TCP connection is established
  • What layers exist in the OSI model
  • How HTTPS/TLS works at high level
  • What a socket is and why servers use them
  • How routing tables work
  • Why firewalls matter and how they work

docs.title: Practical Skills
docs.text:
• Can run ip addr show and explain output
  • Can run netstat -an and identify connection states
  • Can use ping, traceroute, dig for debugging
  • Can read a routing table
  • Can check what's listening on your system
  • Can use tcpdump to see packets on wire
  • Can check TLS certificate details
  • Can understand CIDR notation (10.0.0.0/8)

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text:
You now have the foundation! Ready to dive deeper?

→ Module 1: Networking Fundamentals - Deep dive into TCP/IP, sockets, and client-server model with real backend examples.

docs.title: Key Acronyms
docs.text: Acronym Meaning Relevance IP Internet Protocol Addressing TCP Transmission Control Protocol Reliable connections UDP User Datagram Protocol Fast, unreliable DNS Domain Name System Name resolution TLS Transport Layer Security Encryption SSL Secure Sockets Layer Older encryption (now TLS) HTTP HyperText Transfer Protocol Web HTTPS HTTP Secure Web + encryption CIDR Classless Inter-Domain Routing IP range notation QoS Quality of Service Priority MTU Maximum Transmission Unit Frame size TTL Time To Live Hop count MAC Media Access Control Physical address ARP Address Resolution Protocol IP to MAC mapping ICMP Internet Control Message Protocol Ping, traceroute OSI Open Systems Interconnection 7-layer model VPC Virtual Private Cloud AWS network VLAN Virtual LAN Logical network groups RFC Request for Comments Standard specifications JWT JSON Web Token Authentication OAuth Open Authorization Delegated authentication

docs.title: Port Reference
docs.text:
80     HTTP
443    HTTPS
22     SSH
3306   MySQL
5432   PostgreSQL
6379   Redis
5672   RabbitMQ
27017  MongoDB
3000   Node.js (dev)
5000   Flask/Django (dev)
8000   Django (alt)
8080   Common alternate HTTP

Completed: You've covered networking A-to-Z! You now have the language and concepts to understand the deeper modules. Don't worry if you didn't absorb everything—we'll revisit these concepts with practical examples in Module 1.

Time estimate: 2-3 hours to read, understand, and practice these basics.

docs.title: Networking From Scratch: An Engineer's Guide for Absolute Beginners
docs.text:
Duration: 3–4 hours | Level: Complete Beginner | Prerequisites: None

What This Module Is: A conversational, conceptual guide to networking fundamentals. If someone asks you "What is networking?", this module will give you the answer from first principles. No hand-waving, no jargon left unexplained. Written as if an experienced engineer is explaining this to you over coffee.

docs.title: 0.1 Why You Need to Understand Networking
docs.text:
Let me start with a real scenario:

Your Flask API is deployed to the cloud. A user in Tokyo tries to access it. Their browser sends a request. Your API processes it. But the response never reaches them.

What happened? The user would say "the internet is broken." You, as a backend engineer, need to know:

  • Did the request even arrive at your server?
  • Is your server trying to send a response?
  • Is something blocking the response halfway?
  • Is it a firewall rule? A DNS problem? A routing issue?

This is why networking matters. Without understanding how data actually moves from one computer to another, you're debugging blind.

docs.title: 0.2 The Fundamental Question: How Do Two Computers Talk?
docs.text:
Imagine you and I are in different buildings. I want to send you a message. Here's what has to happen:

  1. I write the message ("Hello")
  2. I put it in an envelope (address it to you)
  3. I put the envelope in the mail system (physical delivery)
  4. The mail system routes it through a network of postal workers and offices
  5. It arrives at your building
  6. You check your mailbox and read it

Computer networking is exactly this, but with data instead of envelopes.

docs.title: The Key Layers (Simplified)
docs.text:
When two computers communicate, we can think of it in layers:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ LAYER 4: Message Layer (What gets delivered?)                │
│ ├─ "Hello" (the actual data)                                │
│ └─ Port number (like apartment number in a building)        │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ LAYER 3: Route Layer (How does it find the destination?)     │
│ ├─ Source IP: 192.168.1.5 (my address)                      │
│ └─ Destination IP: 203.0.113.42 (your address)              │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ LAYER 2: Physical Layer (What cable/radio does it travel?)   │
│ ├─ Source MAC: aa:bb:cc:dd:ee:ff (my network card)          │
│ └─ Destination MAC: 11:22:33:44:55:66 (next hop)            │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ LAYER 1: Hardware (Actual wires, cables, radio waves)        │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

You'll hear these called the OSI Model or the TCP/IP Model. Don't memorize it. Just know: data travels in layers, each one adding a wrapper.

docs.title: 0.3 Concept 1: IP Addresses (How Computers Find Each Other)
The Problem: Computers Need Names Too
docs.text: If I want to send you a letter, I need your address. Computers need addresses too. That's what IP addresses are.

docs.title: What Is an IP Address?
docs.text:
An IP address is a unique label for a computer on a network. Like a street address.

Your home address:  123 Main Street, New York, NY 10001
Your IP address:    192.168.1.5
My IP address:      192.168.1.10

docs.title: IPv4: The Common Format
docs.text:
Most IPs you'll see look like this:

192.168.1.5
  ↑   ↑  ↑  ↑
  |   |  |  └── These 4 numbers are each 0-255
  |   |  |
  └───┴──┘

Each part can be a number from 0 to 255. Why? Because computers think in bits (0 or 1). Eight bits can represent 256 different numbers (0-255). Four groups of 8 bits = 32 bits total.

docs.title: Public vs. Private IP Addresses
docs.text:
Public IP: Your address on the actual internet. Anyone with routing can reach it. - Example: 8.8.8.8 (Google's DNS server) - Your home/office might have one for reaching the internet

Private IP: Only works within your local network. The internet ignores these. - Examples: 192.168.1.5, 10.0.0.50, 172.16.5.200 - Your laptop, phone, and server on the office network likely have these

docs.title: Why This Matters
docs.text: When your Flask API is on a server: - The server has a public IP (so users from the internet can reach it) - Inside the server, there might be a database with a private IP (only the server can reach it)

docs.title: 0.4 Concept 2: Ports (Which Service Do You Want?)
The Problem: One Computer Might Run Many Services
docs.text:
Your server might be running: - A web server on 1 address (serving HTTP) - A database on 1 address (storing data) - A cache server on 1 address (speeding things up)

They all have the same IP address. So how does the computer know which service you want?

docs.title: The Solution: Ports
docs.text:
A port is a number that identifies which service/application you want to talk to.

Think of it like this:

IP Address = The Building
Port       = The Office/Apartment Inside the Building

IP: 192.168.1.5, Port: 80     = The web server
IP: 192.168.1.5, Port: 5432   = The database
IP: 192.168.1.5, Port: 6379   = The cache server

docs.title: Common Ports (Just For Reference)
docs.text:
When you see these, you'll know what service to expect:

Port 20, 21   = FTP (file transfer)
Port 22       = SSH (remote login)
Port 80       = HTTP (web, unencrypted)
Port 443      = HTTPS (web, encrypted)
Port 3306     = MySQL (database)
Port 5432     = PostgreSQL (database)
Port 6379     = Redis (cache)
Port 8080     = Often a secondary web service

You don't need to memorize these. Just know: ports are numbers, and different services listen on different ports.

docs.title: How It All Works Together
docs.text:
User's browser makes a request:
   → 203.0.113.42:443

This means: "Hey computer at IP 203.0.113.42, 
send my request to the service listening on port 443 (HTTPS)"

The computer receives it:
   "Oh, someone is asking for port 443. That's the web server. 
    Let me pass this request to the web server application."

docs.title: The Problem: How Do Computers Understand Each Other?
docs.text:
When you send data to another computer, just sending random bytes is useless. The receiving computer doesn't understand what it means.

It's like mailing a letter in a language the recipient doesn't speak. Useless.

docs.title: The Solution: Protocols
docs.text:
A protocol is a standard set of rules for how computers should format and exchange data.

Think of it as a language that both computers understand.

docs.title: TCP: The Reliable Messenger
docs.text:
TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) is like sending a registered letter.

  • You send data, and the receiving computer confirms: "Yes, I got it."
  • If something gets lost, it's retransmitted.
  • Data arrives in the correct order.
  • Slow but reliable.

When you use TCP: - Browsing websites (HTTP/HTTPS) - Sending emails (SMTP) - Talking to databases - Anything where losing data would be bad

Your computer → [Package with label "PART 1"] → Remote computer
                "Got it!" ← [Acknowledgment]
Your computer → [Package with label "PART 2"] → Remote computer
                "Got it!" ← [Acknowledgment]

docs.title: UDP: The Fast Messenger
docs.text:
UDP (User Datagram Protocol) is like shouting across a crowded room.

  • You send data and don't wait for confirmation.
  • If something gets lost, oh well.
  • Data might arrive out of order.
  • Fast but unreliable.

When you use UDP: - Video streaming (losing one frame is okay) - Online gaming (speed matters more than perfection) - DNS lookups (if it fails, try again) - Real-time voice (a dropped packet won't be noticed)

Your computer → [Shout 1] → Remote computer
Your computer → [Shout 2] → Remote computer
(No confirmation needed. Maybe it heard both, maybe one got lost.)

docs.title: HTTP/HTTPS: The Web Protocol
docs.text:
HTTP (HyperText Transfer Protocol) sits on top of TCP.

It's the protocol that web browsers and web servers use. It defines: - How to ask for a web page ("GET /index.html") - How to send form data ("POST this data") - How to respond ("Here's your page" or "Page not found")

HTTPS is HTTP encrypted. Everything you send is scrambled.

docs.title: 0.6 Concept 4: DNS (How Do Humans Remember Addresses?)
The Problem: Humans Can't Remember "203.0.113.42"
docs.text: You probably visit Google daily. The IP address for google.com changes. And you certainly don't remember 8.8.8.8; you remember google.com.

docs.title: The Solution: DNS
docs.text:
DNS (Domain Name System) is like a phone book for the internet.

When you type "google.com" in your browser:

1. Browser: "What's the IP for google.com?"
2. DNS Server (phone book): "That's 172.217.16.206"
3. Browser: "Thanks! Let me connect to 172.217.16.206"

docs.title: Why This Matters
docs.text:
• Domains are memorable. example.com beats 203.0.113.42
  • IPs can change. If your server moves to a new IP, you just update DNS. Users still type the same domain.
  • You might cache DNS. Repeated requests for the same domain are answered instantly from cache.

docs.title: 0.7 Concept 5: Routing (How Data Finds Its Way)
The Problem: There Are Billions of Computers
docs.text: Your computer doesn't have a direct cable to every other computer on the internet. So how does your data reach its destination?

docs.title: The Solution: Routing
docs.text:
Routing is hop-by-hop delivery, like mail being passed between post offices.

Your Computer (192.168.1.5)
        ↓
   Your Router (192.168.1.1)
   "I need to send this to 203.0.113.42"
        ↓
   ISP's Gateway
   "I need to send this west to the next network"
        ↓
   Regional Network
   "I need to send this to another region"
        ↓
   ...multiple hops...
        ↓
   Destination Network
   "Use this local router to find 203.0.113.42"
        ↓
   Target Computer (203.0.113.42)

docs.title: The Routing Table
docs.text:
Every computer has a routing table that says:

"If you want to reach this range of IPs, send it through that gateway."

For example:
- 192.168.1.0/24         → Use local network (no gateway needed)
- 10.0.0.0/8             → Send through gateway 192.168.1.1
- 8.8.8.8 (and everything else) → Send through gateway 192.168.1.1 (default)

Your computer checks the routing table to decide: "Who should I pass this packet to next?"

docs.title: Why This Matters
docs.text:
• Networks are hierarchical. Not flat. Data hops from router to router.
  • Routing can break. If a router is misconfigured, packets get lost.
  • You might route traffic differently. Internal traffic (to your database) might use one route. Internet traffic uses another.

docs.title: The Problem: Not All Traffic Should Be Allowed
docs.text: Imagine your server. Someone tries to connect to a port that shouldn't be open. They're trying to exploit your system.

docs.title: The Solution: Firewalls
docs.text:
A firewall is a set of rules that says "allow this traffic, block that traffic."

Think of it like a bouncer at a club:

Incoming Request: "I want to connect to 203.0.113.42:5432"
Firewall: "Are you on the whitelist? No? BLOCKED."

Incoming Request: "I want to connect to 203.0.113.42:443"
Firewall: "Yes, that's HTTPS. That's allowed. Go in."

docs.title: Common Firewall Rules
docs.text:
✅ Allow incoming on port 443 (HTTPS)
✅ Allow incoming on port 80 (HTTP)
❌ Block incoming on port 5432 (PostgreSQL)
✅ Allow outgoing to 8.8.8.8 (DNS)
❌ Block outgoing to suspicious IPs

docs.title: The Problem: How Do Computers Know If a Conversation Is Happening?
docs.text: If your computer sends data to another computer, how does the receiving computer know: - Is this the start of a conversation or a random packet? - Should I respond to this? - Is this legitimate?

docs.title: The Solution: Connections
docs.text: A connection is an established communication session between two computers.

docs.title: TCP Connections: The Handshake
docs.text:
TCP connections follow a famous ritual called the Three-Way Handshake:

Client (You)               Server (Remote)

     │                            │
     │───── SYN (let's talk) ────→│
     │                            │
     │←── SYN-ACK (ok, let's) ───│
     │                            │
     │─── ACK (confirmed) ────────→│
     │                            │
     └──── Connection Open ───────┘

Now data can flow back and forth.

docs.title: UDP: No Handshake
docs.text:
UDP doesn't have a connection. It's like yelling into the void:

Client (You)               Server (Remote)

     │                            │
     │─── Here's some data ──────→│
     │                            │
     │─── Here's more data ──────→│
     │                            │
(No confirmation. The server might receive it or not.)

docs.title: Why This Matters
docs.text:
• TCP is reliable but slower (needs confirmation for each packet)
  • UDP is fast but unreliable (no confirmation)
  • Your web browser uses TCP (you want the data to arrive correctly)
  • Video streaming often uses UDP (speed matters more than perfection)

docs.title: 0.10 Concept 8: Bandwidth vs. Latency (What "Fast" Really Means)
Bandwidth: The Width of the Pipe
docs.text:
Bandwidth is the maximum amount of data that can flow per second.

Low bandwidth:    1 Mbps   (enough for email)
Medium bandwidth: 100 Mbps (good for a home network)
High bandwidth:   10 Gbps  (for data centers)

docs.title: Latency: The Speed of the Pipe
docs.text:
Latency is the time it takes for one packet to travel from A to B.

Low latency:   1 ms  (very fast, like talking to a local server)
Medium latency: 50 ms (acceptable for most web apps)
High latency:  200 ms (feels slow, like a video call with lag)

docs.title: The Difference (Critical!)
docs.text:
Bandwidth = How much water flows per second
Latency   = How fast the water travels

A fire hose (high bandwidth) shooting water slow-motion (high latency) 
is less useful than a thin pipe with fast water pressure (low latency).

docs.title: Why This Matters
docs.text:
• Your API might be able to process 1000 requests/second (bandwidth)
  • But if each request takes 200ms to reach you (latency), users feel it's slow
  • A server in Tokyo accessing a database in New York has high latency (~150ms round-trip) even on a fast connection

docs.title: How Data Actually Travels
docs.text:
Your message "Hello" doesn't travel as one big blob. It's broken into small pieces called packets.

Application: "Hello, world! This is a long message."
             ↓
             (break it into pieces)
             ↓
Packet 1: [Packet 1 of 3, containing "Hello,"]
Packet 2: [Packet 2 of 3, containing "world!"]
Packet 3: [Packet 3 of 3, containing "This is..."]

Each packet travels independently and is reassembled at the destination.

docs.title: Packet Structure (Simplified)
docs.text:
Each packet has layers:

┌─────────────────────────────────┐
│ Your actual data (e.g., "Hello")│
├─────────────────────────────────┤
│ TCP header:                      │
│ ├─ Source port: 54321           │
│ ├─ Destination port: 443        │
│ └─ Other info                   │
├─────────────────────────────────┤
│ IP header:                       │
│ ├─ Source IP: 192.168.1.5       │
│ ├─ Destination IP: 203.0.113.42 │
│ └─ Other info                   │
├─────────────────────────────────┤
│ Ethernet header:                 │
│ ├─ Source MAC: aa:bb:cc:...     │
│ ├─ Destination MAC: 11:22:33... │
│ └─ Other info                   │
└─────────────────────────────────┘

Each layer adds its own header. It's like a letter inside an envelope inside a bigger envelope.

docs.title: Why Small Packets?
docs.text: Networks aren't perfect. If you send 1 GB in one chunk and 1 bit gets corrupted, you lose the whole thing. Split into 1000 packets, and you only resend the 1 packet that got corrupted.

docs.title: 0.12 Concept 10: NAT (Network Address Translation – Your Secret Translator)
The Problem: You Have a Private IP, But the Internet Wants a Public IP
docs.text: Your laptop has IP 192.168.1.5 (private). You ask Google for something. Google responds to 192.168.1.5. But that's private! The internet doesn't know how to reach it.

docs.title: The Solution: NAT
docs.text:
NAT (Network Address Translation) translates between private and public IPs.

Your router does this automatically:

Your Laptop (192.168.1.5): "Google, what's the weather?"
         ↓
Your Router: "Wait, I'll translate this."
         ↓
Translation: Change source IP from 192.168.1.5 to YOUR_PUBLIC_IP
         ↓
Google receives request from YOUR_PUBLIC_IP
         ↓
Google responds to YOUR_PUBLIC_IP
         ↓
Your Router: "This is for my laptop. Let me translate back."
         ↓
Translation: Change destination from YOUR_PUBLIC_IP to 192.168.1.5
         ↓
Your Laptop receives the response

docs.title: Why This Matters
docs.text:
• Your private IP Never leaves your network
  • The internet only sees your router's public IP
  • Millions of computers can hide behind one public IP using NAT
  • This is why the world hasn't run out of IP addresses yet

docs.title: 0.13 Real-World Scenario: Putting It All Together
docs.text:
Let's trace what happens when you visit example.com:

step 1: Your Browser
        "I need to visit example.com"

step 2: DNS (Concept 4)
        Browser: "What's the IP for example.com?"
        DNS: "That's 93.184.216.34"

Step 3: TCP Handshake (Concept 7)
        Your computer: "Can I connect to 93.184.216.34:443?"
        Web server: "Yes, here's my response"
        Your computer: "Great, connection confirmed"

Step 4: HTTP Request (Concept 3)
        Your browser: "GET /index.html HTTP/1.1"

Step 5: Routing (Concept 5)
        Your packet travels: local router → ISP → backbone network → server's router → server

Step 6: Firewall (Concept 6)
        Server's firewall: "Port 443? Yep, that's allowed."

Step 7: Web Server
        Server: "Here's your page"

Step 8: Response Routing (Concept 5 again)
        Response travels back: server → router → backbone → ISP → your router → your computer

step 9: Your Browser
        Renders the HTML

Each step involves multiple concepts working together.

docs.title: 0.14 Common Networking Problems (And What They Mean)
"Connection Refused"
docs.text:
Your computer tried to connect, but nothing was listening on that port.
Why: Service isn't running, or firewall is blocking it.

docs.title: "Connection Timed Out"
docs.text:
Your computer tried to connect, but got no response within the timeout.
Why: Firewall is silently dropping packets, or the route is broken.

docs.title: "DNS Resolution Failed"
docs.text:
The domain name couldn't be translated to an IP.
Why: The DNS server is down, or the domain doesn't exist.

docs.title: "Packet Loss"
docs.text:
Some packets are being dropped along the way.
Why: Network congestion, bad hardware, or interference.

docs.title: "Slow Connection"
docs.text:
Could be low bandwidth (slow pipe) or high latency (far away).
Why: Internet congestion, geographic distance, or bottleneck in infrastructure.

docs.title: The 5 Mental Models to Remember
docs.text:
