Characteristics: - Multiple components working together - Organized into layers (UI, logic, data) - Persistent data storage - Used by multiple users - Meant to evolve and scale

docs.title: Separation of Concerns
docs.text: The biggest principle in architecture: each piece should have ONE job.

docs.title: Example: Without Separation
docs.text:
# Bad: one function does everything
def process_order(order_id):
    # Get from database
    connection = connect_to_database()
    cursor = connection.cursor()
    cursor.execute(f"SELECT * FROM orders WHERE id = {order_id}")
    order = cursor.fetchone()
    connection.close()

    # Calculate total
    subtotal = order["price"] * order["quantity"]
    tax = subtotal * 0.08
    total = subtotal + tax

    # Save to database
    connection = connect_to_database()
    cursor = connection.cursor()
    cursor.execute(f"UPDATE orders SET total = {total} WHERE id = {order_id}")
    connection.commit()
    connection.close()

    # Send email
    email_service = EmailService()
    email_service.send(order["customer_email"], 
                      f"Order total: ${total}")

    # Log transaction
    log_file = open("transactions.log", "a")
    log_file.write(f"Order {order_id}: {total}\n")
    log_file.close()

    return total

Problems: - Hard to test (needs real database, email service, file system) - Hard to change (touching one part breaks others) - Hard to read (too much happening) - Can't reuse pieces

docs.title: Example: With Separation
docs.text:
# Good: separate concerns into different functions

def process_order(order_id):
"""Main logic: coordinate other pieces"""
    order = get_order(order_id)
    total = calculate_order_total(order)
    save_order_total(order_id, total)
    notify_customer(order, total)
    log_transaction(order_id, total)
    return total

def get_order(order_id):
"""Database concern: fetch data"""
    # Only deals with database
    pass

def calculate_order_total(order):
"""Business logic concern: calculate"""
    # Only does math
    subtotal = order["price"] * order["quantity"]
    tax = subtotal * 0.08
    return subtotal + tax

def save_order_total(order_id, total):
"""Database concern: persist data"""
    # Only writes to database
    pass

def notify_customer(order, total):
"""Communication concern: send email"""
    # Only sends email
    pass

def log_transaction(order_id, total):
"""Logging concern: record event"""
    # Only writes to log
    pass

Benefits: - Easy to test each piece independently - Easy to change (modify one concern without affecting others) - Easy to read (each function is small and focused) - Easy to reuse (calculate_order_total can be used anywhere)

docs.title: Layers in Architecture
docs.text: Real applications are organized into layers. Think of a sandwich: each layer has a specific job.

docs.title: Presentation Layer (UI)
docs.text:
• What users interact with
  • Displays information
  • Captures user input
  • Doesn't contain business logic
# Simple example: command-line UI
def show_menu():
    print("=== Sales System ===")
    print("1. Add Sale")
    print("2. View Total Sales")
    print("3. Exit")

def get_user_choice():
    choice = input("Choose option: ")
    return choice

docs.title: Business Logic Layer
docs.text:
• The rules of your system
  • Calculations, decisions, workflows
  • Doesn't know about UI or database
  • Reusable from anywhere
def calculate_sales_total(sales_list):
"""Business rule: sum all sales"""
    return sum(sale["amount"] for sale in sales_list)

def apply_discount(amount, discount_percent):
"""Business rule: calculate discount"""
    if discount_percent < 0 or discount_percent > 100:
        raise ValueError("Invalid discount")
    return amount * (1 - discount_percent / 100)

docs.title: Data Layer
docs.text:
• Reads and writes data
  • Talks to database
  • Doesn't contain business logic
  • Doesn't know about UI
def get_all_sales():
"""Data access: fetch from database"""
    connection = connect_to_database()
    cursor = connection.cursor()
    cursor.execute("SELECT * FROM sales")
    data = cursor.fetchall()
    connection.close()
    return data

def save_sale(sale):
"""Data access: write to database"""
    connection = connect_to_database()
    cursor = connection.cursor()
    cursor.execute("INSERT INTO sales VALUES (?)", (sale,))
    connection.commit()
    connection.close()

docs.title: How Layers Work Together
docs.text:
User Input
    ↓
Presentation Layer (UI): "Get user input"
    ↓
Business Logic Layer: "Apply business rules"
    ↓
Data Layer: "Read/write from database"
    ↓
Database
    ↓
Data Layer: "Return data"
    ↓
Business Logic Layer: "Process data"
    ↓
Presentation Layer: "Display to user"
    ↓
User sees output

docs.title: 1. MVC (Model-View-Controller)
docs.text:
A widely-used pattern that separates presentation, logic, and data.

Model = Data and business logic 

class User:
    def __init__(self, name, email):
        self.name = name
        self.email = email

    def validate_email(self):
        return "@" in self.email

View = What the user sees 

def display_user(user):
    print(f"Name: {user.name}")
    print(f"Email: {user.email}")

Controller = Handles user input and coordinates 

def create_user_workflow():
    # Get input from user
    name = input("Enter name: ")
    email = input("Enter email: ")

    # Create model
    user = User(name, email)

    # Validate
    if not user.validate_email():
        print("Invalid email")
        return

    # Save
    save_to_database(user)

    # Display
    display_user(user)

docs.title: 2. Client-Server Model
docs.text:
Two separate pieces: client (requests) and server (provides).

Client (Browser/App)
    ↓
Request: "Get user #5"
    ↓
Server (Web Server)
    ↓
Database: Get user #5
    ↓
Response: User data
    ↓
Client displays data

Why separate: - Client can be web, mobile, desktop - Server can be upgraded without changing clients - Multiple clients can use same server - Each can scale independently

docs.title: 3. Microservices
docs.text:
Instead of one big application, split into small, focused services.

Monolith (one big application):
┌─────────────────────┐
│ User Service        │
│ Product Service     │
│ Order Service       │
│ Payment Service     │
│ Shared Database     │
└─────────────────────┘

Microservices (small focused apps):
┌──────────────┐  ┌──────────────┐  ┌──────────────┐  ┌──────────────┐
│ User Service │  │ Product Svc  │  │ Order Svc    │  │ Payment Svc  │
│ Own DB       │  │ Own DB       │  │ Own DB       │  │ Own DB       │
└──────────────┘  └──────────────┘  └──────────────┘  └──────────────┘
      ↓                   ↓                 ↓                 ↓
    API Calls / Message Queue / Direct Communication

docs.title: APIs: How Pieces Talk
docs.text: An API (Application Programming Interface) is a contract for communication between pieces of code or systems.

docs.title: Internal API - How your code talks to itself
docs.text:
# API: "Here's how to use the sales system"

def get_total_sales(date_from, date_to):
"""
    Get total sales in date range

    Args:
        date_from: Start date (YYYY-MM-DD)
        date_to: End date (YYYY-MM-DD)

    Returns:
        Float: total sales amount

    Raises:
        ValueError: if dates are invalid
    """
    # Implementation
    pass

# How to use it:
total = get_total_sales("2024-01-01", "2024-01-31")
print(f"Total: ${total}")

docs.title: External API - How other systems talk to yours
docs.text:
# Your application provides a web API
# Other applications can call it over HTTP

# Request: GET /api/sales?from=2024-01-01&to=2024-01-31
# Response: {"total": 15000.00, "count": 42}

docs.title: API Contract
docs.text:
An API is a promise: - "I'll accept these inputs" - "I'll return data in this format" - "If something goes wrong, I'll return this error"

Breaking the contract breaks other code that depends on you.

# Original API
def get_user_by_id(user_id):
    return {"name": "Alice", "email": "alice@example.com"}

# WRONG: Changed what we return
def get_user_by_id(user_id):
    return "Alice"  # Now it's a string, not a dict!

# Code that uses this breaks:
user = get_user_by_id(5)
print(user["email"])  # Error! Can't index a string

docs.title: DRY (Don't Repeat Yourself)
docs.text:
Write code once, reuse it everywhere.

# Bad: repeated code
def format_user_name(first, last):
    return f"{first[0].upper()}{first[1:].lower()} {last[0].upper()}{last[1:].lower()}"

def format_product_name(first, last):
    return f"{first[0].upper()}{first[1:].lower()} {last[0].upper()}{last[1:].lower()}"

# Good: one function, reused
def format_name(first, last):
    return f"{first[0].upper()}{first[1:].lower()} {last[0].upper()}{last[1:].lower()}"

user_name = format_name(user_first, user_last)
product_name = format_name(product_first, product_last)

docs.title: SOLID Principles (Advanced, introduced here)
docs.text:
Single Responsibility - One class, one reason to change 

# Bad: User class does too much
class User:
    def load_from_database(self): pass
    def save_to_database(self): pass
    def send_email(self): pass
    def validate_email(self): pass

# Good: separate classes
class User:
    def __init__(self, name, email): pass

class UserRepository:  # Handles data
    def load(self, user_id): pass
    def save(self, user): pass

class EmailService:  # Handles email
    def send(self, email): pass

class UserValidator:  # Handles validation
    def validate_email(self, email): pass

Open/Closed - Open for extension, closed for modification 

# Create a plugin system: easy to add new features without changing existing code
class PaymentProcessor:
    def process(self, payment):
        pass

class CreditCardProcessor(PaymentProcessor):
    def process(self, payment):
        # Process credit card
        pass

class PayPalProcessor(PaymentProcessor):
    def process(self, payment):
        # Process PayPal
        pass

# Add new payment type? Just create a new class, don't modify existing code

docs.title: Exercise 1: Identify Layers
docs.text: Look at a simple application you use (like an email client, note app, etc.). Identify: 1. Presentation layer (what you see) 2. Business logic (what happens) 3. Data layer (where information is stored)

docs.title: Exercise 2: Refactor Code
docs.text:
Take this script and organize it into layers: 

# Current: everything mixed together
import json

data = json.load(open("users.json"))
for user in data:
    if user["age"] >= 18:
        print(f"Email: {user['email']}")
        print(f"Status: Active")

Your task: 1. Separate data loading 2. Separate business logic (age check) 3. Separate display

docs.title: Exercise 3: Design an API
docs.text: Design an API for a "student grade tracker": 1. What inputs does it need? 2. What does it return? 3. What errors might occur?

docs.title: Exercise 4: Separation of Concerns
docs.text:
Identify concerns in this code and separate them: 

def process_student_grades(csv_filename):
    # Read file
    import csv
    with open(csv_filename) as f:
        reader = csv.DictReader(f)
        students = list(reader)

    # Calculate averages
    for student in students:
        total = sum(float(g) for g in student["grades"].split(","))
        average = total / len(student["grades"].split(","))
        student["average"] = average

    # Save to database
    import sqlite3
    conn = sqlite3.connect("grades.db")
    cursor = conn.cursor()
    for student in students:
        cursor.execute(f"INSERT INTO students VALUES ('{student['name']}', {student['average']})")
    conn.commit()
    conn.close()

    # Print report
    print("=== Grade Report ===")
    for student in students:
        print(f"{student['name']}: {student['average']:.2f}")

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
✅ Real software is organized, not just written

✅ Scripts are simple; programs are organized; applications are complex systems

✅ Separation of concerns makes code manageable

✅ Layers separate presentation, logic, and data

✅ Patterns like MVC and client-server solve common problems

✅ APIs are contracts for communication

✅ Good design makes code easy to change

docs.title: What's Next?
docs.text:
Now you understand how software is structured. Let's learn how to think like an engineer making these decisions.

→ Module 4: Thinking Like an Engineer

docs.title: Module 4: Thinking Like an Engineer
docs.text:
Writing code that works is just the starting point. Engineers write code that: - Other people understand - Can be changed safely - Runs efficiently - Scales when needed

This is where craft meets engineering. This is where you move from "making it work" to "making it right."

docs.title: Code Is Communication
docs.text:
Your code will be read far more than it will be written.

You might spend: - 15 minutes writing a function - 6 months reading and modifying it

Most of your code's audience is humans, not machines.

docs.title: Why Code Readability Matters
docs.text:
# Hard to read (clever, but confusing)
result = [x*2 for x in numbers if x%2==0]

# Easy to read (clear intent)
even_numbers = [x for x in numbers if x % 2 == 0]
result = [x * 2 for x in even_numbers]

# Even better (explicit steps)
even_numbers = [num for num in numbers if num % 2 == 0]
doubled = [num * 2 for num in even_numbers]

The second and third versions are longer, but a human can understand them in 3 seconds. The first version requires thinking.

docs.title: Naming: The Most Important Skill
docs.text: Good naming is the most powerful tool for clear code. Bad names make code impossible to understand, even if it's correct.

docs.title: Variable Names
docs.text:
Bad names: 

d = 5                    # What is d?
temp_x = user.get()      # Temporary? Why?
data = [1, 2, 3]         # What kind of data?
a = 25                   # a what?
foo_bar = True           # Meaningless

Good names: 

days_in_month = 5
current_user = user.get()
test_scores = [85, 92, 78]
user_age = 25
is_authenticated = True

Rules: - Name should explain what it contains - Longer names are fine if they're clearer - Use nouns for variables (contains data) - Avoid temp, data, foo, x (unless you're in a short loop) - Use full words: ✅ current_user, ❌ curr_usr

docs.title: Function Names
docs.text:
Bad names: 

def do_stuff(x, y):
    pass

def process(data):
    pass

def calculate(a, b):
    pass

Good names: 

def calculate_total_price(items, tax_rate):
    pass

def fetch_user_by_email(email):
    pass

def validate_credit_card(card_number):
    pass

Rules: - Name should say what the function does - Use verbs: calculate, validate, fetch, process - Be specific: ✅ get_user_by_id(), ❌ get_user() - Shorter function names are better (but not at cost of clarity)

docs.title: Class Names
docs.text:
Bad names: 

class Thing:
    pass

class Handler:
    pass

class Manager:
    pass

Good names: 

class BankAccount:
    pass

class EmailNotificationService:
    pass

class UserAuthenticator:
    pass

Rules: - Use nouns (classes represent things) - Specific, not generic: ✅ BankAccount, ❌ Account - One word preferred: ✅ User, ❌ UserObject

docs.title: Boolean Variables
docs.text:
Bad names: 

flag = True
done = False
x = True

Good names: 

is_authenticated = True
has_admin_rights = False
should_send_email = True

Pattern: Use is_, has_, should_ prefix for booleans.

docs.title: Short Functions
docs.text:
Functions should do one thing, clearly.

Bad: Long function doing multiple things 

def process_order(order):
    # Calculate totals
    subtotal = sum(item["price"] for item in order["items"])
    tax = subtotal * 0.08
    total = subtotal + tax

    # Check inventory
    for item in order["items"]:
        if item["quantity"] > get_stock(item["id"]):
            return {"error": "Out of stock"}

    # Update inventory
    for item in order["items"]:
        reduce_stock(item["id"], item["quantity"])

    # Create shipment
    shipment = {
        "order_id": order["id"],
        "items": order["items"]
    }
    send_to_warehouse(shipment)

    # Send email
    send_confirmation_email(order["customer_email"], total)

    return {"success": True, "total": total}

Good: Small functions, each doing one thing 

def process_order(order):
    total = calculate_order_total(order)
    check_inventory(order)
    update_inventory(order)
    create_shipment(order)
    send_confirmation(order, total)
    return {"success": True, "total": total}

def calculate_order_total(order):
    subtotal = sum(item["price"] for item in order["items"])
    tax = subtotal * 0.08
    return subtotal + tax

def check_inventory(order):
    for item in order["items"]:
        if item["quantity"] > get_stock(item["id"]):
            raise OutOfStockError(f"Item {item['id']} out of stock")

# ... other functions

Benefits: - Easy to understand what happens - Easy to test each step - Easy to change one part without affecting others - Easy to reuse functions

docs.title: Consistent Code Style
docs.text:
Bad: Inconsistent 

def calc_total( price,tax ):
    return price+tax

def calculate_discount(orig_price, percent):
    return orig_price * (1 - percent / 100)

result=calc_total(100,8)

Good: Consistent 

def calculate_total(price, tax):
    return price + tax

def calculate_discount(original_price, discount_percent):
    return original_price * (1 - discount_percent / 100)

result = calculate_total(100, 8)

Style rules (use these consistently): - Spaces around operators: a = b + c (not a=b+c) - Spaces after commas: func(a, b) (not func(a,b)) - Indentation: 4 spaces per level (most common) - Line length: keep lines under 80-100 characters

docs.title: Comments: When and How
docs.text:
Bad comments: 

# Add 1 to x
x = x + 1

# Check if age is greater than 18
if age > 18:
    pass

# Loop through list
for item in items:
    pass

These comments say what the code does. The code already says that.

Good comments: 

# Use the smaller of the two estimates for conservative calculation
x = min(estimate1, estimate2)

# Users must be 18 to enter (legal requirement)
if age > 18:
    allow_access()

# Skip test entries (start with underscore by convention)
for item in items:
    if item.startswith("_"):
        continue

These comments say why the code does it.

When to comment: - Explain non-obvious decisions - Explain why, not what - Document assumptions - Mark temporary hacks (so they get fixed)

When NOT to comment: - To explain obvious code - To restate what variable names already say - To comment out old code (use version control instead)

docs.title: Errors and Exceptions
docs.text: Errors aren't bad—they're information. Good code anticipates errors and handles them.

docs.title: Anticipate Problems
docs.text:
# Bad: assumes input is valid
def parse_age(user_input):
    return int(user_input)

# Test:
parse_age("25")      # Works
parse_age("hello")   # Crashes! ValueError
parse_age("")        # Crashes! ValueError

# Good: handles errors
def parse_age(user_input):
    try:
        age = int(user_input)
        if age < 0 or age > 150:
            raise ValueError("Age must be between 0 and 150")
        return age
    except ValueError as e:
        print(f"Invalid age: {e}")
        return None

# Test:
parse_age("25")      # Returns 25
parse_age("hello")   # Prints error, returns None
parse_age("-5")      # Prints error, returns None

docs.title: Document Assumptions
docs.text:
def calculate_discount(price, discount_percent):
"""
    Calculate discounted price.

    Args:
        price: Product price (must be positive)
        discount_percent: Discount percentage (0-100)

    Returns:
        Discounted price

    Raises:
        ValueError: If inputs are invalid
    """
    if price < 0:
        raise ValueError("Price must be positive")
    if discount_percent < 0 or discount_percent > 100:
        raise ValueError("Discount must be 0-100")

    return price * (1 - discount_percent / 100)

docs.title: Trade-Offs: Speed vs. Clarity vs. Scalability
docs.text: Every software decision involves trade-offs. Good engineers make conscious choices.

docs.title: Speed (Development Speed) vs. Clarity
docs.text:
# Fast to write, hard to understand
users = [u for u in filter(lambda u: u['age']>18, 
    map(lambda u: {**u, 'active': True}, 
        fetch_users()))]

# Takes longer to write, easy to understand
all_users = fetch_users()
adult_users = [u for u in all_users if u['age'] > 18]
active_adult_users = [
    {**u, 'active': True} for u in adult_users
]
users = active_adult_users

Decision: Usually choose clarity. Development is 10% writing, 90% reading and understanding. Invest in clarity.

docs.title: Clarity vs. Performance (Runtime Speed)
docs.text:
# Clear and simple
def find_user(users, target_id):
    for user in users:
        if user['id'] == target_id:
            return user
    return None

# Faster (for large lists)
users_by_id = {u['id']: u for u in users}  # Build index once
def find_user(users_by_id, target_id):
    return users_by_id.get(target_id)

Decision: Usually choose clarity first. Optimize only when you have evidence it's slow. (Premature optimization is a common mistake.)

docs.title: Simplicity vs. Flexibility
docs.text:
# Simple: works for one currency
def calculate_tax(price):
    return price * 0.08  # US tax rate

# Flexible: works for any currency
tax_rates = {
    'US': 0.08,
    'CA': 0.05,
    'EU': 0.19
}

def calculate_tax(price, country):
    rate = tax_rates.get(country)
    if rate is None:
        raise ValueError(f"Unknown country: {country}")
    return price * rate

Decision: Choose simplicity first. Add flexibility only when needed. (Over-engineering is a common mistake.)

docs.title: Refactoring: Making Code Better
docs.text: Refactoring means improving code without changing what it does.

docs.title: Why Refactor?
docs.text: Code gets messy. Refactoring keeps it clean.

docs.title: How to Refactor
docs.text:
1. Test first - Make sure it works before you change it
  2. Make small changes - Change one thing at a time
  3. Test after each change - Ensure it still works

docs.title: Extract Function
docs.text:
# Before: long function
def process_user(user):
    # Validate
    if not user.get('email') or '@' not in user['email']:
        return False
    if not user.get('age') or user['age'] < 18:
        return False

    # Process
    user['email'] = user['email'].lower()
    user['is_active'] = True

    return True

# After: extracted validation
def is_valid_user(user):
    has_email = user.get('email') and '@' in user['email']
    is_adult = user.get('age') and user['age'] >= 18
    return has_email and is_adult

def process_user(user):
    if not is_valid_user(user):
        return False

    user['email'] = user['email'].lower()
    user['is_active'] = True
    return True

docs.title: Replace Magic Numbers with Constants
docs.text:
# Before: what does 12 mean?
if user_age < 12:
    discount = 0.2

# After: clear intention
CHILD_DISCOUNT_THRESHOLD = 12
CHILD_DISCOUNT_RATE = 0.2

if user_age < CHILD_DISCOUNT_THRESHOLD:
    discount = CHILD_DISCOUNT_RATE

docs.title: Simplify Complex Logic
docs.text:
# Before: nested ifs
if email_is_valid:
    if user_is_active:
        if not is_already_subscribed:
            subscribe_user()

# After: early return
if not email_is_valid:
    return
if not user_is_active:
    return
if is_already_subscribed:
    return

subscribe_user()

docs.title: Testing Your Code
docs.text: Before you send code anywhere, test it yourself.

docs.title: Manual Testing
docs.text:
def calculate_age(birth_year):
    current_year = 2024
    return current_year - birth_year

# Test various cases
print(calculate_age(2000))  # 24 (expected)
print(calculate_age(2024))  # 0 (just born)
print(calculate_age(1950))  # 74 (elderly)
print(calculate_age(2025))  # -1 (not born yet—bug!)

docs.title: Systematic Testing
docs.text:
def test_calculate_age():
    assert calculate_age(2000) == 24
    assert calculate_age(2024) == 0
    assert calculate_age(1950) == 74
    # Now I see the bug with future years

test_calculate_age()

docs.title: Test Edge Cases
docs.text:
def divide(a, b):
    return a / b

# Edge cases:
divide(10, 2)      # Normal: 5
divide(10, 1)      # Divide by 1
divide(0, 5)       # Divide zero
divide(10, 0)      # Divide by zero—ERROR!

# Fix it:
def divide(a, b):
    if b == 0:
        raise ValueError("Cannot divide by zero")
    return a / b

docs.title: Exercise 1: Naming
docs.text:
Rename these poorly-named variables and functions: 

x = 5
temp_data = [1, 2, 3]
process(a, b)
class Handler:
    pass

docs.title: Exercise 2: Code Clarity
docs.text:
Rewrite this code for clarity: 

def f(n):
    if n<=1:
        return n
    return f(n-1)+f(n-2)

docs.title: Exercise 3: Comments
docs.text:
Add meaningful comments to this code (say WHY, not WHAT): 

def calculate_price(base_price, quantity):
    if quantity > 100:
        discount = 0.1
    else:
        discount = 0.05
    return base_price * quantity * (1 - discount)

docs.text:
Add error handling to this function: 

def parse_date(date_string):
    parts = date_string.split("-")
    year = int(parts[0])
    month = int(parts[1])
    day = int(parts[2])
    return (year, month, day)

docs.title: Exercise 5: Refactoring
docs.text:
Refactor this code to be clearer: 

def process_data(data):
    result = []
    for i in range(len(data)):
        if data[i] % 2 == 0 and data[i] > 10:
            result.append(data[i] * 2)
    return result

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
✅ Code is for humans to read; computers only need to run it

✅ Good naming is the most powerful clarity tool

✅ Short functions do one thing well

✅ Comments explain WHY, not WHAT

✅ Every design choice involves trade-offs

✅ Refactor constantly; keep code clean

✅ Test your code before trusting it

docs.title: What's Next?
docs.text:
You now understand how to write good code. But you're going to make mistakes. Let's learn how to use AI as a tool to help you, without becoming dependent on it.

→ Module 5: Programming With AI Assistance

docs.title: Module 5: Programming With AI Assistance
docs.text:
AI is powerful. It's also seductive. It can do things for you instantly, which is awesome—and dangerous.

This module teaches you how to use AI responsibly as a programming tool. You'll learn what it's great at, what it's terrible at, and most importantly, how to verify that AI-generated code is actually correct.

docs.title: What AI Is Good At
docs.text:
Explaining concepts 

You: "Can you explain what a decorator is in Python?"
AI: [Clear, multi-example explanation]

Generating boilerplate 

You: "Generate a class for a BankAccount with deposit and withdraw methods"
AI: [Standard, correct implementation]

Helping debug errors 

You: "I'm getting TypeError: 'int' object is not subscriptable when I run [code]"
AI: "This error means you're trying to index something that isn't indexable. In your code, 
    [explanation]. Try [fix]."

Code review 

You: [Share code]
AI: "This is good, but here are potential improvements: [suggestions]"

Writing tests and documentation 

You: "Write docstring and tests for this function"
AI: [Professional docstring and test cases]

docs.title: What AI Is Bad At
docs.text:
Architecture decisions - AI can't understand your full requirements - AI doesn't know your constraints - AI won't make trade-off decisions

❌ "Design my entire application" ✅ "Here's my architecture. Does it make sense? What am I missing?"

Correct implementation (without verification) - AI generates code that looks right but doesn't work - AI makes subtle bugs that compile but fail in edge cases - AI sometimes hallucinates (makes up things)

❌ Copy AI code directly into production ✅ Copy AI code, test it thoroughly, understand it, then use it

Making judgment calls - Should this be a database query or in-memory calculation? - Should we refactor now or later? - Is this code clear enough?

❌ "Tell me what to do" ✅ "Here are the options. Help me think through trade-offs"

Learning - Using AI to do your work means you don't learn - You end up dependent on AI - You can't debug or improve code you don't understand

❌ "Write this entire feature for me" ✅ "I'm stuck on this specific part. Help me understand [concept]"

docs.title: The AI-Assisted Workflow
docs.text: Here's a process for using AI responsibly:

docs.title: Step 1: Understand the Problem
docs.text:
Before asking AI anything, you must understand what you're trying to do.

Bad:
"I need to build an e-commerce site"

Good:
"I need a Python function that:
- Takes a list of product dictionaries with 'name', 'price', 'quantity'
- Calculates total cost including 8% tax
- Validates that price and quantity are positive
- Returns total or raises error if invalid"

docs.title: Step 2: Try It Yourself First
docs.text:
Don't ask AI for help immediately. Try for 10-15 minutes.

Why? You learn by struggling. You understand the problem better. You know what you don't know.

docs.title: Step 3: Ask Specific Questions
docs.text:
Specific questions → useful answers.

Bad questions:
- "How do I use databases?"
- "Help me debug this code"
- "Write a function"

Good questions:
- "I need to connect Python to PostgreSQL. What library should I use and how?"
- "My code crashes with 'TypeError: 'NoneType' object is not subscriptable' at line 42. 
   Here's the code. What's happening?"
- "Write a function that takes a list and returns the sum of even numbers"

docs.title: Step 4: Verify AI's Answer
docs.text:
This is critical. Don't trust AI just because it sounds authoritative.

# AI gives you this code
def calculate_discount(price, percent):
    return price - (price * percent)

# Test it:
print(calculate_discount(100, 0.1))  # What should it return?
# Result: 90

# Is that right? 100 - (100 * 0.1) = 100 - 10 = 90
# Looks good!

# But what about edge cases?
print(calculate_discount(100, 2))  # What should it return?
# Result: -100

# That's wrong! A 200% discount should be rejected, not result in negative price.
# AI didn't handle edge cases.

docs.title: Step 5: Understand the Code
docs.text:
Read AI-generated code as if you wrote it. Trace through it.

# AI generated this
def bubble_sort(arr):
    n = len(arr)
    for i in range(n):
        for j in range(0, n - i - 1):
            if arr[j] > arr[j + 1]:
                arr[j], arr[j + 1] = arr[j + 1], arr[j]
    return arr

# Trace it:
# What does it do? (Sorts array)
# How does it work? (Compares adjacent elements, swaps if needed)
# What's the performance? (O(n²), slow)
# Is it right? (Yes, for this use case)
# Should I use it? (Depends on array size)

docs.title: Step 6: Modify as Needed
docs.text:
AI gives you a starting point. You finish it.

# AI gives you basic function
def get_user(user_id):
    return database.query(f"SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = {user_id}")

# You add:
def get_user(user_id):
"""Get user by ID, with validation"""
    if not isinstance(user_id, int) or user_id <= 0:
        raise ValueError("user_id must be a positive integer")

    user = database.query(f"SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = {user_id}")

    if not user:
        raise UserNotFoundError(f"User {user_id} not found")

    return user

docs.title: Common AI Pitfalls and How to Avoid Them
Pitfall 1: Blind Copy-Paste
docs.text:
# You ask: "How do I download a file?"
# AI gives 20 lines of code
# You copy and paste it without understanding

# Later: something breaks, you have no idea why

Fix: Type it yourself. Understand each line.

docs.title: Pitfall 2: Trusting Without Testing
docs.text:
# AI gives you a function to parse dates
def parse_date(date_string):
    # Implementation
    pass

# You use it immediately without testing

# Later: it fails on some date format and crashes in production

Fix: Write tests before using code.

docs.title: Pitfall 3: Asking AI to Design
docs.text:
# Bad: "Design my user authentication system"
# AI gives you something, but it might not fit your needs

# Good: "I need user authentication. Here's my tech stack and requirements. 
#        Should I use JWT or sessions? Here are the trade-offs I see..."

Fix: Make architectural decisions yourself. Use AI for implementation.

docs.title: Pitfall 4: Not Reading Error Messages
docs.text:
# AI generates code
# You run it and get an error
# You ask AI: "Fix this error"

# Instead, read the error! It tells you what's wrong.

Fix: Read error messages carefully. Ask AI to explain them, not fix them.

docs.title: Pitfall 5: Code You Don't Understand
docs.text:
# AI generates something clever but complex
# You don't understand it, so you don't modify it
# You can't debug it when it breaks

# This is worse than writing simple code yourself

Fix: If you don't understand it, ask AI to explain it. If it's still complex, ask for a simpler version.

docs.title: How to Ask AI Good Questions
Framework: Be Specific
docs.text:
CONTEXT: What are you building? What problem are you solving?
ATTEMPT: What did you try? What happened?
DESIRED: What should happen?
CODE: Show the relevant code

docs.title: Example: Good Question
docs.text:
CONTEXT: I'm building a program to track student grades. I'm 
using Python and storing data in a dictionary.

ATTEMPT: I wrote a function to calculate average grade, but 
it crashes when the list is empty.

DESIRED: The function should return None for empty lists 
instead of crashing.

CODE:
def calculate_average(grades):
    total = sum(grades)
    return total / len(grades)

grades = []
result = calculate_average(grades)  # ZeroDivisionError

AI can now help effectively.

docs.title: Framework: Start Broad, Get Specific
docs.text:
First: "How do I handle errors in Python?"
Then: "How do I use try-except for this specific error?"
Then: "Here's my code. Does this handle errors right?"

docs.title: Framework: Ask About Concepts, Not Just Code
docs.text:
❌ "Write code that does X"
✅ "Explain how X works. Show me an example. Here's code I 
   wrote based on that. Does it use the concept correctly?"

docs.title: Verification Checklist
docs.text: When AI gives you code, ask yourself:

docs.title: Does It Do What I Asked?
docs.text:
# You asked: "Calculate total including tax"
# AI gave you: [code]
# Does it actually calculate total including tax?
# Test with specific numbers

docs.title: Does It Handle Edge Cases?
docs.text:
# What if input is empty?
# What if input is None?
# What if input is negative?
# What if input is extremely large?

# Test all of these

docs.title: Is It Secure?
docs.text:
# Does it validate input?
# Could a user break it?
# Does it access sensitive data safely?

docs.title: Is It Efficient?
docs.text:
# Will it be slow with large input?
# Does it use a reasonable algorithm?
# Are there obviously wasteful operations?

docs.title: Is It Readable?
docs.text:
# Can you understand what it does?
# Are variable names clear?
# Could someone else read this?

# If not, ask AI to make it clearer, or rewrite it yourself

docs.title: Does It Match Your Style?
docs.text:
# Does it match your project's conventions?
# Does it match other code you've written?
# If not, refactor it to match

docs.title: For Explaining Concepts
docs.text:
Good use:
You: "I don't understand how closures work"
AI: [Explanation with examples]

Bad use:
You: "Explain everything about Python"
AI: [Too much, overwhelming]

Best practice: Ask about one concept at a time

docs.title: For Debugging
docs.text:
Good use:
You: "My code returns [X] but I expect [Y]. Here's the code. Why?"
AI: [Explains what's happening]

Bad use:
You: "My code is broken"
AI: [Guesses, might be wrong]

Best practice: Share the error message and code

docs.title: For Generating Tests
docs.text:
Good use:
You: "Write unit tests for this function"
AI: [Good test cases]
You: [Review and modify if needed]

Bad use:
You: [Trust tests without reviewing]

Best practice: Review generated tests, add more if needed

docs.title: For Refactoring
docs.text:
Good use:
You: "Here's my code. How could I make it clearer?"
AI: [Suggestions]
You: [Implement suggestions you agree with]

Bad use:
You: [Use all suggestions blindly]

Best practice: Consider suggestions, use what makes sense

docs.title: Don't use AI when:
docs.text:
1. You're learning fundamentals
  2. Writing functions, loops, conditionals should be muscle memory

  3. Do it 100 times yourself before asking AI for help

  4. You need to make decisions

  5. Architecture, technology choices, trade-offs

  6. These are your responsibility

  7. You don't understand what it gives you

  8. If you can't explain it, don't use it

  9. Ask AI to explain better, or write it yourself

  10. It would be faster to write it yourself

  11. For very simple code, typing it is faster than prompting

  12. This happens more often than you'd think

  13. You're trying to look competent

  14. Pretending to understand AI code makes you incompetent
  15. Admitting confusion and fixing it makes you competent

docs.title: AI as a Learning Partner
docs.text:
The best way to use AI is as a teacher:

Workflow:
1. You try something
2. You get stuck
3. You ask AI to explain (not fix)
4. You understand the concept
5. You write the code yourself

This is learning.

docs.title: Example: Learning to Use Databases
docs.text:
Bad: "Write code to query a database"
→ You get code you don't understand

Good: 
"I'm trying to use SQLite. Explain the basic steps:
1. How do I connect?
2. How do I execute a query?
3. How do I get results?
4. How do I close the connection?

Here's my first attempt: [code]
Does this do it right?"
→ You understand, you write it, you learn

docs.title: Exercise 1: Asking Good Questions
docs.text:
Rewrite these AI requests to be more specific:

  1. "Help me code"
  2. "How do I use lists?"
  3. "Debug my program"

docs.title: Exercise 2: Verification
docs.text:
AI gives you this code. Test it and identify any problems:

def find_max(numbers):
    max_value = numbers[0]
    for num in numbers:
        if num > max_value:
            max_value = num
    return max_value

Test cases: - Normal list: [1, 5, 3, 9, 2] - Empty list: [] - Negative numbers: [-5, -1, -10] - Single item: [42]

docs.title: Exercise 3: Code Review
docs.text:
AI generated this. Review it for clarity, correctness, and efficiency:

def calculate_average(nums):
    if not nums:
        return 0
    return sum(nums) / len(nums)

Questions: - Is it correct? - Should it return 0 for empty list, or None, or raise error? - How would you improve it?

docs.title: Exercise 4: Learning Approach
docs.text: You need to understand decorators. Write out a learning approach: 1. What would you ask AI? 2. How would you test your understanding? 3. How would you practice?

docs.title: Exercise 5: When to Use AI
docs.text:
For each scenario, decide: use AI, or do it yourself? Why?

  1. You're stuck on a syntax error
  2. You need to decide between database systems
  3. You need to write 5 unit tests
  4. You need to understand a concept
  5. You need to generate a lot of boilerplate code

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
✅ AI is a tool, not a replacement for thinking

✅ Understand the problem before asking AI

✅ Verify every piece of AI-generated code

✅ Ask specific questions

✅ Use AI to explain, not to replace learning

✅ Edge cases are your responsibility to think about

✅ Code you don't understand is code you shouldn't use

docs.title: What's Next?
docs.text:
Now you know how to code and how to use AI responsibly. Let's apply it all to real projects.

→ Module 6: Practical Examples & Projects

docs.title: Module 6: Practical Examples & Projects
docs.text:
Theory is important. But programming is learned by doing.

This module walks you through concrete projects, showing you the thinking process, design decisions, and how to apply everything you've learned.

docs.title: Project 1: Grade Tracker
docs.text: A simple program to track and analyze student grades.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
1. Store student names and their grades
  2. Calculate average grade for each student
  3. Calculate class average
  4. Identify students who need help (below 70%)
  5. Generate a report

docs.title: Step 1: Understand the Problem
docs.text: Questions to ask yourself: - What data do I need to store? - What operations do I need to perform? - How will users interact with this? - What could go wrong?

docs.title: Step 2: Design (Before Coding)
docs.text:
Data Structure:
- List of students
- Each student has:
  - Name (string)
  - Grades (list of numbers)

Operations:
- Add grade for student
- Calculate average for student
- Calculate class average
- Find struggling students
- Print report

Format (simple):
- Command-line interface
- Text-based menu

docs.title: Step 3: Pseudocode
docs.text:
# Pseudocode (not real code, just the logic)

Main program:
1. Load or create grade data
2. Show menu loop:
   - "Add grade"
   - "View student average"
   - "View class average"
   - "View struggling students"
   - "Exit"
3. Based on choice, call appropriate function

Functions:
- add_grade(name, grade)
- get_student_average(name)
- get_class_average()
- get_struggling_students()
- print_report()

docs.title: Step 4: Implementation
docs.text:
class GradeTracker:
"""Tracks and analyzes student grades"""

    def __init__(self):
"""Initialize with empty students dictionary"""
        self.students = {}

    def add_grade(self, name, grade):
"""Add a grade for a student"""
        if not (0 <= grade <= 100):
            raise ValueError("Grade must be between 0 and 100")

        if name not in self.students:
            self.students[name] = []

        self.students[name].append(grade)

    def get_student_average(self, name):
"""Get average grade for a student"""
        if name not in self.students:
            raise ValueError(f"Student {name} not found")

        grades = self.students[name]
        if not grades:
            return 0

        return sum(grades) / len(grades)

    def get_class_average(self):
"""Get average grade for entire class"""
        all_grades = []
        for grades in self.students.values():
            all_grades.extend(grades)

        if not all_grades:
            return 0

        return sum(all_grades) / len(all_grades)

    def get_struggling_students(self, threshold=70):
"""Get students below threshold grade"""
        struggling = []

        for name in self.students:
            average = self.get_student_average(name)
            if average < threshold:
                struggling.append((name, average))

        return sorted(struggling, key=lambda x: x[1])

    def print_report(self):
"""Print comprehensive report"""
        print("\n=== Grade Report ===\n")

        # Individual students
        print("Student Averages:")
        for name in sorted(self.students.keys()):
            avg = self.get_student_average(name)
            print(f"  {name}: {avg:.2f}%")

        # Class average
        class_avg = self.get_class_average()
        print(f"\nClass Average: {class_avg:.2f}%")

        # Struggling students
        struggling = self.get_struggling_students()
        if struggling:
            print("\nStudents Below 70%:")
            for name, avg in struggling:
                print(f"  {name}: {avg:.2f}%")
        else:
            print("\nAll students above 70%!")


def main():
"""Main program loop"""
    tracker = GradeTracker()

    while True:
        print("\n=== Grade Tracker ===")
        print("1. Add grade")
        print("2. View student average")
        print("3. View class average")
        print("4. View struggling students")
        print("5. Print report")
        print("6. Exit")

        choice = input("Choose option: ").strip()

        if choice == "1":
            name = input("Student name: ").strip()
            try:
                grade = float(input("Grade (0-100): "))
                tracker.add_grade(name, grade)
                print(f"Added grade for {name}")
            except ValueError as e:
                print(f"Error: {e}")

        elif choice == "2":
            name = input("Student name: ").strip()
            try:
                avg = tracker.get_student_average(name)
                print(f"{name}'s average: {avg:.2f}%")
            except ValueError as e:
                print(f"Error: {e}")

        elif choice == "3":
            avg = tracker.get_class_average()
            print(f"Class average: {avg:.2f}%")

        elif choice == "4":
            struggling = tracker.get_struggling_students()
            if struggling:
                print("\nStudents below 70%:")
                for name, avg in struggling:
                    print(f"  {name}: {avg:.2f}%")
            else:
                print("All students above 70%!")

        elif choice == "5":
            tracker.print_report()

        elif choice == "6":
            print("Goodbye!")
            break

        else:
            print("Invalid option")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

docs.title: Project 2: URL Shortener
docs.text: A service that converts long URLs to short codes.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
1. Generate short code from long URL
  2. Store mapping (short code → long URL)
  3. Retrieve long URL using short code
  4. Handle invalid URLs

docs.title: Step 1: Design
docs.text:
Data:
- Dictionary mapping short codes to URLs
- Or database table

Algorithm:
- Take long URL
- Generate unique short code (could be random, or hash-based)
- Store mapping
- Return short code

Issues to handle:
- What if URL already shortened?
- What if short code collision happens?
- What about URL validation?

docs.title: Step 2: Implementation
docs.text:
import hashlib
import string
import random

class URLShortener:
"""Converts long URLs to short codes"""

    def __init__(self):
"""Initialize with empty mapping"""
        self.url_map = {}  # short_code → long_url
        self.reverse_map = {}  # long_url → short_code

    def _is_valid_url(self, url):
"""Validate URL format"""
        # Simple validation: just check for http(s) and domain
        return url.startswith(('http://', 'https://')) and '.' in url

    def _generate_short_code(self, url):
"""Generate a short code for a URL"""
        # Use first 6 characters of hash
        hash_value = hashlib.md5(url.encode()).hexdigest()
        short_code = hash_value[:6]

        # If collision, keep adding random characters
        while short_code in self.url_map:
            short_code += random.choice(string.ascii_letters)

        return short_code

    def shorten(self, url):
"""
        Shorten a URL

        Args:
            url: Long URL to shorten

        Returns:
            Short code

        Raises:
            ValueError: If URL is invalid
        """
        if not self._is_valid_url(url):
            raise ValueError(f"Invalid URL: {url}")

        # Return existing code if already shortened
        if url in self.reverse_map:
            return self.reverse_map[url]

        # Generate new code
        short_code = self._generate_short_code(url)

        # Store mapping both ways
        self.url_map[short_code] = url
        self.reverse_map[url] = short_code

        return short_code

    def expand(self, short_code):
"""
        Get original URL from short code

        Args:
            short_code: The short code

        Returns:
            Original URL

        Raises:
            KeyError: If short code doesn't exist
        """
        if short_code not in self.url_map:
            raise KeyError(f"Short code not found: {short_code}")

        return self.url_map[short_code]


# Example usage
shortener = URLShortener()

# Shorten URLs
code1 = shortener.shorten("https://www.example.com/very/long/page")
code2 = shortener.shorten("https://github.com/user/repo")

print(f"Short code 1: {code1}")
print(f"Short code 2: {code2}")

# Expand
original = shortener.expand(code1)
print(f"Original: {original}")

# Error handling
try:
    shortener.shorten("not-a-url")
except ValueError as e:
    print(f"Error: {e}")

try:
    shortener.expand("nonexistent")
except KeyError as e:
    print(f"Error: {e}")

docs.title: Project 3: Simple Chat Application
docs.text: A command-line chat between two people.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
1. Person A and Person B exchange messages
  2. Keep conversation history
  3. Display who sent each message
  4. Show timestamp

docs.title: Design
docs.text:
from datetime import datetime

class Message:
"""Represents a single chat message"""

    def __init__(self, sender, text):
        self.sender = sender
        self.text = text
        self.timestamp = datetime.now()

    def __str__(self):
        time_str = self.timestamp.strftime("%H:%M")
        return f"[{time_str}] {self.sender}: {self.text}"


class Chat:
"""Manages conversation between two people"""

    def __init__(self, person_a, person_b):
        self.person_a = person_a
        self.person_b = person_b
        self.messages = []

    def send_message(self, sender, text):
"""Add a message to chat"""
        if sender not in (self.person_a, self.person_b):
            raise ValueError(f"Unknown sender: {sender}")

        if not text.strip():
            raise ValueError("Message cannot be empty")

        message = Message(sender, text)
        self.messages.append(message)

    def get_history(self):
"""Get conversation history"""
        return [str(msg) for msg in self.messages]

    def print_chat(self):
"""Print formatted conversation"""
        print("\n=== Conversation History ===\n")
        for msg in self.messages:
            print(msg)
        print()


# Usage
chat = Chat("Alice", "Bob")

chat.send_message("Alice", "Hi Bob!")
chat.send_message("Bob", "Hey Alice, how are you?")
chat.send_message("Alice", "I'm doing great!")

chat.print_chat()

docs.title: 1. Understand
docs.text: Read the problem 2-3 times. Ask: - What data do I need? - What operations are needed? - What could go wrong?

docs.title: 2. Design (Don't code yet!)
docs.text: Draw it out, write pseudocode: - What classes/functions do I need? - How do they interact? - What's the data structure?

docs.title: 3. Start Simple
docs.text: Build the simplest version first: - Get basic functionality working - Then add features - Then handle edge cases

docs.title: 4. Test as You Go
docs.text: After each piece: - Does it work? - Does it handle errors? - Is the output correct?

docs.title: 5. Refactor
docs.text: Once it works: - Is it readable? - Can I simplify? - Are names clear? - Is there duplication?

docs.title: 6. Add Features
docs.text: Only after basic version works: - File persistence - Better UI - More features - Optimization

docs.title: Mistake 1: Big Bang Approach
docs.text: ❌ Try to build everything at once ✅ Build simplest version, add features incrementally

docs.title: Mistake 2: No Design Phase
docs.text: ❌ Start coding immediately ✅ Spend 15 minutes thinking before writing code

docs.title: Mistake 3: Ignoring Edge Cases
docs.text: ❌ Code works for happy path, breaks on edge cases ✅ Test with empty input, invalid input, extreme values

docs.title: Mistake 4: No Error Handling
docs.text: ❌ Code assumes everything will work ✅ Anticipate what could go wrong and handle it

docs.title: Mistake 5: Over-Engineering
docs.text: ❌ Build a complex system for simple problem ✅ Start simple, add complexity only when needed

docs.title: Key Takeaways

✅ Design before coding

docs.title: Common Mistakes & How to Avoid Them
docs.text: When learning to program, mistakes are inevitable. More importantly, certain mistakes appear again and again across all learners. This guide highlights the most common pitfalls and pragmatic ways to avoid them.

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text:
You read a problem, immediately start typing code, and realize halfway through you didn't understand the requirements.

# ❌ MISTAKE
def process_data(items):
    # Wait... what should this do exactly?
    result = []
    for item in items:
        # I'll figure it out as I go...
        result.append(item * 2)  # Or is it item + 2?
    return result

docs.title: Why It Happens
docs.text:
• Impatience to "get it working"
  • Pressure to produce code quickly
  • Belief that coding is mostly typing

docs.title: The Fix
docs.text:
Always write pseudocode first. Pseudocode is English-like instructions that describe your algorithm.

# ✅ PSEUDOCODE FIRST
"""
Given a list of items:
1. Create an empty result list
2. For each item in the list:
   a. Multiply the item by 2
   b. Add the result to our result list
3. Return the result list
"""

# NOW write the code
def double_items(items):
    result = []
    for item in items:
        result.append(item * 2)
    return result

Time saved: 5 minutes of thinking = 20 minutes of debugging.

docs.title: 2. Mistake: Not Testing as You Go
The Problem
docs.text:
You write 50 lines of code, run it, get 5 errors at once. Now you don't know which line caused which error.

# ❌ MISTAKE - Write everything, then test
def process_user_data(users):
    valid_users = []
    for user in users:
        if user.age >= 18:  # Error 1: user doesn't have .age
            user.status = "adult"  # Error 2: strings aren't comparable
            valid_users.append(user)

    emails = [u.email for u in valid_users]  # Error 3: wrong field name
    send_emails(emails)  # Error 4: function not defined yet
    return valid_users

Running this gives you 4 errors. Which one do you fix first? You have no idea which lines work and which don't.

docs.title: The Fix
docs.text:
Test after every few lines. Create a small test case for each function.

# ✅ CORRECT - Test as you build
def process_user_data(users):
    valid_users = []
    for user in users:
        if user['age'] >= 18:  # Test: does user have 'age'?
            user['status'] = "adult"
            valid_users.append(user)

    return valid_users

# Test immediately
users = [
    {'name': 'Alice', 'age': 25, 'email': 'alice@example.com'},
    {'name': 'Bob', 'age': 17, 'email': 'bob@example.com'},
]
result = process_user_data(users)
print(result)  # Does it work? Good. Move on to emails.

# NOW add the next part
emails = [u['email'] for u in result]
# Test it works before going further
print(emails)

The rule: If you can't test it in under 2 minutes, break it into smaller pieces.

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text:
# ❌ MISTAKE
d = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
x = 0
for i in d:
    x += i * 2
# What does x represent? No idea. Bad variable name.

Weeks later, you come back and can't understand your own code.

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text: Code is read 10 times more than it's written. If it takes you 30 seconds to remember what x means, that's 5 minutes lost per day across a team.

docs.title: The Fix
docs.text:
Name variables for what they represent, not their type.

# ✅ CORRECT
user_ages = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
sum_of_doubled_ages = 0
for age in user_ages:
    sum_of_doubled_ages += age * 2
# Clear. Anyone reading this knows what's happening.

Exception: Single-letter variable names are acceptable only: - In math formulas: y = m * x + b - In short loops: for i in range(10): - In obvious contexts: for user in users:

docs.title: 4. Mistake: Mixing Different Data Types in One Variable
The Problem
docs.text:
# ❌ MISTAKE
data = "42"  # It's a string
result = data + 10  # Can't add string + number
# TypeError: can only concatenate str (not "int") to str

Even worse:

# ❌ EVEN WORSE
user_id = 123  # It's a number
user_id = "unknown"  # Now it's a string. What?
user_id = None  # Now it's None

Next person to read this code is confused.

docs.title: The Fix
docs.text:
Keep one variable's meaning consistent. If it starts as a number, keep it a number.

# ✅ CORRECT
user_id = 123
if some_error_occurred:
    user_id = 0  # Use 0 or -1, not "unknown"

# OR create a new variable for the error case
user_id = None
if valid_user_exists:
    user_id = 123

Better: Use type hints (Python 3.5+):

# ✅ BEST
user_id: int = 123  # Explicitly tells others: this is always an int

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text:
# ❌ MISTAKE
def process_order(order):
    # Connect to database
    # Validate user
    # Check inventory
    # Calculate shipping
    # Apply tax
    # Process payment
    # Send confirmation email
    # Log activity
    # (200 lines of code in one function)

This function does too many things. Testing it requires dealing with all of that complexity.

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text:
• Hard to test: You have to set up everything to test one piece
  • Hard to reuse: Can't use "just the tax calculation" elsewhere
  • Hard to debug: An error could be in any of 200 lines

docs.title: The Fix
docs.text:
Break it into smaller, single-purpose functions.

# ✅ CORRECT
def process_order(order):
    user = validate_user(order.user_id)
    item = check_inventory(order.item_id)
    shipping_cost = calculate_shipping(item.weight, user.address)
    tax = calculate_tax(item.price, user.state)
    total = item.price + shipping_cost + tax

    process_payment(user.payment_method, total)
    send_confirmation_email(user.email, order)
    log_order(order)

    return order

# Each function is small, testable, and reusable
def calculate_tax(price, state):
    rates = {'CA': 0.08, 'TX': 0.0625, ...}
    return price * rates.get(state, 0)

Rule: If your function is longer than a screen, it's probably too long.

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text:
You get an error:

Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "app.py", line 45, in <module>
    user.email = user_data['email']
KeyError: 'email'

Instead of reading the error, you: - Hit "run" again (hoping it fixes itself) - Add a try/catch and ignore the error - Post on Stack Overflow asking "why am I getting an error?"

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text: Error messages are gifts. They tell you exactly what's wrong and where.

docs.title: The Fix
docs.text:
Read the error message bottom-to-top:

KeyError: 'email'
  ↑ What? The key 'email' doesn't exist in user_data

File "app.py", line 45
    user.email = user_data['email']
  ↑ Where? Line 45. I'm trying to access user_data['email']

Traceback (most recent call last):
  ↑ When? When running this code

Action: Check if user_data has an 'email' key. If not, handle it:

# ✅ CORRECT
if 'email' in user_data:
    user.email = user_data['email']
else:
    user.email = None  # or raise an error

docs.title: 7. Mistake: Copying Code Without Understanding It
The Problem
docs.text:
You find a StackOverflow solution, copy it, it works, you move on.

# ❌ MISTAKE - You don't know what this does
result = list(map(lambda x: x**2 if x % 2 == 0 else x, data))
# You copied it. You don't understand it. Bad.

6 months later, you need to modify it. You're lost.

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text:
• You can't debug it
  • You can't explain it to others
  • You'll copy it wrong next time
  • You're not learning

docs.title: The Fix
docs.text:
If you copy code, understand it line-by-line.

# ✅ CORRECT - You understand it step-by-step
data = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]

# The goal: Square even numbers, keep odd numbers as-is
result = []
for num in data:
    if num % 2 == 0:  # Is it even?
        result.append(num ** 2)  # Square it
    else:
        result.append(num)  # Keep original

print(result)  # [1, 4, 3, 16, 5, 36]

Yes, it's longer. But you understand it. And you can modify it.

docs.title: 8. Mistake: Not Committing Code to Git
The Problem
docs.text:
You're working on a feature. You make changes. Something breaks. You try to undo it manually.

# ❌ MISTAKE
# You've been coding for 3 hours without Git commits
# Now you have a bug and can't remember what changed
# You can't revert safely

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text:
• No safety net: You can't go back
  • No history: What did I change?
  • No collaboration: Others can't work alongside you

docs.title: The Fix
docs.text:
Commit frequently.

# ✅ CORRECT
git add .
git commit -m "Add user authentication"

git add .
git commit -m "Fix login validation bug"

git add .
git commit -m "Add email verification"

# Now if something breaks, you can revert to any commit
git revert <commit-hash>

Rule: Commit after every working feature, no matter how small.

docs.title: 9. Mistake: Writing Comments That Repeat the Code
The Problem
docs.text:
# ❌ MISTAKE
# Increment counter
counter += 1

# Check if age is greater than 18
if age > 18:
    # Set status to adult
    status = "adult"

These comments don't add information. They repeat what the code obviously does.

docs.title: The Fix
docs.text:
Comments should explain WHY, not WHAT.

# ✅ CORRECT
counter += 1  # No comment needed; it's obvious

# Users under 18 require parental consent per COPPA regulations
if age > 18:
    status = "adult"

Or document complex logic:

# ✅ COMPLEX LOGIC - docstring is helpful
def calculate_compound_interest(principal, rate, time):
"""
    Calculate compound interest using: A = P(1 + r/n)^(nt)
    Where:
    - P = principal amount
    - r = annual interest rate
    - n = number of times interest compounds per year
    - t = time in years
    """
    n = 12  # Interest compounds monthly
    return principal * (1 + rate / n) ** (n * time)

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text:
# ❌ MISTAKE - Optimizing before proving there's a problem
# You write super-complex code to be "efficient"
# Then you realize the bottleneck was somewhere else

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text:
• Wastes time: You optimize something that doesn't matter
  • Makes code unreadable: Clever code is hard to maintain
  • Late discovery: You find out after months what the real bottleneck is

docs.title: The Fix
docs.text:
Make it work first, make it right second, make it fast last.

# ✅ STEP 1: Make it work (ugly is fine)
def find_user(user_id):
    for user in all_users:
        if user.id == user_id:
            return user
    return None

# ✅ STEP 2: Make it right (readable, tested)
def find_user(user_id):
"""Find a user by ID. Returns None if not found."""
    for user in all_users:
        if user.id == user_id:
            return user
    return None

# ✅ STEP 3: Measure. Is it slow? Profile it.
import timeit
# ... measure ...

# ONLY IF SLOW: Optimize
user_map = {u.id: u for u in all_users}  # O(1) lookup instead of O(n)
def find_user(user_id):
    return user_map.get(user_id)

Rule: Don't optimize what you haven't measured.

docs.title: Summary: The Meta-Mistake
docs.text:
The biggest mistake isn't any single one above—it's not asking for feedback.

  • Show your code to experienced programmers
  • Ask "Is there a better way?"
  • Read other people's code
  • Make mistakes, learn from them, don't repeat them

You'll make mistakes. That's how you learn. The key is making different mistakes, not the same ones over and over.

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text:
• Read Bibliography & Further Reading for books on clean code
  • Review your own code from 3 months ago—do you see these mistakes?
  • Find a mentor or code review partner

docs.title: Bibliography & Further Reading
docs.text: Programming fundamentals are timeless. While tools and languages evolve, the principles in this module are drawn from decades of computer science research and engineering practice. Below are resources that have shaped this curriculum and will deepen your understanding.

docs.title: 1. "Code Complete: A Practical Handbook of Software Construction" by Steve McConnell
docs.text:
Why read it: The bible of practical programming. Not about a specific language—about writing code that another human can understand and maintain.

Key sections for this module: - Chapter 2: Metaphors for a Richer Understanding of Software Development - Part II: Creating High-Quality Code - Chapter 11: Variable Names

Best for: Intermediate. Read after mastering your first language.

docs.title: 2. "The Pragmatic Programmer: Your Journey to Mastery" by Hunt & Thomas
docs.text:
Why read it: Career advice from engineers who've been there. Philosophy over syntax.

Key lessons: - Care about your craft - Think about your work - "Broken Window Theory" in code - Change local state before global state

Best for: Everyone. Even experienced programmers benefit from re-reading.

docs.title: 3. "Clean Code: A Handbook of Agile Software Craftsmanship" by Robert C. Martin
docs.text:
Why read it: How to write code that's maintainable, readable, and professional-grade.

Key chapters: - Chapter 2: Meaningful Names - Chapter 3: Functions - Chapter 4: Comments - Chapter 10: Classes

Note: Some examples are dated (Java-centric), but principles apply everywhere.

Best for: Advanced beginners and professionals. Dense but worth it.

docs.title: 4. "Introduction to Algorithms" by Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest, Stein (CLRS)
docs.text:
Why read it: The definitive algorithm textbook. University standard.

Reality check: Read selectively. All 1312 pages is harsh. Start with specific algorithms you need.

Key sections: - Chapter 1: The Role of Algorithms in Computing - Part I: Foundations (Big-O, sorting basics)

Best for: Computer Science aspirants. Optional for self-taught engineers (focus on applied knowledge first).

docs.title: 5. "Computer Systems: A Programmer's Perspective" by Bryant & O'Hallaron (CS:APP)
docs.text:
Why read it: Understand what's actually happening under the hood. From bits to operating systems.

Key insight: Programming isn't just "write code and hit run." Understanding the machine helps you write better code.

Best for: After you're comfortable with fundamentals. Game-changing perspective.

docs.title: 6. "Design Patterns: Elements of Reusable Object-Oriented Software" by Gang of Four
docs.text:
Why read it: The canonical reference on design patterns. If devs mention "Factory Pattern" or "Observer Pattern," this is where they come from.

Reality: Read it later. You need pattern experience first. This is a reference, not a beginner book.

Best for: Intermediate+. Useful as a reference when you encounter problems.

docs.title: 7. "Refactoring: Improving the Design of Existing Code" by Martin Fowler
docs.text:
Why read it: How to improve code without breaking it. Essential for working with legacy code.

Key concept: Refactoring is changing code WITHOUT changing its behavior. The opposite of "I'll rewrite this."

Best for: Mid-level developers who've written code they now regret.

docs.title: 8. "Fluent Python: Clear, Concise, and Effective Programming" by Luciano Ramalho
docs.text:
Why read it: Goes deep into Python's design philosophy and asks "Why does Python work this way?"

Best for: Python developers who understand basics and want mastery.

docs.title: 9. PEP 8: Style Guide for Python Code
docs.text:
Why read it: The official Python style guide. Read it once, make it a habit.

Link: https://www.python.org/dev/peps/pep-0008/

Time: 30 minutes. Do it.

docs.title: 10. PEP 20: The Zen of Python
docs.text:
Why read it: Philosophy of Python design. Cultural resource.

How to read it: In Python, run import this. It prints Python's design philosophy (19 lines).

docs.title: 11. Martin Fowler's Blog
docs.text:
Link: https://martinfowler.com/

Why: Architecture, design, and industry observations from someone who helped define modern software engineering practices.

Start with: - "Refactoring" - "Code Smell" - "Technical Debt"

docs.title: 12. Steve Yegge's Blog
docs.text:
Link: https://steve-yegge.blogspot.com/

Why: Passionate, opinionated takes on programming language design and software engineering.

Must-read: - "Practicing Programming" - "Code's Worst Enemy"

docs.title: 13. Joel on Software
docs.text:
Link: https://www.joelonsoftware.com/

Why: Joel Spolsky's essays on building software and hiring engineers. Humorous and insightful.

Classics: - "The Joel Test: 12 Steps to Better Code" - "Making Wrong Code Look Wrong"

docs.title: 14. "Structure and Interpretation of Computer Programs" (SICP) by Abelson & Sussman
docs.text:
Level: Academic/Advanced. Taught at MIT using Scheme (a Lisp dialect).

Why read it: Teaches you to think about computation itself, not just syntax.

Reality: Most self-taught engineers skip this one. But if you want to understand the deep principles, it's foundational.

Link: https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262510875/structure-and-interpretation-of-computer-programs/

docs.title: 15. "The C Programming Language" by Kernighan & Ritchie (K&R)
docs.text:
Why read it: Written by people who literally invented C. Shows you how important systems are built.

Benefit: Gives you respect for memory management and why higher-level languages abstract it away.

Best for: Appreciating how far programming has come.

docs.text:

  • Julia Evans (jvns.ca) – Systems, tools, learning strategies

docs.title: 16. LeetCode (Optional)
docs.text:
For what: Algorithm problems. Useful if you're preparing for interviews.

Reality: Don't obsess over this. The problems are somewhat artificial. But practicing is valuable for: - Pattern recognition - Time/space complexity thinking - Problem-solving under pressure

Best for: Interview prep or building coding fluency.

Link: https://leetcode.com/

docs.title: 17. Project Euler
docs.text:
For what: Programming problems rooted in mathematics.

Why: More interesting than algorithm drills. Forces you to think creatively.

Link: https://projecteuler.net/

docs.title: 18. HackerRank
docs.text:
For what: Structured learning paths + problems.

Advantage: Guided curriculum. Start with basics, build up.

Link: https://www.hackerrank.com/

docs.title: 19. "Thinking, Fast and Slow" by Daniel Kahneman
docs.text:
Why read it: Understanding how your brain solves problems and makes decisions. Prevents you from making certain kinds of mistakes.

Key insight: Your brain has two systems—one for quick reactions, one for deliberate thinking. Programming requires deliberate thinking, but your brain defaults to quick reactions.

docs.title: 20. "The Effective Engineer" by Edmond Lau
docs.text:
Why read it: Not about code. About time management, making impact, and growing as an engineer.

Relevant sections: - "Focus on High-Leverage Activities" - "Invest in Your Growth"

docs.title: Podcasts (Learning While Doing Other Things)
docs.text:
• Software Engineering Radio – In-depth interviews with practitioners
  • The Changelog – Open source and software news
  • CoRecursive – Deep technical podcast

docs.title: The Meta-Advice: How to Use These Resources
Don't Read Everything
docs.text: You don't have time. Pick 2-3 that resonate, read them deeply. Skim others.

docs.title: Read in Order
docs.text:
1. First: Code Complete or Pragmatic Programmer (practical, motivating)
  2. Then: Clean Code (you'll understand it better after writing bad code)
  3. Then: Design Patterns or Refactoring (when you need them, re-read the specific part)

docs.title: Re-read Key Books
docs.text: Books like Code Complete change how you think. Read them again every few years.

docs.title: Balance Theory and Practice
docs.text: Don't just read. Write code after every session. Apply what you learned in the next project.

docs.title: Join a Community
docs.text:
• Local programming meetups
  • Online forums (Reddit r/learnprogramming, Stack Overflow)
  • Open source contributors

Learning with others accelerates everything.

docs.title: Final Word
docs.text:
"The best time to plant a tree was 20 years ago. The second best time is now."

These resources have been available for years. Start with one today. Read one chapter. Write some code. Repeat.

You'll get there. Not overnight. But steadily.

docs.title: Real-World Incident: Unsecured Container Registry
docs.text:
Scenario: Attacker gains access to container registry with elevated privileges: - Pushes malicious image - Infects production deployments - Data breach affects thousands of users

What Goes Wrong: - No image signing → Can't detect malicious image - No scanning → Vulnerability missed - No RBAC → Attacker gained admin access - No audit logs → Can't trace attack

Prevention (This Track Teaches): - Scan all images before deploy (Module 3) - Sign images, verify signatures (Module 3) - Implement RBAC on registry (Module 2) - Enable audit logging (Module 4) - Detect suspicious behavior (Module 5)
